title: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters
authors: Ruixi Yu,Dairu Liu,Xuchuan Chen,Zekun Qi,Zekai Li,Zhuo Cao,Luyang Niu,Yingsheng Zhang,Sikai Liang,Ke Fan,He Wang,Li Yi
comment: Tech Report
abstract: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.
introduction:
Frontier vision-language models are beginning to show remarkable capabilities in physical control. Recent studies of GPT-6 Astra demonstrate that a general-purpose model can generate robot actions, perform manipulation, and improve its behavior through physical feedback [20, 80, 43]. What makes these results particularly intriguing is that such capabilities are not acquired primarily from robot demonstrations. Instead, they appear to draw on the broad knowledge developed during large-scale pretraining, including visual perception, spatial understanding, reasoning, and code generation [44, 11]. These observations suggest a compelling possibility: the knowledge needed for more capable robot policies may already exist within frontier VLMs.

Yet most vision-language-action models still rely on relatively small VLM backbones, such as the 2B Cosmos-Reason2 in GR00T N1.7 [58]. While effective, these models may not fully capture the rich knowledge emerging in frontier VLMs.
This raises a fundamental question: can frontier-scale representations unlock greater potential in learned robot policies?

To investigate this question, we introduce ScaleVLA, which scales the VLM backbone of a learned robot policy to 552 billion parameters using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 [15]. Inspired by the action-expert architecture of GR00T [4], we connect a VLM to a trainable diffusion transformer (DiT) that converts multimodal representations into continuous robot actions. Rather than relying on explicit reasoning at every control step, the policy learns to directly translate pretrained representations into actions. We systematically compare VLM backbones ranging from 2B to 552B parameters, holding the action architecture, initialization, robot demonstrations, and optimization budget fixed. This allows us to examine how much robot learning can benefit from stronger pretrained representations without introducing additional action-side supervision or pretrained robot-action experts.

We argue that the value of a robot foundation model should be measured not only by its performance on familiar tasks, but by how efficiently it learns, how well it generalizes, and how precisely it acts. We therefore evaluate ScaleVLA across LIBERO [47], LIBERO-PRO, RoboCasa [54], DexJoCo [74], and real-world manipulation, focusing on three fundamental capabilities.
First, sample efficiency: on LIBERO-Goal, ScaleVLA achieves 87.8% success with only 10 demonstrations per task, surpassing a 2B backbone trained with 50 demonstrations (85.6%).
Second, generalization: under LIBERO-PRO perturbations, it achieves 45.1% average success, compared with at most 31.3% for the smaller backbones, indicating stronger transfer beyond the training distribution.
Third, precise manipulation: on a real bimanual charger-insertion task, it succeeds in 9 out of 10 reference-layout trials, compared with 4 out of 10 for the 2B backbone. The improvement is concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment and insertion rather than reaching or grasping. Together, these results suggest that frontier representations are particularly valuable when robot data is scarce, the environment changes, or fine-grained coordination is required.

Crucially, frontier-scale capacity does not necessarily imply prohibitive inference latency. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash uses a sparse mixture-of-experts architecture, activating only a fraction of its 552B parameters per token [14, 15]. Moreover, ScaleVLA extracts features from the causal encoder of the VLM without autoregressive reasoning or text generation. It achieves a median inference latency of 216 ms per action chunk using four H200 GPUs (table 6). This demonstrates that frontier VLM representations can support practical, subsecond robot control, although at a higher hardware cost than smaller backbones.
On the real robot, lower latency does not translate into faster execution: although ScaleVLA has the highest per-chunk latency of the three policies, it completes successful trials in a median of 114.4 s, 13% less time than π0.5\pi_{0.5} + Action Head (132.0 s), because it aligns and inserts the plug 28% faster (table 8).

Our findings point toward a promising direction for VLA development. Frontier pretrained representations can substantially improve data efficiency, robustness, and contact-sensitive manipulation. Rather than treating frontier VLMs only as high-level reasoning agents, we show that they can serve as the representational foundation of fast, learned robot policies. We hope this work encourages a shift toward fully exploiting frontier-model pretraining as a central ingredient in building more capable and generalizable VLAs.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce ScaleVLA, a VLA framework that connects a 552B frontier VLM to a trainable action DiT, enabling continuous robot control without autoregressive reasoning.

We systematically investigate backbone scaling from 2B to 552B across simulation and real-world manipulation, demonstrating substantial gains in sample efficiency, generalization, and contact-sensitive control.

We demonstrate practical subsecond inference with a sparse frontier VLM, showing that large pretrained representational capacity can be brought into learned robot policies at manageable latency.

1. We introduce ScaleVLA, a VLA framework that connects a 552B frontier VLM to a trainable action DiT, enabling continuous robot control without autoregressive reasoning.

2. We systematically investigate backbone scaling from 2B to 552B across simulation and real-world manipulation, demonstrating substantial gains in sample efficiency, generalization, and contact-sensitive control.

3. We demonstrate practical subsecond inference with a sparse frontier VLM, showing that large pretrained representational capacity can be brought into learned robot policies at manageable latency.

title: SADL: On the Demand-Supply Geometry of Representation Collapse
authors: Junhan Sun,Yigui Feng,Mingzhe Liu,Haoyan Xu,Lei Ye,Ziqi Han,Hanru Bai,Yanzhao Zhang,Hao Zhao,Guofeng Zhang
comment: including references and appendices
abstract: In Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), a well-constrained projector output does not by itself prevent representation collapse. We find that, from initialization, the encoder representation is dominated by a component shared by different inputs. A batch-normalized projector removes this component, so regularization after the projector cannot correct it, and the differences between representations shrink until they collapse. We propose SADL (Supply And Demand Loss), which keeps the original training objective and constrains the encoder directly when needed. SADL compares the representation differences that the projector output demands with the differences the encoder can retain and pass on to the projector, and adds a constraint on the encoder only when supply falls short of demand. It works with different Demand Regularizers and introduces no auxiliary networks, additional trainable parameters, or architectural changes. In single-task and jointly trained four-task LeWorldModel (LeWM) and INTACT experiments, SADL lowers the collapse rate over ten random seeds from 50% to 0%. After one epoch of training, encoder effective rank is 3.4–6.4×\times that of the corresponding baseline without SADL, and latent prediction error falls to 1/20–1/303 of it. Without additional tuning, SADL stays robust as its loss weight spans orders of magnitude, and with several Demand Regularizers INTACT exceeds 95% mean search-free control success. On four image datasets, SADL also consistently improves accuracy and stability across random seeds. These results show that matching the representation differences a regularizer demands with the differences the encoder can supply leads to faster and more stable representation learning in control and image classification.
introduction:
Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn from images and video by predicting latent targets instead of reconstructing every pixel (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024). An encoder EθE_{\theta} maps inputs to a representation HH, which a projector PϕP_{\phi} maps to an endpoint ZZ; existing Demand Regularizers typically constrain the geometry at ZZ (Zbontar et al., 2021; Bardes et al., 2022a; Balestriero & LeCun, 2025). Yet an apparently regular ZZ does not, on its own, certify that HH retains sample variation, or that such variation survives the projection from HH to ZZ. Predictability alone does not ensure a useful representation: suppressing distinctions between samples can also make targets easier to predict, and in a world model, losing these distinctions can turn different states or action consequences into nearly indistinguishable control inputs.

We find that this gap is present from initialization. In LeWM and INTACT, the encoder representation HH is dominated by a component shared by all inputs: sample variation carries about 0.01%0.01\% of its energy at initialization and only 33–5%5\% after one epoch of training with a Demand Regularizer (Section 4.2). Two mechanisms keep it there. First, the batch normalization (BN) in the projector subtracts the batch mean, so the shared direction lies in the null space of the projector Jacobian, and the gradients of the Demand Regularizer and the task loss both vanish along it. Second, the remaining variation grows mainly through the task gradient and concentrates in a few directions, leaving an effective rank of about 1515 in HH; the endpoint gradient reaches these directions but does little to expand them. The projector can remix and amplify existing variation to meet the Demand Regularizer’s requirements, but cannot recover what HH has lost, so ZZ inherits the degradation in milder form (effective rank about 2020).

We find that the problem is not which Demand Regularizer is universally better, but whether the demand capacity of the endpoint matches the supply capacity of the encoder representation.
The answer changes over training and across Demand Regularizers.
Supply has two distinct limitations: the encoder may fail to excite sample-dependent directions, or the projector may fail to transmit them.
We therefore introduce SADL (Supply And Demand Loss), which adds a Supply Regularizer on HH to the Demand Regularizer on ZZ.
SADL reads the demand capacity qq from both the Demand Regularizer and the structure already attained at ZZ, measures the supply capacity kk as the weaker of the sample variation (excitation) in HH and its transmission to ZZ, and corrects HH only while k<qk<q.
On the shared direction, 𝒮\mathcal{S} supplies the nonzero gradient that the other losses lack; on the remaining directions, it lets the weaker ones grow faster. Within a few hundred steps, sample variation exceeds 80%80\% of the energy of HH and settles near 99%99\%, and the effective ranks of HH and ZZ both rise to about 5353. The selected Demand Regularizer remains unchanged; SADL adds no auxiliary networks, learnable gates, or separate regularization schedule.

We evaluate SADL on LeWorldModel (LeWM) and INTACT with multiple Demand Regularizers in single-task and jointly trained four-task control, and examine its generalization to image classification. Across more than ten tested Demand Regularizers, one epoch of joint four-task INTACT training yields at least 92%92\% mean search-free success under the reported evaluation protocols (Appendix Figure 5). By epoch three, the INTACT curves reach approximately 96%96\% mean official Direct success (Appendix Figure 6). Across image self-supervised learning datasets, SADL also serves as a near-zero-overhead plug-in that accelerates convergence while yielding more stable and higher-quality representations.

Our contributions are:

We find that the encoder representation of JEPA-style world models is dominated by a shared component from initialization, that a BN projector leaves this component unconstrained by the downstream task and the Demand Regularizer, and that the resulting degradation of HH carries over to ZZ. We cast it as a mismatch between the demand capacity of ZZ and the supply capacity of HH.

We introduce SADL, a low-overhead, adaptive, one-sided Supply Regularizer that attaches to any Demand Regularizer satisfying the stated conditions and targets an observed supply deficit rather than imposing a fixed upstream distribution, and remains stable over orders of magnitude of its weight without extra tuning.

Across more than ten Demand Regularizers, control and image tasks, SADL prevents collapse, speeds up convergence, and gives more stable representations; ablations of the attention backend, the supply terms, the gate, and the demand show that each component is needed.

1. We find that the encoder representation of JEPA-style world models is dominated by a shared component from initialization, that a BN projector leaves this component unconstrained by the downstream task and the Demand Regularizer, and that the resulting degradation of HH carries over to ZZ. We cast it as a mismatch between the demand capacity of ZZ and the supply capacity of HH.

2. We introduce SADL, a low-overhead, adaptive, one-sided Supply Regularizer that attaches to any Demand Regularizer satisfying the stated conditions and targets an observed supply deficit rather than imposing a fixed upstream distribution, and remains stable over orders of magnitude of its weight without extra tuning.

3. Across more than ten Demand Regularizers, control and image tasks, SADL prevents collapse, speeds up convergence, and gives more stable representations; ablations of the attention backend, the supply terms, the gate, and the demand show that each component is needed.

title: Lazy-MOSAIC: Accelerating Skill-Centric Manipulation Planning with Learned Skill-Effect World Models
authors: Itamar Mishani,Mukund Krishnakumar,Oren Salzman,Maxim Likhachev
comment: Under review
abstract: Long-horizon manipulation tasks require a robot to perform a sequence of physical interactions with its environment, typically combining several different skills. Planning such behaviors efficiently is challenging: given a library of parameterized skills, solutions lie in a vast hybrid space of skill sequences and their parameters, and evaluating each candidate skill’s feasibility and effect with a high-fidelity world model such as a physics simulator is computationally expensive. Mosaic, a recent skill-centric approach, lets the skills guide a non-sequential search toward the regions of this space where they are likely to succeed; however, it pays the full cost of simulation for every parameterized skill it considers. In this work, we introduce Lazy-Mosaic, a lazy planning framework that instead searches over hypothesized skill outcomes. A cheap learned skill-effect world model predicts, in a fraction of a millisecond, a skill’s feasibility and the world state it produces. Lazy-Mosaic then uses these predictions to focus expensive simulation on promising candidate skills and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs only the affected part of the search, while ensuring that every skill in a returned plan is validated in simulation. We evaluate Lazy-Mosaic on cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks of increasing difficulty and demonstrate it on a physical robot, showing that it plans substantially faster than baselines with fewer simulator queries, while matching or exceeding their success rate in every setting. Visit skill-mosaic.github.io.
introduction:
Consider a robot tasked with retrieving a wrench from behind clutter in an automotive workshop (Fig. ). This is an instance of the semi-structured settings we target in this work: the robot knows the workspace and the object types it may encounter, but which objects are present and where they rest varies from task to task. The wrench may lie beyond the gripper’s reach, requiring the robot to push other objects aside and reposition the wrench before attempting a grasp. Solving such tasks with generic skills such as pushing, pulling, grasping, and transporting requires reasoning not only about which skills to compose but also about the world states they produce, since a skill that makes little immediate progress toward the goal may enable a later skill to succeed. A planner therefore needs a world model—any function that predicts the outcome of executing a parameterized skill from a given state—to compare alternative skill sequences, and such models differ in cost and fidelity. Recent skill-based planners use a physics simulator as their world model, relatively accurate but expensive to query [23, 26].

Mosaic [23] is a recently introduced planner of this kind. Rather than growing a search forward from the start state, it conducts a non-sequential search in which skills guide exploration toward regions of the state space where they are likely to succeed. Generator skills, grounded with specific parameters, propose behaviors in these regions, and connector skills link them by solving boundary value problems. This allows Mosaic to discover non-obvious enabling steps, e.g., repositioning an object to allow a feasible grasp. However, every candidate generator and connector is simulated before entering the search graph, whether or not it contributes to the solution. Over 80% of Mosaic’s planning time is spent forward-simulating skills to compute their outcome (Fig. 6).

To address this computational challenge, we draw on ideas from lazy search [3, 8]. Lazy search defers edge evaluation, treating each edge as a hypothesis until it must be resolved. It assumes, however, that the vertices will strictly either be valid or invalid, and that invalidating an edge leaves the rest of the graph unaffected. In Mosaic, vertices and edges are both skills, and the outcome of a skill is known only after it is simulated, violating the assumption that lazy search makes.
In this work, we introduce Lazy-Mosaic, which extends lazy search to graphs whose vertices, not only edges, are hypotheses. It interleaves two world models: a cheap learned skill-effect model, which predicts the outcome of a skill, and an expensive high-fidelity model, here the physics simulator. Lazy-Mosaic builds its graph from the cheap model’s predictions, queries the expensive model for skills along a promising candidate solution path, and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs the graph locally, keeping the state actually produced and every unaffected hypothesis rather than discarding all of them. Only fully simulated grounded skills ever appear in the returned plan. This crucially preserves physics simulation-based validation, helping alleviate the risk of unexpected contact in safety-critical tasks.

Our contributions are twofold:

We introduce Lazy-Mosaic, which extends lazy search to skill-centric planning, where deferring a skill also defers the state it produces, so that vertices as well as edges are hypotheses and an invalidated prediction affects a subtree rather than a single edge.

We show how a cheap learned world model can drive this search, deciding which skills are simulated and in what order, while certification guarantees that its accuracy affects only planning efficiency, never the validity of a returned plan with respect to the high-fidelity model.

1. We introduce Lazy-Mosaic, which extends lazy search to skill-centric planning, where deferring a skill also defers the state it produces, so that vertices as well as edges are hypotheses and an invalidated prediction affects a subtree rather than a single edge.

2. We show how a cheap learned world model can drive this search, deciding which skills are simulated and in what order, while certification guarantees that its accuracy affects only planning efficiency, never the validity of a returned plan with respect to the high-fidelity model.

title: GHySSeg: Real-Time Geometric Ground and Road Segmentation for Hybrid Solid-State LiDAR
authors: Martín Palos,Fernando García
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. HySoLiD-Drive dataset:this https URL
abstract: Hybrid solid-state LiDAR sensors are making their way into production vehicles, yet the data they produce differs structurally from that of the established spinning mechanical sensors behind today’s autonomous-driving datasets: it is ring-free, dense, cluttered, and concentrated in a frontal field of view. The classical geometric methods that autonomous vehicles rely on for drivable space computation and navigation assume the ordered ring-and-column structure of a 360-degree spinning LiDAR and degrade or fail on this data, while learned alternatives are computationally heavy, hard to certify, and trained almost exclusively on spinning-LiDAR data. We demonstrate that the same dense, per-curve geometry is instead an opportunity to close the divide between the industry’s preferred sensors and autonomous-driving research. We present GHySSeg, a purely geometric method that segments ground and drivable road from a single hybrid solid-state LiDAR frame by tracing each scan curve and reading two geometric signatures, a step in height and a fold-back in range, with no training and no graphics processing unit. To evaluate it, we release HySoLiD-Drive, the first public benchmark dedicated to ground and road segmentation on an automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR, comprising 100 manually labeled and 7000 unlabeled frames recorded by two vehicles in real driving. On this benchmark, GHySSeg surpasses both geometric and learned state-of-the-art baselines across ground and road segmentation, reaching an intersection-over-union of 0.907 for road and 0.896 for ground at over 0.96 precision, while running in real time at about 22 milliseconds per frame on a single core.
introduction:
LiDAR (light detection and ranging) is the cornerstone of modern autonomous driving (AD). As an active sensor, it delivers rich three-dimensional (3-D) measurements that stay reliable under poor illumination, even in complete darkness, and that are far denser than those of radar sensors, enabling object detection and classification directly in 3-D for a thorough understanding of the space around the vehicle. Its long range, moreover, lets a vehicle anticipate the road ahead, even at high speed [1].

Spinning mechanical LiDARs, which provide a full 360∘360^{\circ} field of view (FOV), dominate research: they are a mature, well-understood technology, and the public AD datasets and benchmarks are built almost exclusively on them [1]. Their adoption in consumer vehicles, however, faces real barriers. They are expensive; exploiting their 360∘360^{\circ} coverage requires mounting them protruding above the roof, which is neither aerodynamic nor aesthetic and noticeably increases the vehicle’s height clearance; and they rely on moving parts spinning at high speed.

These limitations have already driven a shift in the automotive industry toward solid-state (SS) and hybrid solid-state (HSS) LiDARs. Such sensors sacrifice full 360∘360^{\circ} coverage in exchange for fewer (or no) moving parts, a higher and more concentrated point density, a cleaner and more seamless installation, and, above all, a lower cost [2]. Recent consumer vehicle models, led predominantly by Chinese manufacturers such as Xiaomi, BYD, and NIO, with Western manufacturers such as Mercedes-Benz now following, already integrate SS or HSS LiDARs [3, 4], bringing LiDAR to mass-production vehicles at last, beyond research platforms and robotaxis.

This new technology, however, brings a challenge of its own: the data it produces is structurally different from that of a spinning sensor, as depicted in Fig. 2. HSS point clouds lack the structured ring pattern and the neatly ordered azimuth columns that spinning LiDARs owe to their rotating laser array, and, because the field of view is condensed into a frontal region, they are far denser and considerably less organized.

When facing this seemingly disorganized data, the classical geometric methods that autonomous vehicles rely on for perception, scene-understanding, and path-planning, such as ground filtering, drivable-area and road segmentation, and free-space estimation, degrade or fail outright, because they depend on the ordered ring-and-column structure of a spinning sensor. With the growing diversity of LiDAR manufacturers and models, the field’s dominant answer is learned semantic segmentation [5, 6], in which a neural network labels every point directly from the raw cloud. These models, however, require a graphics processing unit (GPU) for inference that adds cost and energy demand, they behave unpredictably in unseen scenarios, offer little traceability of their errors, and, most importantly, they are trained almost exclusively on spinning-LiDAR datasets such as KITTI [7, 8]. This introduces a domain gap: a model trained on cleanly spaced 360∘360^{\circ} data struggles to generalize to the denser, frontal, more cluttered clouds of a solid-state sensor, even though both are 3-D point clouds [9].

Yet the very properties that break these methods are also an opportunity. The high density, the focused FOV, and the close, non-ring scan lines let an HSS sensor resolve surfaces, curbs, and centimetric steps sharply. In this dense per-curve structure, road boundaries leave a clean geometric signature: a step in height together with a visible bend in the range profile.

This article turns that observation into a method. We propose GHySSeg (Fig. 1), which exploits the specific characteristics of automotive HSS LiDAR data to segment ground and road by pure geometry, without training or running heavy models, without a GPU, and in real time on a consumer-grade CPU, providing reliable and fast drivable-area 3-D detection for demanding autonomous-driving applications.

Because no existing public benchmark specifically targets ground and road segmentation on an automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR as the main sensor, GHySSeg has been developed and validated on an Innovusion (now Seyond) Falcon Kinetic LiDAR [10] mounted on two distinct autonomous vehicles operated by our laboratory at the Universidad Carlos III de Madrid (UC3M). Moreover, to directly address this automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR data scarcity, we release HySoLiD-Drive [11] as part of this work. HySoLiD-Drive is an open benchmark of 100 unique, manually per-point-labeled frames, spanning urban roads, motorways, roundabouts, dense traffic, and sharp turns, together with 7000 unlabeled frames drawn from two continuous drives through Madrid, Spain. It comprises the data we have used to evaluate GHySSeg, and invites the community to build on it and benchmark against our results through an open, transparent leaderboard.

The contributions of this work are the following.

A sensor-native, real-time, single-shot, geometry-only ground and road segmentation method for HSS LiDAR.

A per-curve road-boundary formulation that exploits the density and geometry of HSS data through height-step and range-fold-back signatures.

HySoLiD-Drive, the first public benchmark dedicated to ground and road segmentation on an automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR in real-world driving scenes, released with an open leaderboard.

A real-world evaluation against six baselines with cross-vehicle transfer, displaying state-of-the-art accuracy at real-time CPU cost.

title: Safe Physical Interaction of All-Electric Heavy-Duty Robotic Manipulators via Control Barrier Functions and Variable Impedance Control
authors: Amir Hossein Barjini,Mohammad Bahari,Jouni Mattila
abstract: All-electric heavy-duty robotic manipulators are increasingly expected to operate close to tunnel walls, equipment, and other structures while retaining the force capability required for large-payload tasks. Accurate motion control alone does not address the resulting safety and interaction requirements. This paper develops a safety-aware physical-interaction architecture that combines variable impedance control (VIC) with control barrier functions (CBFs) on top of an established virtual decomposition control (VDC) framework for electromechanical linear actuator (EMLA)-driven manipulators. VIC continuously adapts the task-space stiffness and damping according to predicted proximity and contact risk, whereas a joint-velocity CBF filter enforces Cartesian workspace boundaries and the physical stroke limits induced by the closed-chain lift and tilt mechanisms. To account for nonideal realization of the filtered velocity by the inner VDC/EMLA dynamics, the CBF inequalities are tightened using a measured bound on the joint-velocity tracking error. Four configurations, namely VDC, VIC+VDC, CBF+VDC, and VIC+CBF+VDC, are evaluated under workspace, actuator-limit, and physical-interaction scenarios. VIC reduces the peak and RMS environment-interaction forces by 92.59%92.59\% and 96.33%96.33\%, respectively; both robust CBF configurations maintain positive workspace and EMLA safety margins, while VIC+CBF+VDC reduces the CBF intervention metric by 10.30%10.30\% compared with CBF+VDC.
introduction:
Heavy-duty robotic manipulators (HDRMs) are increasingly used in drilling, mining, construction, forestry, and material handling, where long reach and large payload capacity are required under demanding operating conditions. Achieving reliable and adaptable manipulation in such environments remains challenging because of nonlinear dynamics, strong actuator–structure coupling, and large interaction forces [1, 2]. Electrification is increasingly reshaping the actuation architectures of heavy-duty mobile machines, with recent studies investigating electric and electro-hydraulic actuation concepts to improve energy efficiency, enable energy recovery, and enhance actuator-level controllability [3, 4, 5]. In fully electric implementations, an electromechanical linear actuator (EMLA) combines an electric motor with a mechanical transmission, typically a gearbox and screw mechanism, to generate the linear force required by manipulator joints. Such actuator-level electrification can eliminate hydraulic throttling and enable more direct integration of actuation, sensing, and control, but it also introduces actuator-dependent force, velocity, and stroke constraints that must be considered at the manipulator level [6, 7, 8]. Consequently, safe operation of all-electric HDRMs requires not only accurate motion realization but also explicit treatment of actuator and workspace constraints.

Control of HDRMs must address nonlinear multibody dynamics, varying loads, actuator constraints, and model uncertainty [9]. For hydraulically actuated systems, nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC), data-driven control, and reduced-order task-space NMPC have been investigated for trajectory tracking, obstacle avoidance, and actuator-aware motion [10, 11, 12]. For all-electric HDRMs, virtual decomposition control (VDC) provides a modular model-based framework that has recently been extended to coordinate manipulator and electromechanical actuator dynamics [13, 6, 7]. These approaches improve tracking and command realization, but safety near workspace and actuator limits still requires explicit constraint enforcement.

For admissible physical interaction, the controller must additionally regulate the robot’s mechanical response to contact. Impedance control shapes the dynamic relationship between robot motion and interaction forces [14], while variable impedance control (VIC) adapts the desired impedance, particularly stiffness and damping, as the task or environment changes [15]. Since time-varying impedance parameters can affect closed-loop stability, their adaptation requires careful treatment [16]. Desired impedance allocation has also been incorporated into the modular VDC framework for interaction control [17]. In parallel, sensor-based perception has been shown to support context-aware human–robot collaboration in industrial tasks [18]. Nevertheless, impedance modulation alone does not provide explicit guarantees on hard geometric or actuator constraints.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide a systematic means of enforcing safety by rendering a prescribed safe set forward invariant under appropriate conditions. When incorporated as constraints in quadratic programs (QPs), CBFs can reconcile nominal control objectives with explicit safety requirements [19]. Their use has been extended to robotic kinematics, including velocity-based safety-aware control of manipulators [20]. CBF-QP safety filtering has also been applied to collision-aware motion of long-reach drilling booms [21], and to actuator-aware inverse kinematics of redundant robots [22]. Robust CBF formulations further address disturbances and perturbations that can affect preservation of the safe set [23]. Barrier-based safety has also been integrated with impedance control for constrained robotic interaction [24], while predictive impedance adaptation combined with safety CBFs has been investigated for obstacle avoidance in human–robot collaboration [25]. These studies demonstrate the compatibility of impedance-based interaction control and barrier-based safety, motivating an actuator-aware formulation for all-electric HDRMs.

Despite recent progress in all-electric HDRM modeling and control, safe physical interaction remains insufficiently addressed when workspace constraints and closed-chain actuator limits must be enforced simultaneously. Building on the analytical EMLA/HDRM models and modular control framework in [6, 7], this paper develops an actuator-aware VIC–CBF–VDC architecture. The main contributions are:

a hierarchical framework in which VIC shapes interaction behavior, the CBF layer enforces safety, and VDC with low-level EMLA control executes the resulting commands;

a unified CBF formulation for Cartesian workspace constraints and closed-chain lift/tilt EMLA stroke limits;

robust CBF tightening based on a measured bound on inner-loop joint-velocity tracking error; and

comparison of VDC, VIC+VDC, CBF+VDC, and VIC+CBF+VDC using tracking, safety, intervention, and interaction metrics.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the HDRM, VDC, and EMLA models. Section III introduces the VIC and CBF framework, and Section IV provides the stability and safety analysis. Section V presents the validation setup and results, and Section VI concludes the paper.

title: Hybrid Optimization-Generative Motion Planning for Multiagent Affine Formations
authors: Zhonggang Li,Hongyu Zhou,Raj Thilak Rajan
abstract: Formation maneuver control enables a multiagent system to cooperatively navigate through constrained environments in collective motion. While various formation controllers exist, they rely heavily on high-quality and dynamically feasible reference trajectories provided a priori, making formation motion planning (FMP) essential. To address the computational challenges for high-dimensional joint trajectories faced by conventional constrained optimization-based solutions, this paper introduces a hybrid optimization-generative framework with a focus on affine formations, which provide the necessary spatial flexibility. By formulating the planning task as a constrained Maximum-a-Posteriori estimation, we decouple multiagent objectives to leverage pre-trained single-agent diffusion priors for dynamic feasibility, obstacle avoidance, and smoothness. We then interleave the generative process with projected gradient descent (PGD) to strictly enforce affine geometric constraints with safety guarantees. Simulations demonstrate our framework generates highly smooth, collision-free plans that are readily trackable by common distributed controllers, and outperforms state-of-the-art planners in various metrics.
introduction:
Formation maneuvering is an essential task for multi-robotic systems, aiming to navigate a swarm of robots safely through a potentially cluttered area while maintaining a desired range of geometries. This is often desired in applications such as cooperative object transport [1], satellite interferometry [2], sensing and coverage [3, 4], etc.
Recently, deformable formations [5, 6, 7] have received increasing attention due to the advantages of flexible geometries for complex environments, over conventional rigid body control [8]. In particular, affine formations [6, 9, 10], including translation, rotation, scaling, and shear, have become a popular expressive class. Predominant formation control literature solves stabilization and tracking of maneuvers assuming given references, i.e., the trajectories are assumed to be provided a priori and are inherently collision-free and dynamically feasible. Moreover, in common distributed control [6], followers rely solely on local information. Consequently, if the planned trajectories deviate from a strict affine transformation, the formation cannot be resolved locally, leading to severe tracking degradation. Hence, enforcing affine geometry is essential for such distributed controllers.

Generating a full set of high-quality reference trajectories subject to complex geometry constraints is difficult. Practical approaches typically decouple the problem hierarchically by pairing a simple global path planner (typically artificial potential field (APF) or A*) for the swarm centroid or a leader with a reactive local controller to resolve collisions and geometry [11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. For instance, [12] plans for a formation that allows rotation and anisotropic scaling of the geometry, and it uses APF to traverse a feasible global path for the centroid with coarse shape planning, followed by a model predictive controller (MPC) that refines the shape geometry and resolves collision avoidance at runtime. This paradigm shifts the heavy sensing and computational burden of collision avoidance and geometric maintenance entirely onto the local controller. Consequently, the required complex online solvers can easily overwhelm the limited onboard resources, such as on lightweight or space robots. More fundamentally, this approach is bottlenecked by the quality of the reference trajectory, making it difficult to apply common tracking controllers such as [6], which will inevitably lead to suboptimal maneuvers or tracking failure.

An alternative paradigm to mitigate complexity is to plan within a low-dimensional space parameterized by the formation’s macroscopic geometric variables [1, 16, 17]. Since geometric coupling intrinsically binds the agents, a 2D affine transformation allows the entire swarm’s configuration to be fully described by just 6 degrees of freedom (DOF). Leveraging this reduction, [1, 17] optimize trajectories strictly within the 7-DOF 3D similarity transformation space, while [16] restricts planning to a 33-DOF 2D rigid body transformation. However, planning exclusively within the geometric parameter space is highly susceptible to disturbances. Small perturbations in the macroscopic parameters are often significantly amplified when mapped to the individual agents, resulting in severe non-smoothness and dynamic infeasibility in the actual trajectory domain. As such, these geometric abstractions must be paired with advanced auxiliary space-time smoothers in the trajectory domain. For example, [17] develops a spatiotemporal polynomial optimization framework to guarantee smooth, dynamically feasible flight, embedded in the precomputed geometric references.

Recently, learning-based motion planning has received increasing attention, such as reinforcement learning-based FMP [18]. In particular, generative models such as diffusion models [19, 20] have been successfully applied to robot motion planning [21, 22, 23]. The idea is to internalize the complex, non-convex motion constraints into learned structural priors through a large amount of data. Then, during inference, we sample from this learned prior with mild intervention from conventional optimization using gradient descent for task-specific objectives. Compared with conventional approaches, this optimization-generative method is computationally tractable, with better smoothness and reachability in cluttered settings [22]. However, this approach is currently limited to single-agent planning, as multiagent trajectory data is much more difficult to collect for an arbitrary number of mobile agents. As such, pioneering works for general multiagent motion planning with diffusion models [24] mostly focus on higher-level priority coordination based on single-agent priors. Moreover, diffusion-based motion planning for multiagent flexible formation maneuvers remains unexplored.

In this work, we propose a diffusion-based motion planning framework specifically for multiagent affine formations. We formulate the FMP task as a constrained Maximum-a-Posteriori (MAP) estimation, which naturally translates to a hybrid constrained optimization with generative priors. By decoupling the high-dimensional multiagent objectives, we can leverage pre-trained single-agent diffusion priors to fulfill intra-agent requirements (such as smoothness and obstacle avoidance), while resolving inter-agent interactions, i.e., the formation, through projected gradient descent (PGD). Additionally, a safety distance among agents can be guaranteed by configuring the affine geometry parameters in the projection step. Our proposed approach avoids the need for complex reactive controllers or additional spatiotemporal trajectory smoothers as in conventional methods. The generated trajectories are smooth, strictly affine, and executable by common distributed tracking controllers.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. The general problem formulation and single-agent motion planning with diffusion is introduced in Section II. Then the proposed FMP framework with formation projection and safety guarantees is discussed in Section III. Finally, we validate our algorithm and the quality of the planned trajectories in comparison with state-of-the-art methods in Section IV. We then conclude the discussion with insights into the future directions in Section V. Throughout the paper, we adhere to the following notation conventions for mathematical clarity.

Sets and graphs are represented using calligraphic letters, e.g., 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Vectors of length NN of all ones and zeros are denoted by 𝟏N\bm{1}_{N} and 𝟎N\bm{0}_{N}, respectively, and their matrix versions are similarly 𝟏M×N\bm{1}_{M\times N} and 𝟎M×N\bm{0}_{M\times N}. An identity matrix of size NN is denoted by 𝑰N\bm{I}_{N}. The \opbraces​diag⁡(⋅)\opbraces{\operatorname{diag}}(\cdot) operator creates a diagonal matrix from a vector. Units are enclosed by square brackets, e.g., seconds [s][s].

title: ThinkWAM: Rethinking Latent Futures for Action Refinement
authors: Haoyun Tang,Baqiao Deng,Enjin Zhou,Songwen Tian,Keyao Xu,Bowen Jing,Kun Wang,Ke Ma,Zhandong Mei,Huibin Li
comment: including references and appendix. Project page:this https URL
abstract: World-action models (WAMs) couple action generation with predictions of future states. An initial action chunk may be flawed. A future prediction that is not conditioned on the chunk may fail to reflect the changes that the proposed actions would induce in visual representations, limiting its usefulness for refinement before execution. We introduce ThinkWAM, a latent WAM that establishes bidirectional feedback before execution through a proposal–rethink–refine loop: the policy first proposes a complete action chunk, the proposal corrects multi-horizon future latents through a learned residual, and the corrected latents are injected into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the executable chunk. An affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, both motivated by predictive coding, support this loop, and all prediction stays in latent space. ThinkWAM achieves 98.70% success on LIBERO, 84.76% on LIBERO-Plus without OOD fine-tuning, 85.75%/65.85% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Random, and 65.17% on RoboCasa24. ThinkWAM achieves 64.4%64.4\% mean success across three real-world OOD conditions. The mean two-pass inference latency per action chunk is 153.48 ms on LIBERO, 164.61 ms on RoboTwin, and 101.2 ms on the Galaxea A1Z. Ablations show complementary gains from rethinking and affordance guidance. Diagnostics indicate that proposal-conditioned corrections change both predicted futures and action trajectories, showing that the corrected future representations improve the final action.
introduction:
Robot manipulation requires anticipating what an action will cause. A visually plausible reach can miss an object, an apparently stable grasp can slip, and a locally reasonable motion can leave a later placement incomplete. Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot control, and scalable robot transformers, web-supervised visual-language backbones, and generalist policies have broadened the range of tasks that a single policy can perform [8, 67, 17, 23, 6]. Diffusion and flow-matching action heads further support continuous, multimodal action chunks [13, 27, 7]. Yet the usual decision interface maps the current visual context directly to an action or action chunk, without an explicit representation of what it will cause.

World-action models (WAMs) address this gap by coupling action generation with a predictive representation of the environment [15, 44, 9], and latent-space variants avoid reconstructing every future pixel [18, 3, 26, 58, 19]. These models use future prediction as training supervision, expose future-informed features to the action head, or use predicted consequences to guide action sampling [1]. Here, we study how a complete action proposal can update predicted futures and how those updates can guide action refinement before execution (Sec. 2).

An initial action chunk may be flawed. If future prediction is independent of that chunk, a mistimed grasp and a well-timed grasp can receive the same predicted continuation, limiting its usefulness for refinement. We therefore seek feedback in both directions before execution: predicted futures guide the action, while the proposal updates those futures. We introduce ThinkWAM, a latent WAM that implements this interaction through a proposal–rethink–refine loop (Fig. 1). The policy predicts visual latents at multiple future horizons and uses language features and affordance-guided memory to propose a complete action chunk. The proposal then conditions learned residual corrections to the base future latents. A second pass through the same ActionDiT head consumes the corrected futures and generates the refined action chunk. Sensory–motor accounts motivate this loop: agents predict the sensory consequences of their own actions to guide behavior [36].

Two ideas from predictive coding motivate our representation choices. Predictive coding shapes representations through prediction-error minimization [35]. We use affordance supervision to shape the shared visual context toward where actions make contact, and write a weighted summary of this context into memory. Dynamic predictive coding motivates hierarchical prediction across temporal scales [20]. We therefore allocate more tokens and use finer aggregation for near-future targets than for distant ones.

Our contributions are:

We introduce ThinkWAM, a proposal–rethink–refine architecture that corrects multi-horizon future latents using the policy’s own proposal and injects the corrected latents into a second pass of the same action head, which generates the final action.

We propose an affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, motivated by predictive coding.

We demonstrate strong generalization on LIBERO-Plus, the randomized setting of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa24, and real-world manipulation tasks, with ThinkWAM achieving competitive overall results while maintaining low inference latency.

2. We propose an affordance-guided observation-action memory and a near-fine, far-coarse multi-horizon prediction scheme, motivated by predictive coding.

3. We demonstrate strong generalization on LIBERO-Plus, the randomized setting of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa24, and real-world manipulation tasks, with ThinkWAM achieving competitive overall results while maintaining low inference latency.

title: BoBDeLaN: Bounded-Bandwidth Context Adaptation for Deep Lagrangian Robot Control
authors: Lucas Schulze,Sucheth Shenoy,Jan Peters,Oleg Arenz
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
comment: Submitted to the 9th Annual Learning for Dynamics & Control Conference (L4DC 2027)
abstract:
Learned physics-based models provide structure for robot control, but uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics limit their predictive accuracy.
Context-aware Deep Lagrangian Networks enable adaptation through a latent context inferred from measurement histories while retaining Lagrangian structure for each fixed context. However, this structure alone does not constrain sensitivity to measurement disturbances. We introduce BoBDeLaN, which combines a contracting, gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network context encoder with stable linear filtering to shape disturbance sensitivity across frequencies. This architecture guarantees exponential forgetting of the recurrent initialization and admits a finite-horizon, frequency-weighted bound on context perturbations, which extends to residual torque prediction under a Lipschitz continuity assumption on the context-conditioned dynamics model. We evaluate a low-pass realization within model predictive control on simulated and real hardware manipulation tasks, together with frequency-sensitivity analysis on real-robot data. Compared with an LSTM encoder using the same input filter, BoBDeLaN exhibits reduced high-frequency context sensitivity, lower residual torque prediction error, and smoother motion, with less degradation under injected disturbances.
introduction:
Physics-encoded learning incorporates mechanical structure directly into data-driven robot dynamics models (Piccinini et al., 2026). Approaches such as Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) (Greydanus et al., 2019) and Deep Lagrangian Neural Networks (DeLaN) (Lutter and others, 2019; Lutter and Peters, 2021) exploit this structure to obtain physically consistent models. The resulting inductive bias is useful when data are limited (Watson et al., 2025) and supports integration with model-based control methods, such as model predictive control (MPC). In practice, however, friction, external disturbances, and payload variations can alter the dynamics, requiring adaptation to current operating conditions while preserving the model’s mechanical structure.

Several works have explored this direction by combining physics encoded models with adaptive control. For example, Duong and Atanasov (2021) proposed an adaptive energy controller based on HNNs with learned disturbance features, while Feng et al. (2024) augmented DeLaN with convolutional and recurrent networks to model residual hydraulic actuation effects and friction. Hu et al. (2026) combined DeLaN with adaptive Kalman filtering and noise suppression for contact force estimation. Context-Aware DeLaN (Schulze et al., 2025) conditions a Lagrangian dynamics model on a latent context inferred from measurement histories by an LSTM encoder, enabling adaptation to unknown payloads within MPC. Although the model retains its mechanical structure for each fixed context, this structure does not constrain the sensitivity of the context encoder.

The measurement history contains information about changes in the dynamics together with measurement noise and estimation errors. Perturbations in this history can alter the inferred context and, consequently, the dynamics predictions supplied to MPC. Prediction accuracy on training data alone provides no guarantee on sensitivity to these perturbations or to recurrent state initialization. We therefore require exponential forgetting of the initial state under a common measurement history and bounded sensitivity of the context output to perturbations of that history. These requirements correspond to contraction and finite incremental gain, respectively, and are not guaranteed by standard recurrent architectures such as LSTMs.

Recurrent Equilibrium Networks (RENs) admit parametrizations that guarantee contraction and prescribed incremental integral quadratic constraints (IQCs), including incremental ℓ2\ell_{2} gain bounds, by construction (Revay et al., 2024). These guarantees hold throughout unconstrained optimization of the model parameters. More broadly, stable operator parametrizations have enabled learning-based controller design with closed loop stability guarantees, as demonstrated by Neural System Level Synthesis and magnitude and direction (MAD) policies (Furieri et al., 2022; Furieri et al., 2025). A uniform incremental gain bound, however, does not distinguish perturbations by temporal frequency. Frequency weighting refines this description by specifying how sensitivity varies with the frequency content of the perturbations. For REN based feedback control, Barbara et al. (2025) combine stable input and output filters with the recurrent parametrization to establish robustness guarantees. This construction motivates the composition of a stable linear filter and a certified recurrent model for context inference. The filter specifies the frequency weighting, while the incremental gain bound on the recurrent model yields a corresponding bound on context deviations.

In this work, we introduce BoBDeLaN, a frequency-shaped extension of Context-Aware DeLaN for adaptive robot dynamics learning with Lagrangian structure. We replace the LSTM encoder in Context-Aware DeLaN with a contracting, gain-bounded REN preceded by a low-pass filter. We establish theoretical bounds on context and residual torque prediction sensitivity.

The main contributions of this work are as follows. (i) A novel extension of Context-Aware DeLaN using a REN as the context encoder, enabling frequency-dependent context adaptation with contraction and incremental gain guarantees. (ii) We derive a finite-horizon frequency-weighted bound on context perturbations and, under a regularity assumption on the learned dynamics model, a corresponding bound on residual torque prediction variations along a fixed trajectory. (iii) We evaluate BoBDeLaN on real-robot data, in closed-loop simulation, and in a real hardware pick-and-place task, demonstrating reduced high-frequency context sensitivity, improved residual torque prediction accuracy, and smoother closed-loop behavior under payload variations and disturbances.

title: Cooperative Mobile Manipulation using Learned Dynamical Systems
authors: Saray Bakker,Wendelin Böhmer,Javier Alonso-Mora
comment: Preprint version
abstract:
Cooperative mobile manipulation requires robots to coordinate their motions while ensuring whole-body collision avoidance and preserving task-relevant behaviors.
We propose CALDS (Cooperative Adaptation of Learned Dynamical Systems), a framework that enables mobile manipulators to adapt learned single-agent behaviors for coordinated execution.
Building on individual dynamical systems (DSs) learned from demonstrations, CALDS enables cooperative adaptation through two key components: Cooperative Policy Selection, which identifies compatible combinations of learned policies, and Temporal Adaptation, which ensures collision-free cooperation while preserving the spatial structure and convergence properties of the original behaviors.
We evaluate CALDS across three diverse scenarios: assistive dressing, restaurant cleaning and serving, and drawer opening and object placement.
Quantitative results demonstrate its effectiveness in improving task success and enabling safe, coordinated simultaneous execution while maintaining fidelity to demonstrated behaviors.
introduction:
Mobile manipulators are versatile platforms capable of assisting humans in household tasks (Wu et al., 2023), and performing labor-intensive jobs, such as operating in greenhouses (Sánchez-Molina et al., 2024) or construction sites (Hartmann et al., 2022). In these domestic and professional environments, efficiency rises when robots collaborate with other agents, anticipating on their actions and intentions.
For instance, consider a robot assisting a human in putting on a jacket while another shows how the outfit looks using a mirror, or a restaurant where one robot places a glass on the table-area cleaned by another robot.
Such scenarios require robots to proactively adapt their behaviors to other agents, ensuring both task effectiveness and safety.

lfd (lfd) has emerged as a powerful framework for transferring human skills to robots, with successful applications in manipulators (Reuss et al., 2023; Pérez-Dattari et al., 2024), dual-arm systems (Zhao et al., 2023), and mobile manipulators (Fu et al., 2024; Sundaresan et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2025). However, extending these skills to collaborative behaviors involving multiple mobile manipulators presents several challenges.
Firstly, collecting multi-agent demonstrations is inherently complex, making even a small number of demonstrations difficult to obtain.
Secondly, mobile manipulators operate in cluttered and dynamic environments, requiring whole-body collision avoidance with other robots and surrounding obstacles. Existing approaches often delegate collision avoidance to low-level planners (Sundaresan et al., 2025), whose deviations from demonstrated motions can compromise task execution and push learned policies into off-distribution states, resulting in potentially unreliable or unintuitive actions.
These challenges motivate frameworks that enable collaborative mobile manipulation from small amounts of demonstrations, while accounting for whole-body constraints and anticipating the actions of other agents.

Rather than depending on extensive multi-agent demonstrations, recent approaches have explored composing multi-agent behavior from single-agent demonstrations.
Singh et al. (2025) define cdmp to generate collaborative trajectories leveraging a time-heuristic and end-effector spatial collision avoidance to modulate learned skills.
Furthermore, single-agent demonstrations can be combined with multi-agent cost functions to train coordinated dual-manipulator diffusion policies (Peters et al., 2026). Extending this approach to mobile manipulators, however, requires reliable visual perception for both diffusion-based policy generation and whole-body collision avoidance.
Other approaches learn collaborative behaviors from multi-manipulator demonstrations, while focusing on maintaining global consistency during decentralized execution (He et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2026).
Learning-free task and motion planning (TAMP) methods, such as those using temporal logic (Saha and Julius, 2017) or long-horizon planning frameworks (Hartmann et al., 2022), also offer solutions for collaborative tasks incorporating whole-body collision avoidance. However, their computational demands can limit real-time applicability. Moreover, collision-free collaboration does not necessarily imply efficient execution: sequential motion or waiting for other robots to pass can cause unnecessary delays, while concurrent execution requires explicit coordination to avoid collisions (Rudy et al., 2022).

To address these challenges, we propose calds (Cooperative Adaptation of Learned Dynamical Systems), a framework that enables mobile manipulators to coordinate learned single-agent behaviors in shared workspaces while ensuring whole-body collision avoidance and task constraints (Fig. 1).
Each robot is equipped with a set of learned  ds (ds), which encode diverse strategies for accomplishing the assigned task. These learned ds, such as proposed in (Urain et al., 2022; Pérez-Dattari et al., 2024; Bakker et al., 2026), can be generated from only a few (e.g. 1–10) demonstrated end-effector pose trajectories in S​E​(3)SE(3), while guaranteeing convergence to the desired goal.
calds comprises two centralized stages: Cooperative Policy Selection, which identifies compatible combinations of single-agent policies, and Temporal Adaptation, which adjusts their temporal profiles to achieve collision-free collaboration while preserving the spatial structure, interpretability, and convergence of the original learned ds.
Both stages generate trajectories in which the adapted learned DSs drive the motion at every step, leveraging JAX (Bradbury et al., 2018; Blondel et al., 2022b) and FRAX (Morton and Pavone, 2026) kinematics for batched, differentiable computation.
We validate the proposed framework through quantitative experiments in three collaborative scenarios. We compare calds against existing collaborative policy adaptation (Singh et al., 2025), whole-body collision avoidance via cbf (Singletary et al., 2021) and nominal single-agent policies, demonstrating its effectiveness in enabling safe and task-consistent operation.

title: Polygraph: Large-Scale Multi-Session Trajectory Optimization using Pose Graphs
authors: Petar Lukovic,Tian Yi Lim,Marc Pollefeys,Pablo Speciale,Hermann Blum,Zuria Bauer
abstract: Robots, vehicles, and wearable devices often traverse the same environment many times. Each pass produces its own trajectory from onboard visual or visual-inertial odometry. These trajectories are locally accurate but drift over time and live in unrelated coordinate frames. Turning many such independent trajectories into one globally consistent set is the large-scale multi-session trajectory optimization problem. Existing solutions largely work offline. All sessions must be available up front, one session is fixed as the reference frame, and a single fused map is then optimized. This paper presents Polygraph, a multi-session trajectory optimization pipeline that processes sessions online, one keyframe and one spatial cluster at a time, and never builds a 3D map. Keyframes are grouped into local clusters. When a cluster closes, it is matched against every other session through learned image retrieval. Candidate pairs are verified with sparse feature matching, monocular metric depth, and robust pose estimation. A two-tier consensus gate admits a cross-session edge into the shared pose graph only once independent evidence corroborates it. A cheap incremental solve keeps the graph current, and a periodic robust batch solve prunes outliers. We evaluate Polygraph on stereo outdoor driving, HoloLens and iPad indoor traversals, legged indoor locomotion with a Boston Dynamics Spot, and large-scale outdoor vehicle and handheld routes. Against the closest prior work on the same GPU model, using its reported timings, Polygraph runs faster, commits fewer loop-closure edges, and matches or improves on accuracy.
introduction:
Many robots, vehicles, and wearable devices see the same environment more than once. A delivery robot drives the same warehouse floor every day. A person wearing an AR headset walks through the same building on many occasions. We call each such pass a session. Each session is tracked by the device’s own visual or visual-inertial odometry. This odometry is accurate locally but drifts over time, and every session lives in its own coordinate frame. Two sessions that walk the same corridor have no way of knowing that they did. Recovering that relationship is the multi-session trajectory optimization problem. It means detecting where sessions overlap, using those overlaps to correct drift, and placing every session into one shared frame. Fig. 1 shows what this looks like once solved.

The classical way to detect overlap is to build and maintain a 3D map of visual landmarks and match new observations against it, as in ORB-SLAM3 Atlas [1], Maplab [2, 3], and COVINS [4]. A map gives strong geometric evidence for a match, but is expensive to store and keep optimized; bundle adjustment grows linearly in landmarks and cubically in poses, so this cost grows with every session and with the size of the environment. A well-built map is also rarely what downstream modules want, since planning and navigation seldom consume a landmark cloud directly.

A recent line of work avoids keeping any map at all. Multi-robot systems such as DOOR-SLAM [5], Swarm-SLAM [6], and FLOCC-SLAM [7] treat closures as pose-graph edges directly but still assume every robot is known up front. 2GO [8] instead represents a single session only as a sparse keyframed pose graph, loop closures found by learned image retrieval, verified with sparse feature matching between two views, and lifted to metric scale with a monocular depth prior or multi-view transformer. However, 2GO handles one session at a time. It cannot relate independent sessions to each other, and its consistency check relies on a live trajectory estimate that exists from the first keyframe onward, which a new session does not have.

This paper presents Polygraph, a multi-session trajectory optimization pipeline that closes this gap. Polygraph processes each session online, one keyframe and one spatial cluster at a time. It does not assume that all sessions are available up front, and it does not fix any session as a reference. When a cluster closes, it is matched with every other session by learned retrieval. Candidate pairs are filtered and verified with sparse matching, monocular depth, and robust pose estimation, and reduced to one confirmed match per cluster pair. A cross-session edge only enters the shared graph once a two-tier consensus gate admits it, which protects the graph from spurious matches. A cheap incremental solver keeps the graph current after every cluster, and a periodic batch solve prunes outlier edges. The algorithm is agnostic to the source of the odometry measurements and simply takes calibrated images and odometry edges as input.

We evaluate Polygraph on stereo outdoor driving on KITTI [9], HoloLens and iPad indoor traversals from LaMAR [10], legged indoor locomotion from CroCoDL [11], vehicle and handheld routes from the large-scale outdoor VBR dataset [12] and small-scale indoor EuRoC dataset [13]. Against the closest prior work 2GO on the same GPU model, using its reported timings, Polygraph runs faster, commits fewer loop-closure edges, and
matches or improves on accuracy.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions.

An online, reconstruction-free formulation of multi-session pose graph optimization that needs neither all sessions up front nor a fixed reference session.

A cluster-level matching and joint pose estimation pipeline with a two-tier consensus gate that admits cross-session edges only once they are corroborated.

A characterization of runtime, accuracy, and loop-closure accuracy across a wide range of devices and scenes, including hardware-matched comparison against 2GO and comparison against other similar methods.

1. An online, reconstruction-free formulation of multi-session pose graph optimization that needs neither all sessions up front nor a fixed reference session.

2. A cluster-level matching and joint pose estimation pipeline with a two-tier consensus gate that admits cross-session edges only once they are corroborated.

3. A characterization of runtime, accuracy, and loop-closure accuracy across a wide range of devices and scenes, including hardware-matched comparison against 2GO and comparison against other similar methods.

title: WinDEX: Metric 3D Hand Motion Reconstruction in the Wild for Dexterous Teleoperation and Policy Learning
authors: Hongyu Ma,Hairong Qu,Shiqi Zhao,Yongsong Yang,Kai Shi,Jiahao Ai,Xin You,Peng Yin
abstract:
Human manipulation data are widely used to train robots for human-like dexterity.
However, low-cost, large-scale collection in the wild remains challenging.
Existing methods remain limited in geometrically grounded metric-scale reconstruction, real-world generalization and inference speed.
We present WinDEX, integrating (1) geometric–temporal optimization for metric 3D hand annotation from in-the-wild egocentric stereo videos, combined with visual–inertial SLAM for world-frame reconstruction;
(2) WinDEX-Net, an end-to-end, fisheye-native network combining calibrated stereo, local detail and temporal context, with a data–model flywheel of model-assisted annotation and retraining; (3) distilled models for offline reconstruction and causal streaming, supporting reinforcement learning and teleoperation;
and (4) low-cost CyberCap stereo–inertial capture, forming the WinDEX-Hand dataset with 1,000 hours of training annotations and held-out human-annotated in-the-wild 2D and independent optical motion-capture evaluation sets.
Offline reconstruction runs at 43.61 FPS and causal streaming at 171 FPS.
On held-out data, offline reconstruction achieves state-of-the-art accuracy: 14.5 pixels in-the-wild reprojection error and, with visual–inertial odometry, 37.29 mm world-frame joint error.
We achieve 7.6×7.6\times and 3.6×3.6\times the task success rates of reinforcement learning policies trained with WiLoR and HaWoR motion references, respectively, and demonstrate real-time arm–hand teleoperation.
Project website: https://fruitrabbit.github.io/WinDEX/.
introduction:
Roboticists have long sought to guide dexterous robotic
manipulation using human motion trajectories. Hand poses and trajectories guide
teleoperation
[1, 2, 3, 4] and provide
demonstrations, pose priors, and tracking references for reinforcement learning (RL)
[5, 6, 7]. Hand trajectories also provide
action supervision for video-based policies and vision–language–action
models [8, 9, 10], condition world models that
predict manipulation outcomes [11], and supply geometric
information for grasp synthesis [12, 13].
These applications share a need for reliable 3D hand motion in relation to
the surrounding scene. We adopt metric 3D hand poses and their trajectories
in a gravity-aligned world frame as our 3D hand representations, describing
wrist motion and finger articulation independently of the moving camera
(Fig. 1). Recovering this representation across everyday
environments at scale is our central problem.

Existing acquisition routes include optical motion capture, calibrated
multi-camera rigs, sensor gloves and wearable trackers, and video recording.
Optical systems and multi-camera datasets such as ARCTIC,
DexYCB, HOT3D and AssemblyHands provide detailed reference measurements
[14, 15, 16, 17], but depend on
instrumented environments. Gloves and exoskeletons support portable capture
[4, 18] while retaining hardware on the hands.

Monocular RGB cameras permit egocentric or exocentric recording without
hand instrumentation. More broadly, video collections such as Ego4D and
Ego-Exo4D cover diverse first- and third-person activity
[19, 20], but a single view leaves depth and absolute
scale ambiguous, and external cameras limit recording to their fields of
view. Wearable recording extends coverage
[21, 22]. In particular, head-worn stereo can follow the
wearer without placing equipment on the hands, while a calibrated baseline
provides a geometric constraint on metric depth. Project Aria and Quest
tracking systems demonstrate the potential of wearable multi-view sensing
[23, 24, 25]. Scalable in-the-wild capture still
requires reliable annotation under occlusion, peripheral visibility and
simultaneous camera and hand motion.

To recover metric hand trajectories from these recordings, both model
architecture and training supervision must accommodate wearable capture.
Monocular image and video estimators, including HaMeR, WiLoR, HaWoR and
Dyn-HaMR [26, 27, 28, 29], use appearance
and motion priors to resolve single-view ambiguity. POEM and its successor
exploit calibrated multi-view geometry [30, 31];
ViDiHand integrates localization and reconstruction without an external
detector [32]. For compact fisheye stereo, an integrated
architecture must additionally use the known baseline and viewing rays,
preserve local finger detail, and distinguish hand motion from camera
motion. On the data side, laboratory capture limits environmental coverage,
and tracker-generated labels require independent accuracy evaluation
[16, 22]. Dense, reliable 3D supervision across diverse
natural recordings remains costly. These needs motivate joint localization
and reconstruction with stereo and temporal context, coupled to a scalable
pipeline for producing and checking training annotations.

We present WinDEX, a system integrating wearable capture,
geometric–temporal annotation, learned reconstruction and robot interfaces
(Fig. 2). Low-cost CyberCap collects fisheye stereo RGB and
inertial data without hand instrumentation. To obtain metric supervision, geometric–temporal
optimization fits hands to manually reviewed 2D keypoints, filters 3D labels
by reprojection error, and uses SLAM camera trajectories to recover
world-frame motion.

To address depth ambiguity, preserve finger detail and account for camera
motion, WinDEX-Net combines calibrated stereo, local crops and
odometry-conditioned temporal features for end-to-end, fisheye-native
localization and reconstruction. Predictions accelerate annotation, and
retraining closes the data–model flywheel. WinDEX-Hand separates generated 3D training labels
from evaluation references: human-annotated in-the-wild 2D references
and independent optical 3D ground truth (Section V-C).

To balance accuracy and response time, distillation yields offline
WinDEX-Window and causal, real-time WinDEX-Stream. Hand2Policy uses
pose-tracking rewards for reinforcement learning; Hand2Teleop coordinates
arm–hand teleoperation using only CyberCap stereo and IMU for operator tracking.

Against human-annotated in-the-wild 2D references and optical 3D ground
truth from held-out recordings,
WinDEX-Window achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy and temporal
smoothness. Under matched
training settings and budgets, Hand2Policy reaches 61% mean simulated
grasp–lift–place success versus 8% for WiLoR and 17% for HaWoR, with
policy transfer to physical robots.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

To obtain metric 3D hand annotations from in-the-wild egocentric stereo
videos, we combine geometric–temporal optimization with visual–inertial
SLAM to recover hand articulation and metrically scaled trajectories in a
consistent world frame.

To accelerate reconstruction, we introduce WinDEX-Net, an end-to-end,
fisheye-native network combining calibrated stereo geometry, local hand
detail and temporal context. Model-initialized optimization and retraining
form a data–model flywheel that expands supervision.

To support offline learning and live control, we distill WinDEX-Net
into WinDEX-Window and WinDEX-Stream. Hand2Policy and Hand2Teleop further connect
the models to reinforcement learning with policy transfer and real-time
arm–hand teleoperation, respectively, with validation on physical hardware.

To make collection accessible at scale, we use the low-cost CyberCap
stereo–inertial device for everyday manipulation and construct WinDEX-Hand
from the annotated recordings, with held-out human-annotated in-the-wild 2D
references and independent optical motion-capture ground truth.

Section II reviews related work, and
Section III formulates the system. Sections IV
and V describe metric annotation and model-assisted corpus
construction. Section VI presents the deployment models and
robot interfaces; Section VII reports experiments, followed
by limitations in Section VIII.
