3. 是否属于 VLA：是。理由：论文中提到使用手部轨迹作为动作监督，支持视觉-语言-动作模型的训练，且输入包含视觉信息，输出是机器人动作，符合VLA的定义。

4. 是否属于 Humanoid Loco-manipulation：否。理由：虽然论文涉及手部的遥操作和策略学习，但并未明确提到使用人形机器人平台进行联合的运动和操作控制，因此不符合Humanoid Loco-manipulation的标准。

5. 最终标签总结：
   - World Model: 是
   - VLA: 是
   - Humanoid Loco-manipulation: 否

6. 如果有歧义，请说明最容易混淆的点：
   论文涉及手部运动的重建和遥操作，可能让人误以为是Humanoid Loco-manipulation，但实际上并未涉及人形机器人的整体协调控制，因此在判断时需注意平台的具体类型和任务的性质。

title: Linglong Agent Service: A Runtime for Centralized Agent Reasoning and Distributed Execution
authors: Hua Zhang,Min Jiang
abstract: LLM agents can use remote tools and cloud sandboxes, but integrating reasoning, session state, and heterogeneous execution sites remains a runtime design problem. We present Linglong Agent Service (agentsvc), a self-hosted HTTP service and embeddable Python runtime that treats execution site as a configurable dimension alongside model, tools, and context. A parent service retains inference orchestration, tool descriptions, and conversation history; each inference request selects one child environment for file, shell, terminal, and MCP operations. Direct HTTP and child-initiated WebSocket tunnels carry the same application interfaces, including portable request context and centrally managed updates. The normal core path requires no third-party Python packages, with an optional Windows pseudo-terminal dependency. We further present online_debugger as the process-scale special case of execution-site separation: an instrumented program submits exception evidence, executes session-scoped inspection tools inside the incident process, and resumes the same diagnostic session. Its default prompt requires failing-then-passing reproduction evidence for source changes, while runtime patch activation and failed-call recovery remain unimplemented. We explain the design through constrained expected-utility reasoning, compare concrete mechanisms with Hermes Agent, Pi, Codex, and Claude Code, and report implementation and regression-test evidence. The current evidence establishes executable contracts, not performance advantages, repair accuracy, or production recovery. The source code is open source under the MIT license at https://github.com/mz24cn/agents.
introduction:
An LLM agent acts through tools, and every tool executes somewhere:
inside a process, in a filesystem namespace, under a permission
boundary, and on a machine with particular resources. Existing agents
already reach beyond their own host through SSH, remote MCP servers, and
hosted sandboxes. The remaining engineering question is how to preserve
a coherent agent service when its actions must occur across
infrastructure with different network, installation, and state
constraints.

Consider a coding agent that operates a GPU server behind NAT. The model
provider and conversation history can remain centrally managed, while
commands, files, persistent terminals, and tool-specific resources
belong to the GPU server. Moving only the shell leaves other operations
and their histories to be integrated separately. Running a separate full
agent on every machine is also possible, but can duplicate configuration
and fragment the operator’s view. Neither outcome is inevitable; they
motivate an explicit contract between centralized orchestration and
distributed execution.

Linglong Agent Service, abbreviated agentsvc, explores that
contract in a self-hosted runtime (Linglong Agent Service contributors, 2026a). The implementation
is open source under the MIT license and publicly available at
https://github.com/mz24cn/agents. Its design vision is to
concentrate agent capability in one place and project execution across
IT infrastructure. Here, projection means selecting where
compatible tools execute while retaining centrally managed reasoning and
session state. Infrastructure-wide reach is a design goal subject to
Python availability, network reachability, authorization,
operating-system support, and tool compatibility. It is not a claim that
every device has been supported or tested. Centralized reasoning refers
to inference orchestration: model weights may reside at a local or
remote provider.

The organizing model is

The product notation expresses configurable composition, not
mathematical independence. Execution site is explicit because changing
it should not require changing model-facing tool names, rebuilding an
agent definition, or relocating conversation history. Compatibility
conditions remain: the selected model must support the interaction, the
child must implement the required tools, and paths must resolve in the
intended namespace.

The same argument extends below machine granularity. When an ordinary
program catches an exception, evidence in its traceback and frames may
be useful to an external coding agent. A shell on the same host does not
automatically provide access to those process objects. The included
online_debugger captures evidence and exposes inspection
operations as client-side tools executed by the incident process. This
makes it a process-scale special case of execution-site separation. It
shares the architectural principle with infrastructure remote execution,
while using a different transport and continuation contract.

This paper makes four contributions:

A compositional agent runtime and a design rationale that connects
centralized session assets, low-dependency deployment, and runtime
configuration under an explicit expected-utility criterion.

A compositional agent runtime and a design rationale that connects
centralized session assets, low-dependency deployment, and runtime
configuration under an explicit expected-utility criterion.

A remote-execution design with request-scoped site selection, portable
execution context, parent-side orchestration, and common application
interfaces over direct HTTP and reverse WebSocket transports.

A client-side tool contract and its realization in exception-triggered
diagnosis and source repair, with an explicit separation between
reproduction evidence and runtime recovery.

A bounded comparison with four agent systems, an implementation
evidence inventory, and an evaluation agenda that separates mechanism
correctness from task effectiveness.

The implementation baseline is commit
07d3d23a24f356bf2e59527b762ab66611c34f27, dated November 8,
2026 (Linglong Agent Service contributors, 2026a). Reported regression results come from the
verification record for that baseline. We have no latency benchmark,
controlled repair study, or evidence of general production recovery to
report.

title: ReuseMem: One Memory, Multiple Goals in Robot Manipulation
authors: Yoonseok Kang,Dayeon Jung,Seunghoon Jeon,Wonjib Kim,Dongchul Park
abstract: Robots that work alongside people should be able to use what they have seen when new requests arise. The same experience may later support identifying an object or returning it to its original location, although these uses were unknown during observation. ReuseMem learns to use one visual memory for multiple later manipulation goals. It records visual features independently of future goals, retrieves complementary evidence for each request, and combines it with the current scene through a lightweight action interface. Retrieval is supervised by how well candidate evidence supports expert-action prediction across different current states, linking memory selection to its use in manipulation. Repeated visual features are stored once, and memory computations that remain unchanged during action generation are reused. Experiments on four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios demonstrate reuse of a common recording across different requests. With matched action adaptation, ReuseMem improves joint goal completion on the benchmark tasks by 24.5 percentage points over uniform memory. These findings show that one memory can support multiple later manipulation goals as the scene changes.
introduction:
Memory enables robots to act on information that is no longer visible. In everyday assistance, the same experience may become useful for several requests that arise only later. An earlier observation may identify an object, reveal its original location, or establish the order of events. The robot need not know which of these uses will matter when it observes the scene. This calls for one memory that supports multiple later goals as the environment changes.

Consider a robot observing the contents and original positions of two cases before they are closed and relocated (Figure 1). Bringing the case containing a USB drive to a tray requires remembering its contents; returning it requires its origin. The same experience supplies different facts for different actions. After the transfer, the case must be grasped from the tray, while its destination still comes from the recorded past.

Memory-augmented policies have advanced historical retrieval and its use in control [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Persistent experience systems also reuse past observations for later requests through retrieval and planning [6, 7, 8, 9]. Building on these advances, we ask how the same recorded experience can reliably support different later manipulations. Success on several tasks with separate histories does not directly answer this question. The relevant unit is a common experience, whose usefulness must persist across requests that need different evidence and produce different actions.

Such reuse couples two challenges. The robot must select the past observations needed for each request, then use them with the current scene to generate an appropriate action. Remembering an object’s identity or former position does not specify where to grasp it now. Earlier actions can change the scene while leaving the historical facts valid. Training must therefore connect evidence selection to action under these changing current conditions.

ReuseMem addresses this problem with a goal-independent Writer, a learned Reader, and a lightweight action interface. The Writer retains visual features and separate temporal entries without an advance inventory of objects or relations. The Reader selects complementary observations for each request. Its supervision comes from comparing how well candidate evidence supports expert-action prediction across different current states for the same goal. Historical facts remain fixed while the required actions vary. The action interface then learns from the updated Reader’s selections, combining remembered evidence with current observations through fusion and low-rank adaptation of a frozen pretrained policy.

Practical reuse also requires controlling storage and response time. Recordings often contain many similar views, yet their order can distinguish events relevant to later requests. To limit storage, ReuseMem stores matching visual features once while retaining a separate temporal entry for each observation. To reduce response time, fixed memory projections are computed once per action-sampling call and reused as the action is refined, while the policy still reads the selected memory anew at every step.

Four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios evaluate different goals from common recordings, both independently and in continuous execution. With matched action adaptation, ReuseMem improves joint goal completion by 24.5 percentage points over uniform memory. Ablations and memory interventions examine evidence selection and action use, while storage and response measurements assess the cost of reuse.

Our contributions are:

One memory, multiple manipulation goals. We introduce ReuseMem, a framework that records experience before later goals are known and reuses the same visual memory for different manipulations as the current scene changes.

Action-guided memory learning. We train memory retrieval by comparing how different selections of past observations support expert-action prediction across current states for the same goal. A lightweight action interface learns to combine the selected evidence with current observations.

Efficient memory reuse. We reduce memory storage and repeated computation while retaining the temporal structure of experience. Repeated visual features are shared across temporal entries, and fixed memory projections are reused within each action-sampling call.

1. One memory, multiple manipulation goals. We introduce ReuseMem, a framework that records experience before later goals are known and reuses the same visual memory for different manipulations as the current scene changes.

2. Action-guided memory learning. We train memory retrieval by comparing how different selections of past observations support expert-action prediction across current states for the same goal. A lightweight action interface learns to combine the selected evidence with current observations.

3. Efficient memory reuse. We reduce memory storage and repeated computation while retaining the temporal structure of experience. Repeated visual features are shared across temporal entries, and fixed memory projections are reused within each action-sampling call.

title: ForceHarness: Turning Force into Action and Physics for Frozen Frontier Models
authors: Ke Sun,Kevin Yuchen Ma,Yike Zhang,Yanzhe Chen,Mike Zheng Shou
comment: : 8-page main paper, references, and supplementary material. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show.
Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges.
First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model.
Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about.
Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning.
After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event.
To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result.
To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables.
On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%.
In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys.
Ablations further show that smaller models make significantly better decisions when given physical quantities rather than raw force values.
introduction:
Frontier multimodal models can now control robots directly without task-specific training.
For example, GPT-6 Astra runs behind an API with frozen weights and still controls a robot zero-shot from images through a pose interface [43, 27].
Much of this progress comes from the harness that wraps the frozen model and provides semantic action units [5], virtual camera views [32], agent-written tools and code [13, 17], or low-level VLA skills [44].
However, existing harnesses mainly help the model see and move.

Beyond seeing and moving, many manipulation tasks in the physical world depend on contact forces that images cannot show.
For example, driving a screw requires pressing down while turning until the thread engages, and sorting identical-looking bottles requires comparing their weight.
Existing work brings force into such tasks mainly through learning.
Specifically, force-aware policies [39, 18, 15] and benchmarks [14] add wrist force as a network input to visuomotor policies [6] and vision-language-action (VLA) models [24].
However, this approach requires demonstrations for every task and updates model weights, so it cannot be applied to an API-only frozen model.
Meanwhile, existing harnesses for frozen models that expose contact typically pass raw wrench and tactile values [7, 29] or ask the model to generate force-control code [4, 28].
Yet these designs still leave the model to parse raw sensor numbers or write low-level control without calibrated physical feedback.
We therefore ask: can a frozen frontier model understand force and use it to complete manipulation tasks that cannot be done without it?

Answering this question raises two challenges.
First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model through general skills that regulate force on their own under the model’s direction.
Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams or choose actions from raw numbers alone, so the system must return force in a form the model can reason about.

Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets a frozen frontier model use wrist force without demonstrations or training.
As shown in Figure 1, ForceHarness places three layers between the model and the robot.
At the bottom, a force sensing and calibration layer estimates hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone and removes sensor offsets.
In the middle, self-terminating force primitives address the first challenge by turning common contact skills such as guarded moves, sliding, and insertion into callable tools.
Once called, each primitive regulates force on its own and returns at a contact event.
At the top, a physics translation layer addresses the second challenge by converting each primitive’s force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty estimates and status flags, such as payload mass, contact height, and friction.
At each turn, the model calls a primitive, reads the returned physical quantities, and decides what to do next.
Together, these three layers form a general set of building blocks that bridges a frozen frontier model and low-level force control.

We evaluate ForceHarness on a real robot arm without a wrist force sensor and across two simulation benchmarks, as summarized in Figure 1.
On the real robot, we design six contact-rich tasks and find that ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% without force to 90.0%.
In simulation, the same model with ForceHarness operates from RGB images on the public ForceBench suite [14] and improves from 70.0% to 87.5%, surpassing the force-aware policies trained on that benchmark.
To further compare frozen models with classical controllers and learned force policies under identical conditions, we build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables.
On HiddenPhys, ForceHarness raises the success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 62.1% to 96.4%, matching hand-written expert force controllers and far exceeding Diffusion Policy [6], π0.5\pi_{0.5} [24], and ForceVLA [39] trained on about 200 demonstrations per task.

Our contributions are:

We propose ForceHarness, a three-layer harness of force calibration, self-terminating force primitives, and physics translation that bridges an API-only frozen model and low-level force control without demonstrations or training.

We build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables that includes expert force controllers and learned force policies evaluated on identical seeds.

Experiments on a real robot and two simulated benchmarks show that ForceHarness lets frozen frontier models make full use of force for contact-rich manipulation, outperforming both training-based methods and the same harness without force.

1. We propose ForceHarness, a three-layer harness of force calibration, self-terminating force primitives, and physics translation that bridges an API-only frozen model and low-level force control without demonstrations or training.

2. We build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables that includes expert force controllers and learned force policies evaluated on identical seeds.

3. Experiments on a real robot and two simulated benchmarks show that ForceHarness lets frozen frontier models make full use of force for contact-rich manipulation, outperforming both training-based methods and the same harness without force.

title: CoopDistill: Equilibrium-Guided Multi-Agent Policy Distillation for Cooperative Driving
authors: Shiyu Fang,Sheng Zhao,Jiarui Zhang,Chengkai Xu,Xiaocong Zhao,Peng Hang,Jian Sun
abstract:
Cooperative driving extends autonomous driving from individual vehicle
decisions to joint maneuvers that improve traffic safety and efficiency.
Optimization-based methods impose safety constraints but often fix
paths to simplify multi-vehicle planning, limiting spatial flexibility.
Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) explores alternatives through
interaction, but coordinated learning and safe execution remain
challenging. Their integration nevertheless faces
challenges in exploration efficiency, experience allocation, and
execution reliability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes
CoopDistill, an equilibrium-guided multi-agent policy distillation
framework. A potential-game (PG) formulation provides a fixed-path
longitudinal reference, around which a residual MARL policy learns
longitudinal acceleration, conflict-approach timing, and lateral path
corrections. A hard-case curriculum concentrates experience on
interactions that PG leaves unresolved or substantially delayed.
A comparative rollout selector evaluates the joint consequences of
learned corrections against PG before choosing the executed action.
Experiments in merging, roundabout, and intersection scenarios compare
CoopDistill with six baselines at four connected automated vehicle
penetration levels. Relative to PG, success improves by 2.1–27.1
percentage points and delay decreases by 7.3–27.3%, with no observed
collisions. Code is available at
https://github.com/FanGShiYuu/CoopDistill.
introduction:
As autonomous driving moves toward commercial deployment, vehicles must negotiate shared road space at intersections, roundabouts, and merging areas (Schwarting et al., 2018; Guanetti et al., 2018). In these complex conflict areas, decisions made from an individual vehicle’s perspective may resolve an immediate encounter without coordinating the progression of the interacting group (Rios-Torres and Malikopoulos, 2017). Vehicle connectivity creates opportunities for connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) to exchange motion states and maneuver intentions and coordinate when and where to proceed (Talebpour and Mahmassani, 2016; Wang et al., 2020). Cooperative driving can therefore complement individual autonomy by organizing joint maneuvers aimed at safer and more efficient traffic operation (Rios-Torres and Malikopoulos, 2017; Malikopoulos et al., 2018).

Cooperative-driving methods coordinate vehicle decisions through optimization, multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), or combinations of the two. Optimization and game-theoretic methods represent interactions through explicit objectives and constraints, but joint motion and path planning becomes increasingly demanding as interactions multiply (Malikopoulos et al., 2018; Katriniok et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021). MARL provides maneuver flexibility through environmental interaction, although coordinated exploration and reliable execution remain challenging (Lowe et al., 2017; Kiran et al., 2022; Gronauer and Diepold, 2022). Hybrid methods seek to combine structured coordination with learned flexibility (Hewing et al., 2020; Zanon and Gros, 2021; Bautista-Montesano et al., 2022; Chen and others, 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026). The central question is how to learn useful improvements beyond the optimization reference while retaining its coordination benefits during execution.

Effective integration therefore involves three connected challenges (Fig. 1). 1) Exploration–Convergence Trade-off: Exploring complete longitudinal and lateral actions across several vehicles creates a large joint search space and makes coordinated policies difficult to learn. Confining exploration to the optimizer’s fixed-path decisions reduces that space but also excludes the path changes needed to release spatial obstruction. The challenge is to use the optimization solution to guide exploration without inheriting its maneuver restrictions (Johannink et al., 2019; Gronauer and Diepold, 2022).
2) Insufficient Long-Tail Learning: Fixed-path coordination already resolves many routine encounters, leaving limited improvement to be learned from repeatedly visiting them. By contrast, infrequent interactions involving blocked paths or chains of yielding can leave an entire group of vehicles waiting. These cases require coordinated changes in both motion and path geometry, yet can occupy only a small share of training experience. Identifying such interactions and allocating sufficient experience to them is essential for learning capabilities beyond those of the reference (Bengio et al., 2009; Narvekar et al., 2020).
3) Execution-Time Reliability: Reward-based training does not explicitly enforce the coupled safety constraints of every new interaction (Wang et al., 2026). A learned correction may advance one vehicle while closing another’s available gap, or remain collision-free while reducing collective progress. Execution therefore requires a state-dependent choice between the learned joint proposal and the optimization reference, based on their predicted feasibility and traffic consequences (Garcia and Fernandez, 2015; Brunke et al., 2022).

To address these challenges, we propose CoopDistill, an equilibrium-guided multi-agent policy distillation framework for cooperative driving. A potential-game (PG) formulation first produces a longitudinal coordination reference by maximizing a common potential over fixed-path acceleration sequences. Conditioned on this reference, a shared residual actor generates longitudinal acceleration, conflict-approach timing, and lateral path corrections, extending coordination from fixed-path motion to joint longitudinal–lateral maneuvers. Rollout-evaluated corrections provide action-level guidance, and multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) refines the policy through vehicle interactions. A hard-case curriculum emphasizes scenes that PG cannot clear or clears only after substantial delay. At execution, a comparative rollout selector evaluates the learned joint proposal and PG from the same state, accepting the proposal when it satisfies the feasibility and utility conditions and otherwise retaining PG. The framework thus connects equilibrium-guided exploration, difficulty-directed training, and reference-based execution.

The contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

An equilibrium-guided residual MARL formulation is developed with three action channels for longitudinal acceleration, conflict-approach timing, and lateral path adjustment. The shared policy learns joint corrections around a PG reference and extends the available cooperative maneuvers.

A PG-based hard-case curriculum is constructed by ranking training scenes according to collision, completion, and delay outcomes. Sampling from the difficult subset together with fresh scenes directs experience toward interactions poorly resolved by the reference.

A comparative rollout selector is formulated to evaluate learned and PG joint decisions from the same traffic state. Feasibility checks and a utility comparison determine which decision is executed, and the same selection process is included during training.

title: Multi-CONDOR: Learning Multistable Motion Primitives from Demonstration
authors: Gabriele Giuseppe Di Marzo,Mariano Ramírez Montero,Maximilian Stölzle,Rodrigo Pérez-Dattari,Cosimo Della Santina
abstract:
Dynamical-system-based motion policies provide a framework for learning reactive robot motions with stability and convergence properties.
Many manipulation tasks, however, admit several distinct goals or a continuous set of acceptable outcomes, requiring motion primitives that preserve these alternatives.
Accommodating both goal structures within a unified framework with continuous, autonomous dynamics remains an open challenge.
We propose a CONDOR-based framework, multi-CONDOR, for learning motion primitives with either multiple discrete attractors or a continuous attracting goal contour.
The approach combines imitation learning with losses that encourage agreement between the learned task dynamics and latent reference systems encoding the desired attraction structure.
We provide a Lyapunov-based analysis of the convergence properties of the learned motion dynamics.
We evaluate the framework on simulated benchmarks with discrete goals, qualitative examples with continuous goal contours, and robotic grasping experiments.
In simulation, multi-CONDOR reduces trajectory RMSE by approximately 72% compared with separately learned single-goal motion primitives selected by a state machine.
For tasks with two and three goals, respectively, it reduces the fraction of evaluated initial states ending outside the goal tolerance from StableNODE’s 0.31% and 7.29% to 0% in both settings.
Experiments with a Franka Emika robot arm demonstrate successful grasping of a container by either of its two handles using motions learned from demonstrations.
Together, these results show multi-CONDOR combines motion reproduction with the flexibility to converge to alternative valid outcomes.
introduction:
Imitation learning enables robots to acquire motion skills from demonstrations, providing an accessible way to adapt their behavior to new tasks.
This capability is increasingly valuable as robots enter environments where tasks vary and frequent manual programming is impractical.
General approaches, including generative methods such as diffusion policies [1], can represent complex behaviors, but may require substantial demonstration data [2] and do not inherently provide stability or convergence guarantees.

Dynamical systems provide an established framework for learning motion primitives with stability and convergence properties.
Dynamic movement primitives (DMPs) reproduce demonstrated motions using an internal phase variable that governs their progression [3].
If this phase advances while physical interaction slows or blocks the robot [4], the resulting mismatch can induce unnatural catch-up motions [5].
Other approaches learn autonomous vector fields that determine motion directly from the current task state, without an independent time or phase reference [6, 7, 8, 9].

Standard point-to-point motion primitives typically encode convergence to a single prescribed goal [3, 10].
Many manipulation tasks instead admit multimodal goal behavior: a robot may grasp a container at either of two handles.
Other tasks admit a continuum of acceptable outcomes, such as grasping at any admissible point along its rim.
Selecting one endpoint in advance discards alternatives that may be easier to reach from the current configuration or after a disturbance.
A disturbance can then redirect the motion toward another valid goal, allowing the robot to complete the task without returning to the originally selected endpoint.
Motion primitives should therefore capture both the demonstrated approach behavior and the freedom to converge to multiple isolated goals or a continuous goal set.

Initial work has addressed the discrete multistable case.
Augmented-SVM combines motion dynamics through learned partitions of the state space and modulates their vector fields to preserve the associated attraction regions [11].
StableNODE learns latent dynamics with multiple attractors using a corrective term derived from an energy function [12].
These approaches demonstrate motion generation toward distinct goals, but do not provide a unified framework for learning continuous, autonomous motion dynamics with both multiple discrete attractors and continuous attracting goal sets.

We propose a unified framework for learning motion primitives with continuous, autonomous dynamics and either multiple discrete attractors or a continuous attracting goal contour.
Building on CONDOR [8], we learn a task-space vector field together with an encoding into a latent space equipped with reference dynamics representing the desired attraction structure.
We introduce two reference systems: a Gaussian potential for multiple isolated goals and a radially attracting circle for a continuous goal contour.
We establish sufficient conditions for convergence to our desired set through Lyapunov analysis, and formulate training losses that encourage these conditions alongside an imitation objective.
The resulting framework learns motion toward alternative admissible goals directly from the current state.

We evaluate the framework on two-dimensional demonstration datasets with two and three discrete goals, measuring trajectory reproduction and convergence from initial states distributed throughout the workspace.
We further examine continuous goal contours through qualitative examples and demonstrate robotic grasping with multiple admissible grasping locations.
Together, these experiments assess the framework’s ability to reproduce demonstrated motions while accommodating discrete and continuous goal sets.

title: WiTac: Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations for Contact-Rich Manipulation
authors: Haotian He,Yiyang Chen,Congsheng Xu,Wenchao Yue,Mingze Ye,Shuai Chen,Yi Yang,Yaping Li,Haonan Wang,Weinan E,Wenzhao Lian,Zhijie Deng
abstract:
Similar tactile contacts can call for different corrections depending on the configuration of the hand, object and target.
Rather than supplying touch and wrist vision separately, fusing them before policy injection better grounds tactile features in visual context, yielding more accurate contact representations.
We introduce Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations (WiTac), a pretrained encoder that learns such representations before action generation.
Pretrained on nearly 300 hours of SharpaDex data, WiTac deeply fuses tactile signals with hand motion and wrist views into a comprehensive contact representation.
Conditioning downstream VLA policies (GR00T N1.7 and π0.5\pi_{0.5}) on WiTac substantially improves task success over vision-only base policies across four contact-rich manipulation tasks (+28.8% and +15.0% on average), and further outperforms a wrist-free tactile encoder by 18.8% and 7.5%, respectively.
Offline analyses further show that incorporating wrist vision yields more accurate contact descriptors, stronger joint task–contact discrimination, greater feature stability under tactile noise, and clearer action-direction readout from similar contacts.
Project page: https://wrist-informed-tactile-representations.github.io/.
introduction:
Contact-rich manipulation requires actions that respond jointly to local touch and surrounding task geometry.
When inserting a battery into a slot, similar finger loading can accompany different battery–slot alignments and call for distinct corrective motions.
Local tactile deformation alone leaves this spatial configuration ambiguous, whereas close-range wrist cameras observe the hand, grasped object, and nearby target geometry, providing the spatial reference needed to interpret contact during manipulation.

Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policies such as GR00T [17] and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [18] already receive camera images in their vision-language streams, yet they lack pre-fusion with tactile signals to ground grasp- and contact-related states.
Recent visuotactile designs incorporate touch into policies by supplying standalone tactile features alongside visual streams [9, 25], modulating visual features with tactile signals [15], or encoding discrete residuals from visually predicted touch [30].
However, separate tactile inputs leave local touch ungrounded in the surrounding visual geometry, while visual modulation and residual coding do not directly form continuous contact representations that preserve detailed touch within its wrist visual context.

To address this limitation, we introduce Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations (WiTac), a pretrained encoder that fuses touch with wrist vision before policy injection to produce grounded visuotactile contact tokens (figure 1).
Pretrained on nearly 300 hours of synchronized dexterous manipulation data from SharpaDex v1.0 [20], WiTac summarizes each finger’s tactile history with robot state and wrist-relative fingertip kinematics, then queries wrist patch features through cross-attention to form finger-level contact tokens.
Pretraining jointly supervises contact-state and history reconstruction, masked wrist-feature recovery, and action-conditioned wrench-response prediction, encouraging the tokens to retain physical contact detail as they incorporate visual context.
During policy learning, the frozen WiTac encoder conditions VLA policies through a lightweight gated cross-attention interface alongside their native visual, language and state inputs.
Across four real-world contact-rich tasks, WiTac consistently boosts closed-loop success on both GR00T N1.7 and π0.5\pi_{0.5} over vision-only base policies (+28.8% and +15.0% on average) and its wrist-free variant WiTac-NW (+18.8% and +7.5%), while offline analyses confirm improved contact reconstruction, joint task–contact discrimination, noise stability, and action-direction readout.

Our contributions are:

We propose WiTac, a pretrained contact encoder that fuses tactile histories, hand kinematics, and wrist observations into finger-level contact tokens before action generation, through joint physical and visual supervision.

We demonstrate the utility of frozen WiTac representations across two VLA backbones and four real-world contact-rich tasks, achieving higher success than vision-only policies and wrist-free tactile encoding on every task.

Through representation analyses, we show that WiTac provides more accurate contact descriptors, stronger joint task–contact discrimination, lower feature drift under tactile noise, and more accurate action-direction readout than wrist-free encoding.

1. We propose WiTac, a pretrained contact encoder that fuses tactile histories, hand kinematics, and wrist observations into finger-level contact tokens before action generation, through joint physical and visual supervision.

2. We demonstrate the utility of frozen WiTac representations across two VLA backbones and four real-world contact-rich tasks, achieving higher success than vision-only policies and wrist-free tactile encoding on every task.

3. Through representation analyses, we show that WiTac provides more accurate contact descriptors, stronger joint task–contact discrimination, lower feature drift under tactile noise, and more accurate action-direction readout than wrist-free encoding.

title: FlowRow: Learning Navigation Behaviors in Agricultural Environments with Long-Horizon Goal-Conditioned Flow Matching Policies
authors: Utkarsh Bajpai,Cédric Pradalier,Stéphanie Aravecchia
abstract: Autonomous monitoring and intervention in semi-structured agricultural environments, such as orchards and vineyards, require mobile robots to navigate to locations across diverse field configurations. This entails performing navigation behaviors including in-row driving, row turning and skipping, and inter-row traversal. Recent learning-based approaches have enabled robust in-row navigation from onboard perception, but navigation across rows typically requires a priori knowledge of field geometry to specify and tune row-transition maneuvers, preventing arbitrary transitions between rows. We address this challenge by framing navigation in these environments as a goal-directed navigation task, where a long-horizon goal is expressed relative to the robot and a planner generates local paths based on the goal and the robot’s perceptual observations. We present FlowRow, a flow-matching-based local planner which models the distribution of diverse agricultural navigation behaviors as SE⁡(2)\mathrm{SE}(2) paths using the long-horizon goal and depth perception. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce RowNavBench, a navigation benchmark for semi-structured agricultural environments developed in Isaac Sim, comprising 900 episodes across grape vineyards, lemon orchards, and apple orchards with varying row lengths, row and plant spacings, plant positions, and weed growth. FlowRow achieves 87% success, compared to 44% for the strongest generative behavior cloning baseline retrained on the same demonstrations. We will release our benchmark, data, and code upon acceptance.
introduction:
Autonomous mobile robots are increasingly deployed in agricultural fields for precision intervention tasks such as crop inspection, and harvesting, which require reliable navigation to target locations. Such robots operate in semi-structured environments such as orchards, vineyards, and greenhouses, where crops are arranged in rows separated by navigable corridors with headlands at their ends. Large fields require long-horizon navigation, while crop rows constrain how the robot can traverse the environment. A target location may be spatially close to the robot yet lie in another row, requiring the robot to first move away from it, transition through a headland, and approach it from a different direction. The appropriate trajectory therefore depends not only on the target location, but also on the surrounding row structure. This gives rise to distinct navigation behaviors, including in-row driving, headland turning, and row skipping, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). Agricultural environments also vary considerably in vegetation density and obstacle distribution. Vegetation growth can narrow corridors or alter their apparent structure, while rocks, weeds, and other obstacles can reduce free space. Dense canopies can attenuate or obstruct GNSS signals, and uneven terrain or loose soil can induce wheel slippage and odometry drift. Together, these factors make long-horizon agricultural navigation challenging.

In this work, we consider the problem of goal-directed navigation in semi-structured agricultural environments. Specifically, we consider a robot initialized in an unknown row-crop field with headlands at the ends of the rows. The robot has no prior map or knowledge of field geometry, such as crop and row spacing, but can perceive its surroundings through onboard perception. Given a relative goal position, the robot must navigate to it while avoiding obstacles and performing navigation behaviors, including in-row driving, headland turning, row skipping, or combinations thereof.

Existing agricultural navigation systems often rely on tracking pre-computed reference paths generated from known field geometry [15]. While effective, these approaches can degrade from localization errors under canopy, and environmental variation. Recent perception-based methods reduce dependence on localization by using onboard sensing for localization-free in-row navigation [2, 18].
Such methods estimate the row centerline for row following, while row transitions are handled separately through rule-based maneuvers that assume known row geometry [4]. As a result, these methods do not support navigation to arbitrary goal positions and are limited to turning into the adjacent rows without row skipping or traversing to non-adjacent rows. In contrast, we unify these navigation behaviors through a single goal-conditioned policy which performs local planning driven by egocentric perception, as illustrated in Fig 1 (b).

The main contributions of this paper are:

We introduce FlowRow, a flow-matching policy trained entirely in simulation for long-horizon, goal-directed local planning in unknown, semi-structured agricultural environments. FlowRow requires no prior knowledge of environment geometry and supports in-row navigation, row turning, row skipping, and inter-row transitions.

We introduce FlowRow, a flow-matching policy trained entirely in simulation for long-horizon, goal-directed local planning in unknown, semi-structured agricultural environments. FlowRow requires no prior knowledge of environment geometry and supports in-row navigation, row turning, row skipping, and inter-row transitions.

We introduce RowNavBench, a simulation benchmark comprising 900 episodes across variations in row length, row spacing, row curvature, and vegetation conditions. We evaluate FlowRow on RowNavBench against depth-based local planning baselines, demonstrating over 40% higher success across the benchmark.

We evaluate FlowRow under localization errors against an oracle that tracks a pre-planned global reference path, and show that local planning with FlowRow is more robust to localization errors and results in fewer navigation failures. We further validate FlowRow with a real-world zero-shot deployment.

1. We introduce FlowRow, a flow-matching policy trained entirely in simulation for long-horizon, goal-directed local planning in unknown, semi-structured agricultural environments. FlowRow requires no prior knowledge of environment geometry and supports in-row navigation, row turning, row skipping, and inter-row transitions.

2. We introduce RowNavBench, a simulation benchmark comprising 900 episodes across variations in row length, row spacing, row curvature, and vegetation conditions. We evaluate FlowRow on RowNavBench against depth-based local planning baselines, demonstrating over 40% higher success across the benchmark.

3. We evaluate FlowRow under localization errors against an oracle that tracks a pre-planned global reference path, and show that local planning with FlowRow is more robust to localization errors and results in fewer navigation failures. We further validate FlowRow with a real-world zero-shot deployment.

title: Inverse Kinematics in Endoscopic Scenarios using MoveIt
authors: Marc Bestmann,Timon Engelke,Rebecca Rodeck,Gerko Wende
abstract:
Inverse kinematics are critical in many robotic applications, yet standard MoveIt-based solvers struggle in confined scenarios.
This paper provides a benchmark of the available solvers and compares multiple practical modifications for improving the performance of the solvers.
Splitting the IK problem into two parts results in the best performance, leading to a 100% success rate under 100 ms in an endoscopic tank scenario.
introduction:
Inverse kinematics is one of the most fundamental problems in robotics [1, p.29].
Over the decades, numerous algorithms utilizing analytical and numeric approaches have been proposed.
For most typical robotic setups, e.g. a robotic arm which grasps objects from a conveyor, one can choose from a set of proprietary and open-source solutions that will work reliably.
However, most of these approaches break if the environment in which the robot works becomes more confined.
This can be observed in endoscopic scenarios in which a robot enters through a small opening into a confined space.
While being a niche, these scenarios are of high importance in the field of maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) as well as in medicine [2].

In this paper, we investigate why current approaches fail in these scenarios and how usable results can be achieved.
We focus on open-source solutions for the widespread MoveIt2 framework [3] to make the results applicable for many users.

Our main contributions are:

Performance analysis of different approaches that improve MoveIt IK solvers in collision-rich environments

Adaption of RelaxedIK for MoveIt

Creation of an IK benchmarking software (EBIKE)

title: ROSE: A Shared Cross-Embodiment Facial-Motion Latent Space for Humanoid Robot Expression
authors: Yongji Fu,Man Cao,Yi Zhou,Fei Lin,Mark F. Hansen,Guanqun Cao
abstract: Natural, coherent full-face dynamic expressions are central to making humanoid robots socially approachable, yet existing systems commonly realize only limited lip motion or scripted expressions. The limitation is both physical and algorithmic. A compact head leaves little room for densely packed, independently controllable actuation; meanwhile, learned systems often generate an avatar video, landmarks, or facial parameters and then infer actuator commands through visual retargeting. This render-and-invert path adds latency and artifacts, and it does not reliably transfer generated behavior to a physical robot. We present ROSE (RObot facial expression through Shared motion Embeddings), a framework that integrates biomimetic hardware, cross-embodiment motion representation learning, and multimodal motion generation. On the hardware side, we build a flexible tendon-sheath transmission structure that integrates 34 actuators into a 19.5 cm biomimetic head. By decoupling actuator placement from facial action points, it enables coordinated full-face expression within a compact volume. On the algorithmic side, ROSE-VAE learns an identity-independent shared facial-motion latent space from human, digital-human, and robot observations. ROSE-Flow directly maps text, audio, or their combination to trajectories in this motion space without using video as a generator input. ROSE-Act then converts these trajectories into constrained actuator commands. Our system demonstrates how high-density biomimetic hardware and a shared executable facial-motion representation can jointly unify cross-embodiment learning, multimodal generation, and physical robot expression.
introduction:
Imagine a humanoid robot turning toward a visitor and answering a question about an exhibit. Its answer may be accurate and its voice natural, yet the interaction can still feel distant if its face remains largely still or moves out of sync with speech. In face-to-face communication, facial movements help people interpret not only what is said but also the speaker’s intent and engagement. Coordinating facial expression with speech and context is therefore an important part of making a humanoid robot feel socially present and approachable. [1, 2, 3].

Reproducing expressive facial motion requires coordinated actuation within a compact head. Previous robotic faces have explored pneumatic and motor-driven mechanisms coupled with compliant skin [4, 5]. These mechanisms provide the physical capacity for expression, but controlling them requires translating desired facial movements into actuator commands compatible with the robot’s mechanical constraints.

Existing approaches often address facial-motion generation and robot execution in separate stages. In the generation stage, audio-driven face animation methods produce visual or parametric outputs, including 3D meshes [6] and portrait videos [7]. In the execution stage, these outputs are translated into robot actuator commands, for example through visual self-modelling or retargeting of generated facial motion [8, 9]. These image- and parameter-based pipelines benefit from learned facial-motion priors, but connecting the two stages requires converting between representations. Image-based outputs must be analyzed to recover facial motion, while parametric outputs must be mapped to the target robot’s actuator configuration and motion limits. This motivates a shared facial-motion representation that connects human, digital-human, and robot observations with conditional motion generation and actuator control.

We therefore propose ROSE (RObot facial expression through Shared motion Embeddings), illustrated in Fig. 1. ROSE connects motion encoding, text- and audio-conditioned generation, and robot execution through a shared facial-motion latent space. Generated motion is mapped to constrained actuator commands without intermediate image reconstruction.
Our contributions are:

A shared facial-motion representation across embodiments. ROSE-VAE (variational autoencoder) factorizes identity and motion and learns a shared motion basis with orthogonality regularization across human, digital-human, and robot observations. Its motion coefficients provide a common representation for observation encoding, conditional generation, and actuator mapping.

Text- and audio-conditioned motion generation. ROSE-Flow combines text conditioning with frame-local audio attention in a dual-stream Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MMDiT). A staged training strategy with model merging unifies audio-to-motion, text-to-motion, and joint text–audio-to-motion generation.

Direct latent-to-actuator execution. ROSE-Act learns to translate shared motion latents into actuator states from paired robot images and actuator states, enabling execution without intermediate image reconstruction. We demonstrate this capability on a compact face robot.

A compact biomimetic face robot. We develop a face robot integrating 34 actuators through a flexible tendon-sheath transmission. By decoupling actuator placement from facial action points, the design supports coordinated full-face expression within a compact head.

title: TacBridge: Learning Unified Tactile Representations through Cross-Sensor Correspondence
authors: Yongji Fu,Yijiong Lin,Yi Zhou,Yi Qi,Guanqun Cao
abstract: Optical tactile sensors record tactile videos that capture local deformation and its temporal evolution during contact, supporting robot manipulation, force estimation, and tactile representation learning. Differences in imaging geometry, background appearance, illumination, resolution, and deformation response lead to sensor-dependent observations of the same contact across GelSight, DIGIT, GelSlim, TacTip, and other optical tactile sensors. This variability limits representation transfer and the joint use of multi-sensor data. We introduce TacBridge, a framework for learning unified representations from multi-sensor tactile videos through cross-sensor correspondence. Specifically, multi-sensor masked tactile-video pre-training learns spatiotemporal representations across sensors. We then train the same masked model jointly on same-sensor and cross-sensor reconstruction, using paired source and target videos of matched contact events. Experiments on cross-sensor translation and downstream perception demonstrate the cross-sensor generalization and task transferability of the learned tactile representations.
introduction:
Optical tactile sensors use embedded cameras to record local elastomer deformation during contact, providing robots with fine-grained tactile feedback. They have been widely used for object-property recognition, slip detection, force estimation, and contact-rich manipulation [1, 2, 3]. By capturing local contact details, this high-resolution tactile feedback complements external vision and conventional force sensing in tasks such as small-part localisation and insertion, grasp-outcome prediction, and cloth-texture recognition [4, 5, 6]. Different from a single tactile image, tactile videos further capture the temporal evolution of local deformation as contact is established, maintained, and released.

The growing diversity of tactile sensors has fragmented tactile data into sensor-specific domains. Sensors such as GelSight, DIGIT, and GelSlim differ in their optical layouts, elastomer materials, and illumination, shaping how they capture contact. Even for the same object, contact location, and motion trajectory, their tactile videos can exhibit markedly different appearances and deformation patterns. This variability makes it difficult to combine data across sensors and learn transferable tactile representations.
Recent sensor-invariant and multi-sensor representation learning has begun to reduce this fragmentation by embedding heterogeneous tactile observations into shared feature spaces [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12].

However, learning from multiple sensors does not by itself reveal which differences arise from the sensing device and which reflect changes in the underlying physical interaction. We argue that event-level cross-sensor correspondence can provide a more direct constraint. When different sensors observe the same contact event, their recordings may differ substantially in appearance and temporal response while sharing the same underlying interaction. Such paired observations explicitly link sensor-specific views, helping the model separate device-induced variation from shared contact content.

In this work, we use such event-level correspondence to learn tactile representations across different tactile sensors. Specifically, TacQuad provides synchronized real observations from DIGIT, GelSight Mini, and DuraGel [8], while ToucHD-Sim provides matched simulations of an interaction under nine optical sensor appearances [13]. In both datasets, paired tactile videos capture the same underlying interaction under different sensor conditions. This pairing grounds cross-sensor learning in a shared physical interaction, rather than relying on unpaired distribution-level alignment.

Building on these, we encode sensor identity as a switchable conditioning signal, allowing the same tactile interaction to be represented in different sensor domains. The spatiotemporal encoder is first pre-trained with masked autoencoding, then trained with event-level correspondence from TacQuad and ToucHD-Sim to separate sensor-specific variation from the underlying physical interaction. Finally, we evaluate the learned representation through controllable cross-sensor translation and downstream robotic tactile perception tasks.
Our contributions are:

We introduce a correspondence-based framework for learning unified tactile video representations from paired observations of matched contact events across heterogeneous optical tactile sensors.

We develop a latent translator that maps source tactile features to their target-sensor counterparts, reusing the learned encoder and decoder for controllable cross-sensor tactile video translation.

We demonstrate that the learned representation transfers effectively to downstream robotic tactile perception tasks and generalises to new tactile data, achieving strong performance with a frozen encoder and lightweight prediction heads.

title: Transferable Neural CBFs via Generalized Closure
authors: Nishant Jayesh Bhave,Parthib Khound
comment: . Submitted to the 2027 American Control Conference (ACC 2027)
abstract:
Classical control barrier functions (CBFs) provide safety constraints for controllers, but designing
them by hand is difficult for underactuated vehicles and the resulting safe sets can be overly
conservative. Neural CBFs can learn more informative barriers from data, yet a learned barrier is
usually verified only for one fixed obstacle configuration. We study whether one neural barrier can
be reused across environments by expressing the state relative to each obstacle. The key gap is that
these relative coordinates may discard information needed to predict their own evolution. We give a
generalized closure condition that represents this missing information as a residual and a lifting
theorem that transfers a verified relative-coordinate barrier to every obstacle in a family. A rank
test also identifies when symmetry alone cannot justify the transfer. We validate the conditions on
a double integrator, a planar aircraft, and a 12-state quadrotor. Coordinates that fail the test
lead to obstacle penetration or to a barrier condition that fails near hover, whereas body-frame
coordinates close exactly for the quadrotor. The resulting barrier transfers to new maps without
retraining and is effective in the reported deployment and fast-start experiments.
introduction:
Control barrier functions (CBFs) turn a safety specification into a constraint on the input that a
quadratic program enforces online [1], and the same program can filter the
output of any nominal controller [2]. The barrier
itself must be constructed, and that is the bottleneck. For systems with bounded inputs in which the
input reaches the obstacle constraint only after several integrations, high-order CBFs
[3] give a systematic construction, but the designer chooses the function and its
gains, and nothing guarantees that the resulting constraint can be met within the input bounds. On
underactuated vehicles, whose ability to stop depends on attitude and rates as well as on distance
and velocity, such a barrier is hard to make both valid and informative. Hamilton–Jacobi reachability computes the
largest safe set, the viability kernel [4], on a grid, at a cost
exponential in the state dimension [5], and learned value functions extend it to higher dimension for a fixed environment and without
formal guarantees [6].

A third approach is to learn the barrier from its defining inequalities [7]. A
learned function is a certificate only if those inequalities hold, and a growing line of work verifies
learned barriers formally
[8, 9, 10, 11]. In each of these works, the
verified object is one barrier for one fixed environment, verified in full-state coordinates, so that
any change of the environment requires retraining and reverification.

Shared and compositional constructions remove the dependence on the environment. A shared network is
evaluated on the local configuration of each agent [12, 13], or
one network h1h_{1} is trained in coordinates relative to a single obstacle, evaluated once for each
obstacle of a map, and combined by a smooth minimum [14] or, as here, by one
constraint per obstacle. The object to verify then lives on
the relative coordinates of one obstacle, whatever the number and placement of the obstacles. Such
networks transfer across maps in practice, but none of these constructions is formally verified, so
the transfer rests on conditions that are never checked for the learned function. Equivariance results evaluate the barrier at a transformed full state, so no information is
lost [15], but coordinates chosen for learning often discard information on
which the dynamics depend.

This paper states when the per-obstacle construction is valid. For the barrier condition to transfer,
the relative coordinates must
determine their own time derivative, up to a residual whose range they determine, and then a barrier
condition on h1h_{1} that holds on a compact set of relative coordinates holds for every obstacle in
every map. A rank test shows in advance when symmetry alone cannot guarantee this. Coordinates that
fail it penetrate obstacles on a planar aircraft and fail the condition near hover on a 12-state
quadrotor. Body-frame coordinates pass it, and the barrier learned in them is deployed on new maps
without retraining. We check the hypotheses on sampled boxes and states, so the result is a
statistical estimate of where they hold, not a proof over the whole domain, and the deployed
controller adds discrete-time safeguards that the theory does not cover. The contributions are the
following:

Generalized closure and a lifting theorem: a per-obstacle barrier condition that holds on a
compact set of relative coordinates holds for every obstacle in every map, and if one input meets all
obstacle constraints the state stays safe until it leaves the lifted domain, with the missing
information made explicit as a residual (Theorem 5,
Corollary 6).

A rank condition, comparing the rank of the coordinates with N=n+p−dimGN=n+p-\dim G, that is necessary for symmetry to guarantee closure and can be checked before training, and explicit residual sets for three systems
(Proposition 8, Table I).

Body-frame relative coordinates that close exactly for the full 12-state quadrotor, and a barrier
learned in them, checked at sampled states, and deployed without retraining on maps not seen in
training
(Proposition 14, Section VII).

title: Driving the Style: Velocity-Conditioned Whole-Body Control from Motion Demonstrations
authors: Murad Dawood,Oezge Drama Berkenkamp,Antonio Gonzales Marin,Nutan Chen
abstract:
Achieving human-like behavior on humanoid robots has advanced rapidly by leveraging motion-capture demonstrations rather than hand-crafted cost functions.
Adversarial imitation supplies a style signal that lets a policy fulfill a task while adhering to a desired style, but is difficult to transfer to hardware. Whole-body tracking through reinforcement learning instead deploys reliably and imitates demonstrations faithfully, but the resulting policies are conditioned on the future reference, so they require a reference trajectory at runtime and can fail when the motion differs from the training data.
We train a humanoid policy directly with whole-body tracking rewards while restricting its actor to compact locomotion commands and robot observations. Reference motion supervises the reward and privileged critic, without supplying reference joint trajectories to the actor or requiring teacher distillation. The demonstrated style is thereby encoded in the policy through the tracking reward, so the robot reproduces the whole-body style under commanded velocities.
Trained on a single random-walk motion and commanded with velocity profiles from held-out motions, our policy reaches at least 98% success in simulation and completes every trial on the Unitree G1. On held-out slow walking, whole-body tracking drops to 2% success and command-conditioned distillation to 56%, and both fail on the real robot. On the trained motions, the joint position error of our policy stays within 8% of whole-body tracking, and it has a higher style coverage than adversarial motion priors (AMP), which fell on the real robot without a safety crane.
introduction:
Humanoid robots have shown the ability to successfully perform a variety of tasks by imitating human motions [1, 2]. This has motivated the capture and generation of extensive motion datasets through motion-capture systems [3, 4, 5]. However, these datasets do not account for the physical constraints of the robot, such as its kinematic and dynamic limits [6]. As a result, imitating the datasets directly through supervised learning yields policies that fail to execute reliably on the robot. Reinforcement learning (RL), on the other hand, is able to learn locomotion policies through exploration that exploits the robot’s own dynamics and kinematics [7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. This has made RL a promising approach for learning stylized locomotion behaviors from motion references [12, 13, 14].

Existing pipelines for learning stylized locomotion follow one of three strategies. Adversarial training provides the RL agent with a reward signal about the style [12, 15, 16, 17]. Whole-body tracking instead combines multiple rewards to imitate the reference motion by tracking joint positions, joint velocities, and the positions and velocities of key body links [6, 13, 18, 14]. A third strategy distills a privileged, reference-conditioned teacher into a student that observes only deployable inputs together with a history of past observations [19]. Each of them has a cost in reliability, in controllability, or in how the policy is trained.

Adversarial approaches have seen great success in computer graphics [12, 16]: beyond imitating a style, they allow the policy to be driven at runtime without a reference trajectory. However, their deployment to the real world is challenging because of the weighting between the style reward and the task reward. Emphasizing the style can lead to unsuccessful deployment on the real robot (e.g. jittery motions and stumbling), while emphasizing the task reward enables successful deployment at the cost of weaker style imitation. Whole-body tracking, on the other hand, can deploy reliably on real robots while imitating the reference motion to a great extent. However, these policies are conditioned on the future reference of joint positions and velocities, so they require the reference trajectory at runtime and the whole-body motion must come from a recorded clip. Command-conditioned distillation can give the student a low-dimensional command interface, but the student learns by imitating the actions of a reference-conditioned teacher rather than from the task reward, so its behavior is limited by what the teacher does.

To close this gap, we present a velocity-conditioned whole-body controller that deploys reliably and can be steered at runtime, without distillation from a privileged teacher. We train a tracking policy with an asymmetric actor-critic: the critic observes the full reference motion, while the actor observes only proprioception, the anchor orientation error, and a planar base velocity command. The demonstrated style is thereby encoded in the policy through the tracking reward, so the robot reproduces the whole-body style under a commanded velocity (Fig. 1). Our key observation is that different locomotion motions often share the base velocities of the training motion while their joint trajectories differ: forward walking, sidesteps, and turning all reduce to base-level goals. A policy conditioned on the velocity command, and not on the reference joints, is therefore less dependent on the joint trajectories of the training clip and can transfer to such motions. At deployment, its inputs can be computed from the base trajectory of a motion clip or, without a clip, from a gamepad. In our experiments, we drive it with velocity profiles from held-out motion clips, so that tracking and style can be measured against ground truth. We compare our approach with all baselines on the Unitree G1, in simulation and on real hardware..

In summary, our contributions are:

A velocity-conditioned whole-body tracking policy, trained directly with RL and an asymmetric actor-critic, whose actor observes only proprioception, the anchor orientation error, and a planar velocity command, without distillation from a privileged teacher.

Simulation and hardware results. Trained on a random walk and commanded with the velocity profiles of three held-out motions, our policy reaches at least 98% success in simulation and completes every hardware trial, while whole-body tracking and command-conditioned distillation fail on slow walking. Compared with AMP, our policy runs on the real robot without support, while AMP fell in both attempts without a safety crane, and it tracks the reference more closely with a higher style coverage. On the trained motions, its mean joint position error stays within about 8%8\% of the reference-conditioned tracker.

An analysis of the policy inputs, showing that 87 to 100% of the held-out velocity commands lie close to the training data, compared with 19 to 87% of the reference joint frames, together with ablations on mirrored data, symmetry training, and smoothed, gamepad-like motions.

Compared with AMP, our policy runs on the real robot without support, while AMP fell in both attempts without a safety crane, and it tracks the reference more closely with a higher style coverage. title: QTOP: Scaling Humanoid Motion Tracking with Quantile Critics
authors: Markus Peschl,Dana Kianfar,Daniel Dijkman
abstract: Learning human motion tracking policies through reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a core capability that underpins a majority of recent progress in humanoid whole-body control. However, achieving generalization to unseen motions at high fidelity requires jointly scaling training to thousands of GPU and dataset hours. This work hypothesizes that motion tracking is inherently compute-bound because training on a diverse set of motions introduces learning interference, similar to multi-task RL. To tackle this, we propose Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP), which improves sample efficiency by introducing a distributional advantage estimate conditioned on state and reference pairs. QTOP outperforms on and off-policy RL baselines both in simulation and real-world tracking scenarios on multiple datasets by up to 10%. Furthermore, we establish a scaling law for QTOP and find that, aside from scaling predictably, dataset size has minimal impact on performance for moderately sized GPU hour regimes.
introduction:
Humanoid motion tracking aims to learn policies conditioned on reference motions, allowing humanoid robots to generate motor commands that faithfully reproduce diverse behaviors in real time. Over the past few years, motion tracking has rapidly evolved from learning individual skills [1, 2] to training generalist policies on thousands of motions [3, 4, 5, 6] with remarkable results on real robot hardware. A key enabler of modern trackers is the utilization of human motion datasets as a rich source of behavioral supervision as well as massively parallelized RL in simulation to converge to a stable and general controller.

As a result, the central challenge is no longer learning individual motions, but optimizing a single policy over a heterogeneous collection of tracking tasks. While the desired behavior is explicitly specified through reference frames at high frequency, different motions can induce distinct state visitation and return distributions, making optimization challenging [7]. Conventional RL algorithms, such as PPO, typically aggregate these diverse learning signals through a single scalar value function, which can lead to overly conservative policies [8]. The resulting tracking errors, although often small, can accumulate over the course of a rollout and become particularly detrimental for loco-manipulation tasks, where accurate global position, orientation and timing are required to grasp objects with high dexterity.

A common strategy to eliminate such tracking errors is to scale both motion datasets and simulation throughput [4, 6, 9]. Larger datasets expose policies to a broader range of behaviors, while increased compute enables faster convergence to robust imitation. This scaling recipe has proven highly effective, but it requires substantial compute resources of over 10410^{4} GPU hours, which is out of reach for most robotics researchers. Secondly, it does not address whether additional data and compute contributes equally to performance. We hypothesize in this work that general motion tracking is inherently multi-task, which makes the task compute-bound even at small dataset scales. To address this, we introduce Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP), a PPO-based training recipe for large-scale humanoid motion tracking that combines Muon optimization with a distributional value critic. Instead of assigning credit using only a scalar return residual, QTOP estimates the return distribution conditioned on each observation-reference pair and reinforces rollouts according to how favorable their realized returns are relative to this local distribution. This converts tracking difficulty across motions and contact regimes into a calibrated advantage signal, enabling more effective policy improvement.

Using QTOP, we study how motion-tracking performance scales jointly with training compute and motion-dataset size. We construct nested subsets of the same motion corpus for multiple seeds and train policies over a grid of dataset sizes and optimization budgets, allowing us to separate the marginal benefit of reference data from additional RL compute. Across the low-to-moderate data regime considered in our experiments, we find that increasing the dataset size improves performance only when paired with sufficient compute, while additional training compute remains the dominant bottleneck. Together with existing results at substantially larger data scales [6], our findings suggest that an important understudied direction is not only how to collect larger motion corpora, but how to design learning algorithms that can effectively exploit them.

Finally, we evaluate QTOP against strong PPO baselines and representative off-policy alternatives on both academic held-out tracking benchmarks and our own motion capture dataset. QTOP consistently achieves the best tracking performance and transfers to improved real-world tracking on a Unitree G1 under a fixed data and training budget. This points to learning algorithms that can more effectively exploit large reference-conditioned motion datasets as an important direction for future research.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

We identify multitask optimization as a central bottleneck in large-scale humanoid motion tracking.

We introduce QTOP, combining PPO, Muon optimization and a custom distributional critic for advantage estimation using return quantiles for scalable training.

We characterize the joint scaling of tracking performance with dataset size and compute. We show that QTOP continues to benefit from additional compute, whereas increasing dataset size yields comparatively smaller gains in practical regimes.

We find that QTOP consistently outperforms well tuned on- and off-policy RL methods on held-out datasets.

3. We characterize the joint scaling of tracking performance with dataset size and compute. We show that QTOP continues to benefit from additional compute, whereas increasing dataset size yields comparatively smaller gains in practical regimes.

4. We find that QTOP consistently outperforms well tuned on- and off-policy RL methods on held-out datasets.
