title: Non-Imaging Optical Tactile Sensors for Robotics: Transduction Principles, System Integration, and Robotic Applications
authors: Hao Wu,Yu Feng,Haotian Guo,Huichan Zhao,Changsheng Wu,Jianshu Zhou
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
During contact, robots sense contact loads and object motion to guide their actions. When grasping fragile objects, grip force must be regulated to maintain a stable grasp without excessive compression. When an object begins to slip, the robot must correct its action promptly [1, 2]. When exploring soft tissues or compliant materials, their mechanical responses must be assessed by considering both the applied load and the indentation process. Bending of soft fingers can also affect sensor outputs, making it necessary to distinguish external contact from self-deformation for accurate interpretation of tactile signals. These requirements have driven the development of tactile devices for robotic end effectors [3, 4, 5, 6, 7], and they broaden as dexterous hands and soft grippers take on more varied contact tasks [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16].

Tactile sensors acquire contact signals through different transduction mechanisms and readout methods. Common sensing principles for soft robotic tactile skins include resistive, capacitive, magnetic, pneumatic and optical transduction [17]. Electronic skins for prosthetics have pursued mechanical durability, stretchability, biodegradability and the sensing of diverse stimuli over large areas [18, 19]. Capacitive sensors generate capacitance signals through changes in electrode spacing, effective area or dielectric properties, whereas resistive sensors convert deformation into resistance signals through changes in conductive pathways or contact resistance [20, 21, 22, 23, 24]. Multimodal electrical sensors read different stimuli separately through decoupled sensing mechanisms or structural arrangements [25, 26, 27]. Magnetic tactile sensing uses deformation of a magnetic elastomer or displacement of an embedded magnet to alter the local magnetic field, which is then measured by a magnetic field detector [28, 29, 30, 31].

Optical tactile sensing converts contact into changes in light propagation or emission [3, 32]. In vision-based tactile sensing, a camera records contact-layer topography or marker displacement, from which tactile information is reconstructed using images [33, 34, 35]. Such sensors can be grouped into marker-based and intensity-based transduction [36], and an open-source family of dual-material 3D-printed skins tracks internal pins with a camera [37]. Camera readout gives these sensors high spatial resolution, but the hardware can be bulky compared with thin-film sensors, and the response speed is generally limited by the camera frame rate, mostly 30–90 frames/s, and by the computation of the tactile model [36]. Photodetector arrays used in place of cameras resolve only several millimeters but sample at 1 kHz or more [36]. This review focuses on non-imaging optical tactile sensing, which acquires contact information by measuring optical intensity, wavelength, spectra or the temporal characteristics of light emission (Figure 1) [3, 38, 39]. Vision-based tactile sensing that uses images of the contact surface as tactile input falls outside the scope of this review. Line-scan cameras that sample fixed waveguide output ports and cameras used solely for calibration do not acquire images of the contact surface and are therefore classified as non-imaging readout, whereas charge-coupled device (CCD) prototypes that image the fingertip contact surface are excluded [40, 41, 42].

Optical tactile sensing allows contact structures and signal readout locations to be designed separately according to installation requirements. Optical fibers connect sensitive regions to light sources and detectors, allowing some electronic components to be located away from the contact area [43]. Soft waveguides and flexibly encapsulated optical fibers can be arranged along fingers or curved skins to transmit optical signals while accommodating surface deformation, making them suitable for compliant fingers, underwater contact and remote detection [3, 4, 44]. Optical-fiber transmission sections convey contact information through optical signals rather than conductive currents, enabling electrical isolation and reducing the influence of electromagnetic interference on signal transmission. For distributed suction cups or local interaction, discrete emitters, photodetectors and integrated optoelectronic chips can also form local readout units, allowing the sensing layout to accommodate the robot’s installation space and contact requirements [45, 46].

Optical encoding also provides different means of observation for multipoint and multiparameter sensing. Multiple fiber Bragg gratings can be wavelength-division multiplexed along a single fiber, connecting several sensitive regions through one transmission path. Changes in the color and optical intensity of soft lightguides can encode deformation locations, and distinct resonance responses can distinguish contact force from temperature [38, 47, 48]. These observables can support tactile coverage, differentiation between self-deformation and external contact, and multivariable feedback.

Optical tactile sensing has developed along imaging and non-imaging routes for about four decades (Figure 2). In the 1980s, two lines developed in parallel. One imaged the contact: frustrated total internal reflection at a light-conducting plate or waveguide formed a contact imprint that a solid-state camera digitized [49, 50], and coherent fiber bundles carried light reflected from a deformable skin to a television camera [51]. This line later led to retrographic sensing with a reflective elastomer skin [52] and to the vision-based sensors outside the scope of this review. The other line read light intensity element by element. A stacked light-emitting diode (LED) matrix, photodetector matrix and pressure-receiving layer formed a 15 × 15 array with 2 mm pitch [53]. Fibers arranged in four overlapping layers served both as microbend force sensors and as signal paths [54]. In a modular sensor for a multifingered hand, the unit was a cantilever that reflected light from an emitting fiber into a receiving fiber [55]. Miniaturization followed. A finger-shaped waveguide first read with a CCD camera [56] was converted to a position-sensitive detector that outputs the centroid of the scattered light [42], and a surface-emitting laser fed back by an external mirror served as both light source and interferometer [57]. In the 2000s, a single LED matrix acted as both emitter and detector [58], modules of photo-reflectors under urethane foam covered the curved surfaces of a humanoid robot [59], and fiber Bragg grating arrays and gratings embedded in robot end effectors introduced wavelength encoding [38, 60]. Prismatic-tip fiber arrays for dexterous hands, transparent and polymer-waveguide skins, and soft waveguides in prosthetic and deep-sea fingers then brought the approach to compliant robots [61, 62, 63, 3, 44]. Since 2019, three-dimensional lightguide lattices, pillar arrays read by quadrant photodiodes, color-encoded stretchable lightguides, Ruffini-type grating skins, micro/nanofiber multi-axis sensors, mechanoluminescent fibers and an octopus-inspired soft arm have extended the readout to networks, spectra and emitted light [64, 40, 47, 4, 65, 39, 45].

Existing reviews have discussed the role of touch in manipulation from the perspectives of tactile integration in dexterous hands, the hierarchy of tactile information from raw signals to contact, object and action levels, and trends in robotic manipulation [66, 67, 68]. Early surveys already listed optical transduction among tactile sensing principles [69, 70], with freedom from electrical interference and easy separation of the sensor from its processing electronics as its attractions [69]. Reviews specific to fiber-optic tactile sensing have since covered modulation mechanisms, flexible packaging, array integration and intelligent algorithms [71], as well as principles, fabrication and data processing [72]. Others address sensors based on fiber Bragg gratings, micro/nanofibers, specklegrams and Fabry–Pérot interferometers [73], and micro/nanofiber tactile sensors together with soft actuators [74].

This review organizes non-imaging optical tactile sensing around a central question: how can contact states be encoded into optical observations, reliably inferred under changing conditions, and used to guide robotic action? We connect mechanical load transmission, optical encoding, readout architecture and tactile inference to examine this question across device families ranging from reflective and waveguide-based sensors to fiber gratings, interferometric structures and mechanoluminescent devices [38, 39, 54, 64]. The framework emphasizes three considerations: the identifiability of contact variables, the system-level constraints on spatial coverage and feedback timing, and the evidence connecting tactile measurements to robotic task outcomes. These considerations guide the analysis of transduction principles and device design, system integration, information decoupling and reconstruction, performance characteristics and robotic applications, and provide a basis for identifying priorities for practical deployment. Figure 1 provides an overview of the transduction mechanisms and robotic applications examined within this framework.

title: Selective Sensor Acquisition for Multimodal Place Recognition
authors: Margaux Edwards,Tobias Fischer,Michael Milford
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Multimodal Place Recognition (PR) can improve robustness, but most systems rigidly read and process every sensor for every query, even when the primary sensor is sufficient, with implications for energy consumption, second sensor update rate, and domain-specific considerations such as passive stealth. We introduce selective, controllable sensor acquisition, where a user specifies a desired second sensor usage rate and the system acquires the additional sensor only when the primary sensor’s estimated performance is sufficiently poor. An online threshold adjustment achieves the requested usage rate by adapting to recent primary sensor performance, directing additional sensing towards queries where fusion is most likely to help without calibration specific to sensor modality, PR method, or environment. The approach requires only a PR method that produces a match score and applies to both single-frame and sequence-based PR. Our system, across multiple datasets, PR descriptors, and sensor combinations, recovers 55% of the available PR performance gain while using the second sensor on only 25% of queries, and 81% while using it on 50%. We further analyse alternative acquisition decision mechanisms and usage-rate control methods, and examine performance when the second sensor is stronger than, comparable to, or weaker than the primary sensor.
introduction:
Place recognition (PR) can benefit from both introspective methods that estimate whether a recognition result should be trusted, and multimodal approaches that combine information from multiple sensors [1, 2, 3]. Introspective methods typically assess the performance of a primary sensor [4, 5], while multimodal PR improves robustness by fusing complementary sensor information [6]. However, existing fusion approaches generally assume that observations from all required sensors have already been acquired and processed, with many learned architectures explicitly requiring paired or synchronised inputs [7, 8, 9]. Consequently, all sensors must be polled, encoded, and matched even when additional sensing contributes little to the final recognition result. This can be undesirable in deployed systems subject to constraints on energy, computation, or sensor utilisation [1, 10, 11, 2].

In this work, we instead treat multimodal PR as a selective acquisition problem: information from a secondary sensor is acquired and processed only when the estimated performance of the primary sensor indicates that it is needed. We additionally allow the user to specify a desired duty, defined as the fraction of queries for which the secondary sensor is used. Our method dynamically adapts the acquisition threshold from recent primary sensor performance estimates to achieve this requested duty. This concentrates additional sensing on queries for which fusion is most likely to be beneficial, without requiring separately calibrated thresholds for different sensor modalities, PR methods, or environments.

In particular, we make the following contributions:

Selective acquisition from primary sensor’s estimated performance:
We formulate multimodal PR as a selective acquisition problem and introduce a gate, based on per-query estimated primary sensor performance that decides whether to process a second sensor observation before it is polled, encoded or matched.
We evaluate the gate with single-frame and sequence-based PR, comparing recognition accuracy against state-of-the-art acquisition methods [4, 12], primary sensor introspection methods [13], and randomly selecting the second sensor at matched sensor use.

A user-specified duty rate for a second sensor:
We propose a recent-history-based method for dynamically adjusting primary sensor match acceptance threshold to achieve a desired overall utilisation duty for the second sensor.

title: AVD: A Multi-Sensor Teleoperated Wheelchair Platform with Safety-Aware Control
authors: Namai Chandra,Madhur Thareja,Boby George
abstract:
Electric wheelchairs predominantly rely on manual joystick interfaces,
which present critical barriers to independent mobility for individuals
with severe motor and visual impairments. This paper presents AVD
(Autonomous Vehicle Drive), a dependable teleoperation
architecture for assistive mobility that unifies perception,
communication, embedded control, and remote supervision in a single
low-cost platform built entirely from commercially available hardware.
The central engineering contribution is a safety-oriented design
framework: control authority follows a static hierarchy, a manual
emergency stop and the occupant’s joystick pre-empt remote commands,
and the on-board sensing layer has stop-only authority. The
compute design partitions primary and safety functions and specifies a
heartbeat-driven safe-state transition for the fault cases considered.
The sensing stack this framework depends on is characterized against
measured data: per-channel acquisition latency, a 2 025-scan LiDAR
degradation campaign spanning five target configurations and a control under water
mist, airborne dust, and direct aperture occlusion, and attitude
measurements across static inclines to 47∘47^{\circ}. The lowest pooled
environmental-condition mean retained 76.6% of the clear-baseline
forward-sector yield, and no scan lost the sector completely. A logged
vibration-induced inertial dropout occurred while LiDAR and camera
logging continued, illustrating complementary channel behavior. The
result is a documented prototype and an explicit validation path for
a deployable wheelchair implementation.
introduction:
Mobility is a prerequisite for social participation,
economic inclusion, and quality of life. Approximately 80 million
people worldwide require a wheelchair, while access is estimated at
only 5–35% depending on the country [1]. Among those who do own powered
wheelchairs, the dominant paradigm remains a manual proportional
joystick, a modality inaccessible to individuals with quadriplegia,
severe tremors, or profound visual impairment. Simpson
[2] identified four unmet needs in powered wheelchair
technology: safe navigation in dynamic environments, environmental
awareness, adaptability to residual motor capacity, and affordability.
Two decades later these gaps remain largely unaddressed in
commercially available devices [3]. Academic smart
wheelchair research has produced sophisticated navigation systems
[4, 5], but the distance between laboratory
prototype and deployable product is rarely bridged [6, 7], in part because of cost, system complexity, and
limited public implementation detail.

Research responses cluster into two groups. The first replaces the
joystick with an alternative input modality; the second pursues
on-board autonomy through SLAM, path planning, and obstacle avoidance,
which demands expensive sensing, dedicated computing, and controlled
environments (Section II). AVD takes a third position.
It treats the remote human as the navigator and asks a narrower
engineering question: what architecture and responses are needed to
drive the vehicle toward a safe state under the fault cases considered?
Fig. 1 shows
the resulting architecture, and Section III develops the
two commitments that follow from the question: stop-only authority for
the on-board sensing layer, and a compute partition that keeps the
element responsible for safety separate from the element most likely
to fail.

A dependable teleoperation architecture for assistive
mobility, integrating perception, communication, embedded control, and
remote supervision in one system intended for operation in real
environments.

A dependable teleoperation architecture for assistive
mobility, integrating perception, communication, embedded control, and
remote supervision in one system intended for operation in real
environments.

A fault-tolerant safety framework employing
hierarchical control authority, watchdog monitoring, communication
supervision, and fail-safe state transitions, with an explicit
response and validation status for the single-fault cases considered
(Section III-C, Table II).

An experimental characterization methodology for the
sensing stack such a platform depends on, applied here through
controlled laboratory validation: per-channel acquisition latency, a
2 025-scan degradation campaign, and attitude characterization to
47∘47^{\circ} (Section IV). Kilometre-scale field
deployment is the next milestone and is not claimed here.

A modular, low-cost prototype on commercially available
hardware, with public sensor-interface software that supports
reproduction and extension toward shared autonomy and remote assistive
care.

title: ACiT: Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers
authors: Haixiang Wu,Zhihao Guan,Yang Yang
abstract: Visuomotor policies condition action prediction on visual and proprioceptive observations. While historical proprioceptive sequences carry rich dynamic priors, current methods treat them as equal to high-dimensional vision, causing the proprioceptive signal to be overwhelmed. To identify what is lost in equal-conditioning fusion, we analyze proprioceptive data and find that strong inter-joint coupling is the key action-determining structure. This finding aligns with the neural sensorimotor loop, in which proprioception first forms a body-centered prior and vision is later calibrated via parietal remapping. Inspired by this, we propose ACiT, Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers, which reinforces historical joint-coupling as the primary condition with vision as a later calibration. This design is instantiated through three modules: Inverted State Encoding builds a proprioceptive prior via per-joint tokens and inter-joint self-attention. State-Visual Grounding lets joint tokens query visual evidence, making vision goal- and calibration-only. Inverted Action Chunking decodes per-joint trajectories independently. ACiT improves success rates on most LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, with the largest gains on those that require dynamics and coordination. The same conditioning design transferred to the VLA backbone π0\pi_{0}-ACiT yields significant gains with better execution efficiency.
introduction:
Visuomotor policies predict actions from multi-view observations and
proprioception. Early work conditioned on a single current state, where ACT maps
the current joint state and images to an action chunk [41]. Diffusion
Policy conditions on a short observation history instead [8]. A single frame proved insufficient to resolve action ambiguity, while
history carries dynamics and hidden-state information, so proprioceptive history
was explicitly incorporated. Recent models such as A2A and Chronos explicitly model proprioceptive history [12, 42].
Another line discretizes historical states or actions into tokens to better
integrate with LLM backbones, at the cost of losing continuous coupling
structure [28, 22, 14]. Reconstruction-only tokenization can also
erode control-relevant information [16]. These works validate the value
of using history from both continuous and discrete directions, and state history
is becoming a consensus for action prediction.

These advances have not converged at the conditioning interface. First,
mainstream methods map historical proprioceptive states as an independent
modality, either discretely or continuously, and place them alongside a pooled
global visual vector as conditions for action generation. This naive fusion lets
high-dimensional, low-SNR visual features entangle and dominate the conditioning,
leading to degraded robustness or spurious
shortcuts [15, 38]. Second, we analyze the state history and the
action itself: the effective dimensionality of the action distribution is far
below the number of joints, and joints are strongly coupled,
as shown in Fig. 1(a)(a). However, existing
methods model temporal dependencies and pack all joints into one vector, so the
inter-joint coupling, a structure critical to action, can only be implicit
inside the token.

Therefore, how to encode historical state information, how to fuse modalities,
and how to feed the result into action decoding is an open problem. Inspired by
neuroscience, the human chain from peripheral proprioception to body-centered
action generation is as follows (Fig. 1(b)(b)): muscle and joint receptors
continuously encode joint angle, velocity, and tension and project through
large-diameter myelinated afferents [29, 36].
The somatosensory cortex and posterior parietal cortex aggregate proprioceptive
history into a body-state representation, forming a body-centered
prior [2, 1]. The posterior parietal
cortex then remaps visual goals from retinal coordinates into
body-centered coordinates, with proprioceptive context modulating this
remapping [2, 10]. Finally, the
parietal-motor pathway sends the calibrated body-centered representation to
action generation [37, 23]. The key
computational asymmetry is that proprioception provides a continuous,
low-latency body-state stream, whereas visual goals are remapped and integrated
into the body-centered representation afterward.

We map this sensorimotor loop to Bayesian cue integration: the fast, continuous
proprioceptive stream forms a prior over the body state, visual goals provide
goal evidence (a likelihood-like term), and calibrating the prior yields a
posterior-like body-centered representation for action generation. Based on
this, we propose ACiT on top of ACT, the smallest architecture that still
carries the full interface (multi-view images, proprioception, and a chunked
action decoder), so that the encoder and the head stay fixed while only the
conditioning changes. It has three modules. First, Inverted State
Encoding compresses each joint’s entire history into a token and directly
models inter-joint coupling with self-attention. Second, State-Visual
Grounding treats vision as a per-joint goal-calibration signal and does not let
it directly enter the encoder. Third, Inverted Action Chunking treats
each joint as a token on the action side, and each joint independently generates
its complete trajectory chunk. The decoder does not need to translate between
“visual coordinates” and “joint coordinates”. The historical proprioceptive
sequence and action generation share a more consistent feature space.
To separate the interface from the backbone, we port the same conditioning to a
pretrained VLA and obtain π0\pi_{0}-ACiT, which keeps π0\pi_{0}’s architecture and changes
only how the state enters it.
Experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks show that
ACiT and π0\pi_{0}-ACiT improve success on most tasks, with improved robustness
under visual perturbations, especially on tasks that depend on dynamics and
joint coordination.

Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate the conditioning interface as Bayesian sensorimotor cue integration, with history as the prior and vision as the calibration evidence, and realize it as an explicit asymmetric fusion.

We propose ACiT, which uses three inverted Transformer modules to

We validate ACiT on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, where it

title: TaF-Foundation: Wrench-Grounded Cross-Sensor Tactile Representations
authors: Jiaming Jiang,Yuzhe Huang,Baokun Yang,Hao Liang,Li Gao,Haoran Guo,Pei Lin,Shengcheng Luo,Chenxi Xiao,Wanlin Li,Ziyuan Jiao
comment: including supplementary material
abstract: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich manipulation, yet heterogeneous sensing mechanisms and observation formats hinder cross-hardware transfer. Since physical contact is governed by Newtonian mechanics, we ground tactile representations in six-dimensional wrenches, establishing a common physical reference across sensing mechanisms. Specifically, we pair tactile observations from all sensors with wrench measurements, enabling shared physical supervision without requiring direct tactile-to-tactile pairing between sensors. To support learning at scale, we develop a dedicated acquisition platform and collect over 100 million paired tactile observations and wrench measurements from 24 sensors spanning four families of sensing principles. Building on this dataset, our framework combines sensor-specific input adaptation with a shared tactile encoder. By learning to reconstruct wrenches, the encoder maps observations from different sensors into a shared, continuous feature space grounded in contact physics. To leverage these representations for manipulation, we introduce TaF-Policy, which integrates tactile features with visual observations and robot states to generate action chunks. We evaluate the learned representations through wrench estimation, cross-sensor retrieval, few-shot adaptation to unseen sensors, and robotic manipulation. On the core benchmark, our method reduces single-frame force RMSE by 17.1 % and improves cross-sensor retrieval R@1 by 13.11 percentage points over the strongest baseline. In manipulation experiments, TaF-Policy achieves average success rates of 51.33% across three simulated tasks and 46.25% across four real-world tasks, compared with 47.33% and 23.75%, respectively, for the strongest baselines evaluated on the same task sets. Project page: https://mrjiangjm.github.io/TaF-Foundation/.
introduction:
Reliable manipulation requires robots to understand both what they see and how they physically interact with the world [3]. Vision provides rich information about objects and scenes, but contact states are often difficult to infer from visual appearance alone [25, 19]. Tactile sensing therefore complements vision by capturing physical interactions, making it particularly valuable for contact-rich manipulation [22, 38, 37]. However, tactile sensors rely on heterogeneous sensing mechanisms and produce contact responses in different formats [33, 1, 12, 21, 29, 11]. This heterogeneity makes it difficult to integrate and reuse tactile data across sensors and tasks, limiting the scalability of tactile representation learning.

To improve the scalability and reusability of tactile representations, recent work has explored several representation learning strategies. Self-supervised learning with shared architectures provides a common framework for learning reusable features across tactile observations [10, 35]. To explicitly address sensor heterogeneity, cross-sensor alignment methods learn shared features from paired tactile observations collected under matched contact conditions [2, 28]. More recently, several pioneering works have explored grounding tactile representations in physical contact properties, particularly force-related information [5, 7, 15]. Despite this progress, existing approaches remain limited in sensor diversity and scale, leaving generalization to heterogeneous and unseen sensor hardware insufficiently explored. Moreover, independently collected tactile datasets lack a shared physical reference for comparing contact states across sensors, making it difficult to establish a physically meaningful metric space for representation learning. Therefore, we study an unanswered question: can large-scale supervision from directly measured physical quantities enable tactile representations to generalize across heterogeneous sensors, including unseen hardware?

Our key insight is that although different sensing mechanisms capture distinct manifestations of contact, the underlying physical interactions obey the same Newtonian mechanics. We therefore propose grounding tactile representations in six-dimensional wrenches, which quantify net contact forces and torques and characterize the mechanical interactions underlying manipulation. By independently pairing observations from each sensor with directly measured wrenches, we establish a shared physical supervision signal without requiring coordinated data collection across sensor pairs. This provides a common quantitative reference for comparing interactions across heterogeneous sensing modalities.

To support large-scale learning, we develop a hardware platform that synchronously records tactile observations and six-dimensional wrenches, collecting over 100 million tactile–wrench pairs from 24 sensors across four sensing families: optical, magnetic, pressure-based, and piezoresistive (Fig. 2). We also establish a benchmark for evaluating representation quality and cross-sensor transferability. Building on this dataset, we develop a unified tactile encoder that maps heterogeneous observations into a shared continuous feature space. Sensor-specific input adapters accommodate different observation formats, while a shared Transformer aggregates tokens through a learnable physical query. We align tactile embeddings with targets from a momentum-updated wrench encoder and use a shared decoder to reconstruct measured wrenches, grounding cross-sensor representations in physical interactions. For downstream manipulation, we introduce TaF-Policy, which combines tactile features, visual observations, and robot states to generate action chunks.

Comprehensive benchmarks were conducted using learned representation. Our encoder reduces single-frame force
RMSE from 2.799 N to 2.321 N, a relative reduction of 17.1 %,
and improves cross-sensor retrieval R@1 from 21.27% to 34.38%,
a gain of 13.11 percentage points, compared with the strongest
baseline for each metric.
For downstream manipulation, TaF-Policy achieves an average
success rate of 51.3% across three UniVTAC
simulation [4] tasks, outperforming the
strongest evaluated baseline at 47.3% by 4.0 percentage points.
On the three real-world tasks evaluated by all methods,
TaF-Policy achieves an average success rate of 40.0%,
compared with 18.3% for the strongest baseline,
a gain of 21.7 percentage points.
These results support the utility of wrench-grounded tactile
representations for both cross-sensor perception and
contact-rich manipulation.

Our main contributions are as follows:

Large-scale tactile–wrench data infrastructure.
We develop a dedicated acquisition platform and collect over 100 million tactile–wrench pairs from 24 sensors spanning four sensing families.

Wrench-grounded unified tactile representations.
We introduce a unified tactile encoder with sensor-specific input adaptation and shared encoding. Wrench reconstruction and alignment with targets from a momentum-updated wrench encoder ground the representations in measured forces and torques.

Cross-sensor benchmark and manipulation policy.
We establish a benchmark for heterogeneous tactile sensors and demonstrate improvements in wrench estimation and cross-sensor retrieval. We also introduce TaF-Policy and evaluate its use of the learned representations in simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.

1. Large-scale tactile–wrench data infrastructure.
We develop a dedicated acquisition platform and collect over 100 million tactile–wrench pairs from 24 sensors spanning four sensing families.

2. Wrench-grounded unified tactile representations.
We introduce a unified tactile encoder with sensor-specific input adaptation and shared encoding. Wrench reconstruction and alignment with targets from a momentum-updated wrench encoder ground the representations in measured forces and torques.

3. Cross-sensor benchmark and manipulation policy.
We establish a benchmark for heterogeneous tactile sensors and demonstrate improvements in wrench estimation and cross-sensor retrieval. We also introduce TaF-Policy and evaluate its use of the learned representations in simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.

title: SG-ODOM: Event-Driven Proprioceptive State Estimation with Stability-Gated Contact Updates for Legged Robots
authors: Francesco Iotti,Chiyun Noh,Franco Angelini,Manolo Garabini,Ayoung Kim,Maurice Fallon,Frank Dellaert
abstract:
Reliable proprioceptive state estimation for legged robots fuses inertial sensing with kinematic sensing from leg encoders. The latter assumes a foot is stationary during the gate; however, physical foot touchdown does not necessarily provide a stationary reference for odometry, particularly during impact and load transfer. Repeatedly applying kinematic corrections throughout the same contact phase can introduce redundant or unreliable information. We present SG-ODOM, a proprioceptive odometry framework that uses stability-gated contact selection to schedule kinematic updates. Following physical touchdown, a stability gate accepts the contact for state estimation only after the foot reaches a sufficiently stable support condition. The resulting validated touchdown event triggers an estimator correction, while additional timeout updates bound the maximum duration of uninterrupted IMU propagation.
The framework is evaluated on multiple legged platforms, both quadrupedal and humanoid robots, against representative state-of-the-art proprioceptive estimators. Across the evaluated sequences, SG-ODOM demonstrates competitive or superior estimation accuracy, reducing  RPE (RPE) by up to 25%25\% compared to the baseline estimator on outdoor sequences from the GrandTour dataset. We make our source code publicly available.

introduction:
Reliable legged locomotion requires stable, low drift, low latency and high-frequency estimates of the robot’s base motion. Proprioceptive odometry commonly uses the  IMU (IMU) for high-rate state propagation and leg kinematics for state updates [3, 18]. Leg kinematics help correct accumulated inertial drift by relating the robot base to feet in contact with the environment. Such indirect state measurements assume that the selected contact frame provides a stationary reference.

However, physical contact does not in itself ensure a stationary reference, particularly during touchdown and load transfer. A foot may sustain a substantial  GRF (GRF) while still bouncing or settling on the ground [23]. Contact information should therefore indicate whether the foot provides a stable reference for estimation.

Even when a contact provides a stable reference, it remains unclear whether kinematic corrections need to be applied at the full joint-sensing rate. Consecutive measurements within the same contact phase are strongly correlated and may therefore provide limited additional information. Moreover, frequent kinematic corrections can repeatedly introduce errors caused by slip or residual foot motion. These errors can distort the estimated base motion and introduce spurious changes in the state estimate. Conversely, overly sparse corrections increase the duration of IMU-only propagation and allow inertial drift to accumulate. This raises the question of how frequently kinematic corrections should be applied relative to inertial propagation.

In this work, we propose SG-ODOM, a stability-gated, event-driven proprioceptive odometry strategy that preserves high-rate IMU propagation and contact processing while selectively applying kinematic corrections. A physical touchdown is accepted for estimation only after the foot reaches a sufficiently stable contact condition, avoiding corrections during the transient phase following impact. These validated touchdowns initiate immediate contact-triggered updates, while, during unchanged contact conditions, timeout-triggered updates are applied at a lower rate than the joint-encoder measurements, but frequent enough to avoid prolonged IMU-only propagation, as illustrated in Fig. 1.

We implement this proposed strategy using two estimator configurations: an  InEKF (InEKF), and a fixed-lag smoother. Both configurations share the same sensing, contact, and update interfaces, allowing the effect of estimator formulation to be examined under consistent conditions. Robot-specific sensing and kinematic processing are handled in a separate front end, enabling the same estimation back end to be used across quadrupedal and humanoid platforms.

Our contributions are as follows:

An event-driven proprioceptive odometry strategy that
separates high-rate IMU propagation and contact evaluation
from kinematic correction timing, using validated touchdowns
for immediate contact-triggered updates and timeout-triggered updates to
limit IMU-only propagation.

An event-driven proprioceptive odometry strategy that
separates high-rate IMU propagation and contact evaluation
from kinematic correction timing, using validated touchdowns
for immediate contact-triggered updates and timeout-triggered updates to
limit IMU-only propagation.

A stability-gated contact classifier that distinguishes
physical touchdown from estimation-valid support, accepting
contacts only after loading and force-stability conditions
persist, past the impact transient.

An evaluation on three legged platforms with ablations
showing that stability gating improves accuracy for both
estimators and that lower correction frequencies can preserve
or improve accuracy. The fixed-lag configuration achieves
approximately 25% lower average translational RPE than the
onboard ANYbotics estimator across seven GrandTour missions.

An open-source GTSAM-based implementation with shared sensing,
contact, and update interfaces supporting both an InEKF and
a fixed-lag smoother, with a robot-specific front end.

The framework is evaluated on sequences from the GaRLILEO dataset [26] (Boston Dynamics Spot) and the GrandTour dataset [14] (ANYbotics ANYmal D), and on a self-collected dataset with the Unitree G1, as illustrated in Fig. 4. The evaluation examines the effect of contact classification and update frequency, and compares the two SG-ODOM configurations with existing proprioceptive and manufacturer-provided estimators.

from kinematic correction timing, using validated touchdowns

physical touchdown from estimation-valid support, accepting
contacts only after loading and force-stability conditions
persist, past the impact transient.

3. An evaluation on three legged platforms with ablations
showing that stability gating improves accuracy for both
estimators and that lower correction frequencies can preserve
or improve accuracy. The fixed-lag configuration achieves
approximately 25% lower average translational RPE than the
onboard ANYbotics estimator across seven GrandTour missions.

contact, and update interfaces supporting both an InEKF and
a fixed-lag smoother, with a robot-specific front end.

title: Design of the Secure Smart Scooter with Automatic Lane Detection
authors: Hamid Reza Ghaeini,Nils Ole Tippenhauer
comment: Published in 16th IEEE International Conference on Service Operations and Logistics, and Informatics (IEEE SOLI 2022)
abstract:
The authors present a prototype of an electric scooter that uses computer vision to determine driving lanes and automatically modify vehicle configuration. Scooters steer on sidewalks, bike paths, or car lanes. The government imposes speed limits on the lanes in which electric scooters drive. Featuring computer vision, electric scooters can determine driving lanes and automatically modify vehicle configuration. However, such systems’ safety is still a concern, and research into such vehicle systems’ safety and security aspects is proceeding. First, we will present our vehicular setup. Then,
we will present our implemented scooter with safety constraints. Finally, we present our security prototype for such an electric scooter.
introduction:
The transportation systems are evolving day by day with integrated technologies such as adaptive cruise control, lane detection, positioning, artificial intelligence and low power wireless communication. One of the goals of an Intelligent Transportation System (ITS) is to support different modes of transportation and traffic management in order to provide users with more relevant information and a safer, more coordinated and ”smarter” use of the transportation network.

The scooter itself, has computing devices that are responsible for the control of the vehicle, and enhanced mobility features such as automatic lane detection. A popular means of transportation in urban areas is the electric scooter, which coupled with other public transportation options can improve mobility and reduce the need for personal mobility devices [3, 7, 12, 6]. E-scooters, however, need to be revisited due to the legal framework for these vehicles, and the technology used in them must be adapted to the vehicle technology requirements and the legal framework. The direct interaction of the vehicle and pedestrian lane makes it challenging to design and implement such a mobility medium’s safety and security requirements. According to the legal frameworks of Germany, electric scooters can only drive at a defined maximum speed in pedestrian, cycling, and car lanes. For example, the scooter is limited to 6 KM/H in the pedestrian lanes.

Driver assistance systems and autonomous vehicles require lane detection to form the driving settings. One of the primary tasks of autonomous driving is detecting the road or drivable portion of an unstructured road. Only colour cameras can detect the road or drivable portion in such a muddled road. The literature has discussed road and lane detection for more than four decades, and many promising solutions exist for automobiles today. The authors of [1] explored road and lane detection methods. Lanes and roads can be perceived in several ways, but monocular vision is the most common. Although most works do not discuss it directly, they acknowledge it as a viable choice. Our scooter is cost-effective and delivers reliable performance thanks to a similar approach, which incorporates computer vision. By the way, our discussion of computer vision performance will not take place in this paper, and this paper concentrates on the secure design of such a scooter.

A cruise control advanced driver assistance system known as an adaptive cruise controller (ACC) automatically adjusts the vehicle’s speed and distance from the vehicle ahead to preserve a reasonable safety span. Control depends on device information from vehicle sensors [9, 13, 11]. Such systems may use a measuring instrument, an optical device, or a camera device. This allows the vehicle to brake when it detects that it is approaching another vehicle and to accelerate again when traffic permits. Similarly, we determine the vehicle’s maximum speed based on the computer vision component. We enforce the top speed based on the lane detected by our prototype from the visual component to the motor controller. We smoothly transition from the current speed to the desired speed by logarithmic increasing or decreasing the speed in a two-second time window [4]. This is critical for maintaining smooth acceleration to ensure the safety of the system [10, 8, 14, 5].

In our prior work [4], we have presented the safety requirements of an electric scooter and the implementation of those safety requirements. This paper discusses the system’s security requirements to maintain functional, control and safety applications secure. To our collective knowledge, this paper is the first paper that presents the requirements for the secure design of electric scooters. Our design can also be extended to other motor controllers, such as autonomous driving systems. The rest of the paper will present the vehicular setup, security requirements of vehicular devices, and our proposed design of the secure scooter.

title: ARMFUL: Learning Whole-Arm Grasp Configurations for Single-Arm Pickup of Large Objects
authors: Xinyi Yu,Yunshuang Li,Daniel Seita,Gaurav S. Sukhatme
abstract:
Many everyday objects, such as storage boxes, baskets, and
chairs, are too large or heavy for a gripper to grasp, yet a single arm can
still pick them up by wrapping around and supporting them. Such grasps are
hard to learn: wrapping motions are difficult to teleoperate, and existing
datasets contain little whole-arm pickup data. We introduce WAG
(Whole-Arm Grasp Dataset), the first large-scale dataset for single-arm pickup
of large objects, with 1.7 million joint configurations across 793
objects. We sample configurations directly in joint space, execute each through
squeeze and lift primitives in simulation, and stress-test survivors
under active shaking and external forces. To demonstrate the utility of
WAG and accomplish the whole-arm pickup task, we develop ARMFUL, a whole-arm pickup pipeline that pairs a diffusion model trained on WAG, generating whole-arm grasps from the object’s point cloud, with a motion planner that reaches them collision-free before the same squeeze-and-lift execution. In simulation, ARMFUL reaches 85.4% lift success
on training and 69.9% on held-out objects, and it lifts the
object in 70 of 100 trials on a physical Franka arm across 10 IKEA objects.
introduction:
Robotic grasping has made substantial progress with a range of
end-effectors, such as parallel-jaw
grippers [1], dexterous
hands [2], and suction
grippers [3]. However, end-effector-centric grasping
remains
fundamentally limited when objects are too large to be securely grasped
or their weight exceeds the end-effector’s payload limit, e.g., chairs, tables, and large storage boxes. Picking up and transporting them requires
using the entire arm,
motivating whole-arm manipulation to overcome the geometric,
kinematic, and force limitations of end-effector-only manipulation.

Unlike conventional grasping, a whole-arm grasp cannot be specified by
a single end-effector pose. Its success depends on the full joint
configuration and contacts established along multiple links, making the
interaction more sensitive than conventional small-object grasping to
the object’s geometry and physical properties, such as mass distribution
and surface friction. This makes it difficult to design grasping
strategies that generalize across objects. Learning offers a promising
alternative but requires whole-arm grasp data. Existing large-scale
manipulation datasets primarily capture end-effector interactions
(Section II). Large-scale simulated datasets with
automatically generated labels have supported learning-based gripper and
dexterous-hand grasping [2, 4, 5, 6, 1, 3, 7],
but comparable data for whole-arm grasping remain unavailable.

To fill this gap, we first introduce WAG (the Whole-Arm
Grasp Dataset), a large-scale dataset generated and stress-tested
entirely in simulation (Fig. 1), together with ARMFUL, a
learning-and-planning pipeline for single-arm pickup of large objects
(Fig. 2). To build WAG, we sample whole-arm grasp
configurations in joint space and test the candidates in a GPU-parallel
simulation using two scripted primitives: squeeze and lift.
Only joint angles that survive arm shaking and external forces are
retained.
To demonstrate the usefulness of this dataset, we develop ARMFUL, which uses a diffusion model trained on WAG to learn whole-arm grasp configurations from an object’s point cloud.
It then plans a
collision-free approach to a learned configuration and executes the
same squeeze-and-lift sequence.
In simulation, ARMFUL outperforms heuristic and retrieval
baselines. We also validate the pipeline on 10 IKEA objects in the real world.
Our key contributions are as follows:

We construct WAG, the first large-scale whole-arm grasp dataset for single-arm pickup of large objects. It contains 793 diverse objects and approximately 1.7 million grasp configurations.

We introduce a perturbation-based stress test that evaluates each grasp and jittered copies of it under base-joint shaking and external forces, retaining only robust configurations and helping increase the dataset quality.

We demonstrate the utility of WAG and accomplish the
full whole-arm pickup task through ARMFUL, a
whole-arm grasping pipeline trained on the dataset. ARMFUL combines
a diffusion model over grasp configurations with collision-free
approach planning. It reaches 85.4% and 69.9% lift success on training
and held-out objects in simulation, outperforming heuristic and
retrieval baselines, and lifts the object in 70 of 100 trials on a
physical robot.

1. We construct WAG, the first large-scale whole-arm grasp dataset for single-arm pickup of large objects. It contains 793 diverse objects and approximately 1.7 million grasp configurations.

2. We introduce a perturbation-based stress test that evaluates each grasp and jittered copies of it under base-joint shaking and external forces, retaining only robust configurations and helping increase the dataset quality.

3. We demonstrate the utility of WAG and accomplish the
full whole-arm pickup task through ARMFUL, a
whole-arm grasping pipeline trained on the dataset. ARMFUL combines
a diffusion model over grasp configurations with collision-free
approach planning. It reaches 85.4% and 69.9% lift success on training
and held-out objects in simulation, outperforming heuristic and
retrieval baselines, and lifts the object in 70 of 100 trials on a
physical robot.

title: Learning and Verifying Progress: Closed-Loop Agentic Planning with Progress-Enhanced Execution for Long-Horizon Vision-Language Navigation
authors: Kangjie Zhou,Sukai Wang,Yuhan Xiao,Qinghang Liu,Zhejia Wen,ChunXuan Jiao,Wei Shan,Guanghui Ren,Maoqing Yao,Chang Liu
abstract: Long-horizon vision-language navigation (VLN) requires agents to track instruction progress and recover from local errors before they propagate across subtasks. However, executors trained on expert trajectories encounter policy-induced state shifts during deployment, and their stop signals do not reliably indicate subtask completion. We introduce Learning and Verifying Progress for VLN (LeaP-VLN), an agentic VLN system that couples progress-aware execution with independent progress verification through plan–execute–verify–recover cycles. LeaP-VLN leverages progress both explicitly, through a progress verifier that verifies subtask completion before the agent advances and triggers dual-phase recovery upon route deviation, and implicitly, by co-training the executor on progress reasoning and action prediction to enhance the executor’s progress awareness and corrective control. To adapt the executor to this closed-loop interface, we propose a two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum: behavior cloning on expert demonstrations, followed by joint training on demonstrations, expert action corrections, and progress-reasoning supervision. Policy-generated trajectories expose the executor to both intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask state shifts, aligning training with the deviations encountered during closed-loop execution. Extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE demonstrate state-of-the-art success rates among monocular methods trained without additional navigation datasets, while real-world experiments further validate the effectiveness of LeaP-VLN in long-horizon navigation.
introduction:
Vision-language navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow a natural-language route instruction in a previously unseen environment [1, 2, 3]. In long-horizon settings, instructions specify sequences of landmark transitions and spatial relations. The agent must therefore predict appropriate actions while inferring from evolving egocentric observations which parts of the instruction have been completed and what remains to be executed. Moreover, local execution errors or instruction misinterpretations can compound across successive subtasks, causing increasing drift from the intended route and making subsequent stages harder to complete. Reliable long-horizon VLN requires progress tracking, accurate subtask execution, and recovery from local failures.

Existing VLN approaches differ in how they organize instruction interpretation and action execution, as illustrated in Fig. 1. End-to-end policies built on vision-language models (VLMs) map the complete route instruction, the visual history, and the current observation directly to actions [4, 5, 6]. Route understanding, progress tracking, and action prediction are integrated into a single policy, leaving instruction progress implicit and subtask transitions difficult to control explicitly.
Hierarchical planner–executor systems separate high-level route reasoning from low-level control: a planner specifies target locations, waypoints, local instructions, or modular skills, and an executor carries out the corresponding navigation actions [7, 8, 9, 10]. This separation makes intermediate navigation goals explicit, but reliable execution still depends on the executor’s ability to handle policy-induced deviations and the planner’s ability to assess subtask outcomes. Two challenges arise at this interface. First, executors trained on expert demonstrations face policy-induced state shifts during closed-loop execution, including intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask boundary shifts. Second, unverified subtask transitions can propagate local failures into inaccurate route-progress estimates. Existing recovery strategies either replan from a potentially deviated state [11, 9] or backtrack without correcting instruction grounding [12]. Reliable execution therefore requires handling both intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask state shifts, verifying subtask outcomes, and coupling state recovery with instruction re-grounding.

To address these gaps, we introduce LeaP-VLN, a closed-loop agentic VLN system that exploits subtask progress on both sides of the planner–executor interface (Fig. 1, bottom). On the planner side, progress is handled explicitly. A high-level multimodal agent decomposes the route instruction into local subtasks and orchestrates plan–execute–verify–recover cycles. An independent verifier assesses subtask completion and route alignment using the observed execution history. The agent advances only after completion is verified, and the corresponding terminal state is stored as a trusted recovery anchor. Upon route deviation, dual-phase recovery restores a trusted execution context and re-grounds the pending subtask for a refined retry. On the executor side, progress awareness is learned implicitly by co-training the executor on progress reasoning and action prediction. We propose a two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum that first initializes the executor through behavior cloning on expert demonstrations, then co-trains it using these demonstrations and expert-corrected intra- and inter-subtask policy rollouts. Learning to reason about progress content improves action prediction while promoting progress–action consistency, aligning the executor’s decisions with the internal subtask progress.

Our contributions are summarized as follows.

We introduce LeaP-VLN, a closed-loop agentic navigation system for long-horizon VLN that integrates progress-aware execution, progress verification, and dual-phase recovery to maintain route alignment and limit error propagation across subtasks.

We develop a two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum for training a low-level VLN executor. By co-training action prediction and progress reasoning on expert demonstrations and policy-generated trajectories, the curriculum trains the executor to handle intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask state shifts during closed-loop execution.

We achieve state-of-the-art success rates on R2R-CE and RxR-CE among monocular methods trained without additional navigation datasets. Component ablations evaluate the contributions of agentic planning, progress-enhanced training, and test-time verification and recovery, while real-world experiments further validate the effectiveness of LeaP-VLN in long-horizon navigation.

1. We introduce LeaP-VLN, a closed-loop agentic navigation system for long-horizon VLN that integrates progress-aware execution, progress verification, and dual-phase recovery to maintain route alignment and limit error propagation across subtasks.

2. We develop a two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum for training a low-level VLN executor. By co-training action prediction and progress reasoning on expert demonstrations and policy-generated trajectories, the curriculum trains the executor to handle intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask state shifts during closed-loop execution.

3. We achieve state-of-the-art success rates on R2R-CE and RxR-CE among monocular methods trained without additional navigation datasets. Component ablations evaluate the contributions of agentic planning, progress-enhanced training, and test-time verification and recovery, while real-world experiments further validate the effectiveness of LeaP-VLN in long-horizon navigation.

title: JEPTERA: A Platform Agnostic JEPA-Assisted Model Predictive Planner for Urban UAV Navigation
authors: Gibran Fathoni Belva,Mansur Arief,Ahmad Alfan Alfian Irfan
comment: . Submitted to conference
abstract: Urban navigation for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) requires planning that accounts for environmental geometry, vehicle dynamics, and moving obstacles. This paper presents JEPTERA, a navigation architecture that integrates a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), Model Predictive Control (MPC), PID control, and a safety layer. JEPA predicts the UAV’s motion response to candidate commands for MPC action selection, while the safety layer checks trajectories against occupied space and predicted obstacle motion. Simulator adapters and platform-specific YAML configurations separate the planning core from simulator interfaces. An ablation study evaluated six configurations across three gym scenarios, totaling 180 runs. The complete architecture achieved the highest aggregate success rate, completing 28 of 30 runs. Additional tests completed one route across three city maps without collisions. Separate integration tests demonstrated operation in Gazebo/ROS 2, MuJoCo, and CARLA without modifying the core planning logic. These results support the feasibility of the integrated architecture for simulated urban UAV navigation and its portability across simulator interfaces.
introduction:
Autonomous UAVs require reliable navigation in dynamic urban environments. Buildings that constrain the airspace, along with moving obstacles, necessitate online planning based on continuously updated observations [1, 2]. Such conditions demand a planning system capable of accounting for environmental geometry, the UAV’s motion constraints, and the predicted movement of obstacles, in order to determine safe maneuvers while still achieving the desired objectives [3].

Model predictive control (MPC) selects actions by optimizing predicted motion under system objectives and constraints [4, 3]. The Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) provides a framework for prediction in representation space [5], subsequently explored through I-JEPA for images and V-JEPA 2 for action-conditioned robot planning [6, 7]. These developments highlight the potential of representation space prediction for UAV navigation among static and dynamic obstacles.

Although MPC–PID with a safety layer provides reliable navigation, its performance may degrade in complex dynamic environments where anticipating obstacle motion is essential [3]. This limitation motivates integrating JEPA-based motion prediction with MPC to improve navigation reliability under challenging conditions.

This paper proposes JEPTERA, a platform-agnostic UAV navigation
architecture integrating JEPA-based motion prediction, MPC, PID control, and safety layer. Simulator adapters and platform-specific YAML configurations decouple the planning core from platform interfaces. Evaluation includes component ablations, navigation across three urban maps, and cross-simulator integration tests.

To summarize, our main contributions are threefold.

a planning architecture combining JEPA-based motion prediction with MPC, PID control, and a safety layer;

a shared planning core integrated across simulators through adapters and platform-specific YAML configurations; and

an evaluation comprising 180 ablation runs, navigation across three urban maps, and cross-simulator integration tests.

title: Stability Principle Inherent in Wheel Gait of Planar X-shaped Walker Generated Using Constant Torque Drive and Mechanical Stoppers
authors: Fumihiko Asano,Cong Yan
comment: . Published in the Proceedings of IEEE ICRA 2026. This author version corrects the author names in one reference; the scientific content remains unchanged
abstract: Since the late 19th century when the first walking toys were developed, it has been known that mechanical stoppers of the hip joint is crucial for generating stable passive dynamic walking. Recent research on passive-dynamic and limit-cycle walkers has also confirmed that mechanical stoppers at the hip and knee joints are effective for generating stable walking motion, but theoretical research on how this mechanical constraint enhances the overall gait stability remains insufficient. This paper introduces a planar X-shaped walker equipped with mechanical stoppers at the hip joint, and investigates the effect of the mechanical constraint on the stability of the wheel gait generated by constant torque drive on a downslope. By simply falling forward while using the stoppers to constrain itself to the target impact posture, the robot can generate a highly stable wheeled gait. We divide the motion of one step into four phases, derive approximate analytical solutions for the state error transition function matrix in each phase using a linearized model, and analyze the increase or decrease in the state error norm using metrics such as its maximum singular value. Numerical simulations demonstrate that while two phases are unstable in terms of the increase in the state error norm, the remaining two phases are stable.
introduction:
Through his pioneering research on passive dynamic walking, McGeer demonstrated that the passive compass-like biped robot can generate stable walking motion on downslopes by repeatedly performing the natural swinging motion of the legs based on gravity and the collision of stance-leg exchange [1]. Simultaneously, he showed that passive-dynamic walkers with knee joints require mechanical stoppers to be attached to both knees for stable motion generation [2]. Walking toys also possess stoppers somewhere on their bodies and utilize this mechanical constraint to walk down slopes with a steady, rhythmic gait [3, 4]. Through these pioneering studies and toy development, insights emerged that using mechanical stoppers to maintain impact postures as consistently as possible is effective for generating continuous walking motion and enhancing the stability of hybrid zero dynamics [5, 6].

The rimless wheel (RW) is also a commonly used model for analyzing passive dynamic walking [7, 8]. It possesses a distinct, self-evident stability compared to the aforementioned passive-dynamic walkers for the following reasons. The RW with a symmetrical shape occurs each collision in the same posture, resulting in a constant ratio of kinetic energy immediately before and immediately after collision. Simultaneously, the restored mechanical energy per step due to gravity also remains constant. Consequently, the generated motion is always period-1 and asymptotically stable. The above can be easily explained using the recurrence formula for kinetic energy immediately before impact, indicating gait stability at an obvious level. In the wheel gait addressed in this paper, however, the inclusion of kinetic energy-loss term that is difficult to describe analytically immediately makes stability analysis extremely challenging. While the convergence of gait descriptors is very similar to that of a RW, the difficulty in providing a mathematical explanation is worlds apart.

This paper examines the stability principles inherent in wheel gaits generated while constrained to target impact postures using mechanical stoppers, employing the following methods. First, we derive the equations of motion, collisions, and constraint conditions for a planar 2-DOF X-shaped walker. We then numerically demonstrate that a stable wheel gait can be generated on a downward slope by causing the mechanical stopper on the swing leg to collide with the stance leg, causing the robot to fall forward. Next, using a linearized model approximating the equation of motion around an unstable equilibrium point, we derive the state error transition function matrices for the two swing phases and the two collision phases. For the two collision phases, we derive the matrices directly using the collision equations from the nonlinear model. By calculating the eigenvalues and maximum singular values of these matrices, we can gain some insight into the trend of increase or decrease in the state error norm during each phase. Furthermore, by sequentially multiplying the four matrices to reduce dimensions, we can derive the state error transition function from the angular velocity error of the entire body immediately before impact to the next. Through numerical simulations, we clarify that walking speed and convergence characteristics change depending on the magnitude of the constant torque applied to the hip joint, and that while two of the four phases are unstable, the remaining two are stable.

title: ExtremeDrive: A Real-World Dataset and Benchmark for Critical Driving
authors: Xinhan Li,Yuhong Jiang,Shiyue Zhao,Junzhi Zhang,Chengkun He,Ruihai Ma,Shijie Zhao,Wenxuan Cheng,Jinbo Lv,Tao Liu
abstract:
Existing autonomous driving datasets and benchmarks provide extensive resources for routine driving, yet real-world data covering safety-critical scenarios and extreme environmental conditions remain limited.
To address this gap, we present ExtremeDrive11
1
          
          
          
        Toolkit and evaluation assets: https://github.com/XinhanLi21/ExtremeDrive, a real-world dataset and benchmark covering emergency maneuvers, complex traffic interactions, and adverse conditions such as slippery or snow-covered roads, alongside routine driving.
The dataset comprises 589 driving scenes curated from a larger pool of real-world driving recordings, with calibrated and aligned multisensor data and reviewed annotations of road structure and traffic participants.
We further establish a benchmark to evaluate planned trajectories through simulated vehicle execution, measuring safety-related metrics and driving performance.
Experiments at equal training set sizes show that incorporating critical driving data reduces trajectory prediction errors and improves mean critical-success rates in critical scenarios.
ExtremeDrive provides a unified resource for learning and evaluating autonomous driving in safety-critical scenarios and extreme environmental conditions.
introduction:
Autonomous driving datasets and benchmarks provide observations and evaluation tools for developing and assessing driving systems [1, 2].
However, most datasets commonly used for autonomous driving focus on routine driving scenarios and basic driving maneuvers, with particularly limited coverage of emergency maneuvers and extreme environmental conditions [3, 4].
This imbalance leaves fewer opportunities to learn from and evaluate driving behavior under critical conditions.

Rare but consequential driving events are central to the long-tail challenge of autonomous driving: their low frequency makes them difficult to cover, while failures can have serious safety consequences [5].
Complex traffic interactions, low light, wet or slippery roads, and snow-covered roads introduce additional challenges in perception, decision making, and vehicle response.
Strong performance under routine driving conditions does not establish planning capability in critical scenarios.
Real-world critical driving data are therefore needed to study these challenges and support the development of safer driving systems.
To support learning and evaluation, these data must also be consistently processed and supplemented with reliable annotations of road structure and traffic participants [6].

Building on these data and annotations, assessing the ability to respond safely in critical scenarios requires suitable evaluation criteria.
Trajectory accuracy measures agreement with the recorded trajectory, but does not by itself establish whether a planned response can be executed safely [7, 8].
Different responses may also be safe, so reproducing a single recorded trajectory should not be the sole criterion for success.
Vehicle response and surrounding road and traffic constraints must be considered when assessing executed outcomes [9].
These needs motivate combining real-world critical driving data with evaluation that accounts for both trajectory accuracy and execution-based safety metrics.

To address these challenges, we introduce ExtremeDrive, a real-world dataset and benchmark for critical driving (Fig. ).
It covers critical scenarios involving complex traffic interactions and adverse conditions, alongside routine driving conditions.
The dataset provides calibrated and aligned multisensor data, vehicle states, and reviewed scene annotations from recordings collected on real roads.
The accompanying benchmark evaluates planned trajectories through simulated vehicle execution, measuring driving performance and safety-related metrics in critical scenarios.

Our contributions are threefold:

(1) We construct ExtremeDrive, a real-world dataset for critical driving, from curated recordings collected with an instrumented vehicle on real roads.
It covers emergency maneuvers during hazardous traffic interactions, including evasive steering and emergency braking, as well as extreme driving environments such as slippery roads and roads covered by snow or ice.
The dataset provides calibrated and aligned multisensor observations with annotations of the traffic environment across complete scenes.

(2) We establish a unified benchmark for comparing planning performance under shared vehicle execution settings.
It assesses planned trajectories through a shared tracking and vehicle execution interface, measuring collision avoidance, road compliance, progress, and comfort, with a dedicated critical-success criterion.

(3) We validate the value of critical driving data and benchmark representative planning methods.
Controlled experiments quantify the prediction benefit of critical driving data at equal training set sizes, while comparisons of representative planning methods characterize trajectory accuracy and execution performance.

title: sqrtVINS-Based 360 Visual-Inertial SLAM Systems: Hilti-Trimble SLAM Challenge 2026 Entry
authors: Jungwoo Lee,Hogyun Kim,Jiwon Choi,Jinyong Jeong,Younggun Cho

abstract:
This report describes our submission to the 2026 Hilti-Trimble SLAM Challenge.
The system is a 360-camera visual-inertial pipeline that uses only the provided dual-fisheye image streams and IMU measurements.
First, raw images are preprocessed with low-light enhancement [7] and static/dynamic masking [4], and then fed into a VINS\sqrt{\text{VINS}} [9] frontend as the local odometry, with deep learning-based SuperPoint features [2], ELSED line segments [10], and LightGlue matching [8].
The resulting trajectory is refined using a GTSAM-based backend that performs tightly-coupled factor graph optimization with SALAD global descriptor [3] and visual bundle adjustment (BA) [1].
The backend performs local-to-global structureless BA, tightly regularized intrinsic and extrinsic refinement, and global scale adjustment supported by the known inter-camera baseline and cross-view constraints.
The design targets long indoor sequences with dark regions, repetitive corridors, dynamic objects, and limited geometric parallax, while keeping the pipeline reproducible in the provided ROS2 workspace.
Fig.  demonstrates that our proposed method aligns well with the floorplan across several indoor sequences.
introduction:
Our visual-inertial SLAM system is summarized in Fig. 2.
We model the 360 camera as two calibrated fisheye views under the extended and unified camera model (EUCM) projection model and represent all poses in the cam0 frame (Sec. I-A).
First, raw fisheye frames are conditioned by static masking, low-light enhancement, and dynamic-object suppression before any feature extraction (Sec. I-B).
Next, we pass the conditioned images to a VINS\sqrt{\mathrm{VINS}}-based frontend [9] that estimates locally metric visual-inertial odometry using SuperPoint point features [2], LightGlue matching [8], and ELSED line segments [10] (Sec. I-C).
We then detect and geometrically verify loop closure and short-term cross-camera constraints using SALAD global descriptor [3] before inserting them into the factor graph (Sec. I-D).
Finally, a GTSAM-based backend [5] then jointly optimizes cam0 poses, extrinsic and intrinsic parameters, and a global scale variable via EUCM-compatible structureless smart projection factors [1] (Sec. I-E).
Since loop closure and BA can revise earlier poses using later observations, the exported trajectory is non-causal.

First, we model the 360 camera as two calibrated fisheye views using the EUCM [6].
The optimized trajectory is represented in the cam0 frame, where each graph node 𝐓k∈SE⁡(3)\mathbf{T}_{k}\in\mathrm{SE}(3) denotes the cam0 pose at frame kk.
The cam0 observations are projected directly from 𝐓k\mathbf{T}_{k}, while cam1 observations are projected through a shared rigid transform 𝐄01=𝐓cam0→cam1\mathbf{E}_{01}=\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{cam0}\rightarrow\mathrm{cam1}}, allowing both fisheye views to constrain one cam0 trajectory without duplicate per-frame camera nodes.

Next, before feature extraction, we apply three conditioning steps to each raw fisheye frame.
Static masks remove invalid fisheye regions and fixed image artifacts.
Low-light enhancement [7] then improves contrast in dark indoor regions.
Finally, YOLO26 detector/segmentation outputs [4] conservatively suppress features on potentially moving objects.

We then build the frontend on VINS\sqrt{\mathrm{VINS}} [9].
Point tracking uses SuperPoint [2] and LightGlue [8] on the conditioned fisheye images, with state-predicted matching to improve robustness during fast motion and repetitive indoor appearance.
To complement point features in low-texture indoor regions, we add a line-feature branch that detects line segments with ELSED [10] and maintains their temporal associations via line matching.
These line observations are incorporated through an MSCKF-style update inspired by PL-VIWO [11].
Rather than enforcing a full Manhattan-world model, we adopt a vertical-world, or weak Manhattan-world, assumption: gravity provides a reliable vertical reference, while horizontal directions remain unconstrained.

Following odometry estimation, loop closure uses global image descriptors [3] to propose visually similar keyframes while rejecting immediate temporal neighbors, followed by SuperPoint-LightGlue geometric verification over valid cam0/cam1 view pairings.
We add accepted loop candidates as EUCM-compatible smart projection factors, keeping loop closure consistent with the keyframe BA formulation.
Beyond long-range loop closure, we search a bounded temporal window for short-term cross-camera matches that connect nearby non-consecutive observations across the two fisheye views.
These constraints are particularly useful during turns, corridor motion, and near-revisits, where structure observed in one fisheye view quickly reappears in the other.
Because the verified matches span the calibrated inter-camera baseline, they also provide local metric evidence that supports the graph-wide scale correction.

Finally, the backend optimizes a factor graph over cam0 poses, camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters, and a global scale variable.
Consecutive frontend estimates provide relative pose factors, while all visual constraints are represented as EUCM-compatible structureless smart projection factors [1] instantiated for keyframe BA, geometrically verified loop closure, and short-term cross-camera tracks.
