title: Vision-Language Grounded Semantic Navigation for Autonomous Mobile Robots
authors: Ravindran Vasoor Saravanan,Chittin Varunav Ravi,Madhumita Singh,Thirulok Sundar Mohan Rasu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Language-guided navigation enables mobile robots to interpret natural language commands and navigate toward user-specified targets in unstructured environments. However, integrating open-vocabulary visual perception with classical robotics pipelines for mapping and navigation remains a challenging problem. In this work, we present a complete ROS2-based system that combines frontier-based exploration, open-vocabulary object detection using Grounding DINO, depth-based 3D localization, and semantic mapping to enable end-to-end vision-language grounded navigation in simulation.
The system accepts natural language commands such as “go to the yellow box,” detects candidate objects from RGB images using text prompts, estimates their positions in the world frame, and generates navigation goals executed by the Nav2 stack. In a Gazebo-based indoor environment with a TurtleBot3 robot, the system autonomously explored the room, detected three of the five target objects, and successfully executed both natural language navigation commands tested, without task-specific training. The results indicate that open-vocabulary grounding models can be integrated into classical navigation pipelines, though performance is limited by detection uncertainty, depth-based localization error, and incomplete exploration coverage. These findings highlight both the feasibility and current limitations of deploying vision-language grounded navigation systems using lightweight, CPU-only architectures.
introduction:
Autonomous mobile robots in human environments must do more than move from point A to point B: they must understand their surroundings in terms that humans naturally use. When a user says “go to the blue box” or “find the red cylinder,” the robot needs to understand both the spatial layout of the environment and the semantic properties of the objects within it. This problem, known as vision-language grounded navigation, combines simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), open-vocabulary computer vision, and natural language processing (NLP).

Traditional navigation systems model the world as a geometric entity consisting of walls, obstacles, and free space. Semantic mapping extends this by adding labels to objects, but most systems can only recognize a fixed set of object types learned during training [1]. This leads to two key limitations. First, adapting a closed-vocabulary system to a new domain requires collecting labeled data and retraining the detector. Second, the system can only recognize objects it was trained on, making it difficult to handle new or unseen object descriptions at runtime.

Recent vision-language models, especially Grounding DINO [2], address this by allowing open-vocabulary object detection using text prompts. Users can describe objects in natural language, and the model attempts to find them in images. When combined with language-driven planning systems such as SayPlan [3] and LM-Nav [4], these capabilities open the door to robots that can be instructed in ordinary English.

However, integrating these models with standard navigation systems is still challenging. Grounding DINO is slow on CPU (about 5–10 seconds per image), detections can be noisy when multiple objects are present, and keeping detections consistent with the SLAM map and user commands requires careful system design. In this work, we focus on addressing these challenges within a unified system.

This work presents an integrated system that combines open-vocabulary perception with classical robotics components. Our main contributions are:

ROS2-based integrated pipeline: We implement a ROS2 Humble–based system combining frontier-based exploration, Grounding DINO object detection, depth-based 3D localization, semantic mapping, and command parsing. These components are coordinated through a state machine managing transitions between exploration, perception, and navigation.

ROS2-based integrated pipeline: We implement a ROS2 Humble–based system combining frontier-based exploration, Grounding DINO object detection, depth-based 3D localization, semantic mapping, and command parsing. These components are coordinated through a state machine managing transitions between exploration, perception, and navigation.

Frontier selection with failure handling: We implement a frontier selection strategy that scores candidate frontiers based on size and distance. The system tracks repeated navigation failures and adjusts behavior to reduce the likelihood of getting stuck in difficult regions, such as concave areas or unreachable goals.

Rule-based natural language command parsing: We implement a simple regex-based parser to extract key elements such as action, object category, and visual attributes (e.g., color), enabling consistent interpretation of navigation commands.

Experimental validation in simulation: The system runs on Ubuntu 22.04 with ROS2 Humble using CPU-only PyTorch, without requiring GPU acceleration. We demonstrate end-to-end operation from autonomous exploration to language-guided navigation in a Gazebo-based indoor environment with geometric objects.

The complete source code for this system is publicly available as open-source software on GitHub (see repository link on the title page).

The system operates in two main phases. During the exploration phase, the robot autonomously navigates an unknown environment using a frontier-based strategy. At regular intervals (approximately every 1.5 meters), Grounding DINO processes the current camera image to detect objects, which are then localized in 3D using depth-based projection and added to a semantic map. During the query phase, the user issues natural language commands that are parsed and matched against the semantic map to generate navigation goals, which are executed by the Nav2 stack.

title: AsymEEF: Bimanual Manipulation with Asymmetric End Effectors
authors: Xiaokang Sun,Ningyue Wang,Kunqi Xu,Guangqi Jiang,Jianglong Ye,Yong Wu,Xueyan Zou
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Teleoperated demonstrations are costly to collect and rarely reusable across end-effectors with different kinematics and action spaces. This burden grows in bimanual manipulation, where each end-effector pair may require new data. We present AsymEEF, a framework for executable cross-end-effector demonstration generation and unified bimanual policy learning. Given a small source dataset, AsymEEF transfers demonstrations to heterogeneous combinations of two-, three-, and five-fingered end-effectors without additional teleoperation. Kinematic teacher anchors provide geometric supervision, while sparse real-world X-Calib anchors correct discrepancies in grasp execution. A shared encoder maps wrist poses and actuator states to a morphology-agnostic latent space, and a morphology-conditioned decoder reconstructs target commands. Generated trajectories undergo replay filtering for task-level executability. The representation also supports a unified bimanual visuomotor policy trained across multiple pairs. Across four simulated and six real-world tasks, AsymEEF improves replay success over adapted transfer baselines, achieves a mean replay-valid expansion gain of 16.6×\times in simulation, and is evaluated through downstream policy training on real robots. Project website: https://asymeef.vercel.app/.
introduction:
High-quality demonstrations are central to imitation learning for robotic manipulation, yet collecting them through teleoperation is time-consuming and costly [1, 2, 3]. Reusing these demonstrations across end effectors is challenging because the recorded actions are tied to the source hardware’s action space, while the resulting motions and interactions depend on its kinematics and contact behavior [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Directly transferring these actions to another end effector may therefore fail to reproduce the demonstrated interaction. This motivates data-generation methods that not only expand datasets across object types and positions but also support demonstration reuse across end effectors.

We study transfer among morphologically and kinematically distinct two-, three-, and five-fingered end effectors, which we collectively call hands. Our objective is to reuse demonstrations from limited source hand types across other hands and bimanual pairs. Source hands may be selected for cost, usability, or existing teleoperation support. For example, when the target hands support the required interactions, demonstrations collected with A+AA{+}A can generate data for A+BA{+}B and B+AB{+}A without separately teleoperating each target pair. Here, AA and BB denote hand types ordered from left to right.

We consider two identical robot arms equipped with different combinations of hands. Collecting demonstrations separately for every pair presents two challenges. First, operators using heterogeneous pairs must coordinate both arms while accommodating differences in control mappings, mounting geometries, and contact behavior. Second, effective teleoperation of individual pairs does not eliminate the collection burden across combinations: NN hand types available on each arm yield N2N^{2} ordered pairs. Generating demonstrations for multiple target pairs from a few source pairs offers an alternative to repeated manual collection.

Existing data-generation methods expand small sets of seed demonstrations into larger datasets [1, 2], while cross-end-effector methods support demonstration reuse and policy learning through action alignment and shared latent spaces [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. However, the joint problem of executable demonstration generation and unified policy learning for bimanual systems with morphologically heterogeneous end-effector pairs remains largely underexplored.

A shared representation of hand states can support both objectives. Hands with different joint structures can realize similar interactions through different joint configurations, with correspondences in interaction location, approach direction, and finger spacing relative to object size. Encoding these correspondences in a common latent space supports transfer and provides a consistent action representation for a single policy trained across hand pairs.

We introduce AsymEEF, a framework that integrates cross-end-effector demonstration generation with unified bimanual policy learning, as illustrated in Figure 1. The Shared EEF-State Encoder maps the states of different hands into a shared latent space. Cross-end-effector decoding then produces candidate trajectories for target hand pairs, while quality checks and task-replay validation identify usable demonstrations. The same representation supports a unified latent bimanual visuomotor policy that jointly predicts latent actions for both arms from visual observations and robot states. These predictions are decoded into commands for the corresponding end effectors. We evaluate demonstration generation and policy learning on contact-rich simulated and real-world tasks. Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate executable cross-end-effector demonstration generation across homogeneous and heterogeneous bimanual pairs of two-, three-, and five-fingered hands.

We formulate executable cross-end-effector demonstration generation across homogeneous and heterogeneous bimanual pairs of two-, three-, and five-fingered hands.

We introduce AsymEEF, combining cross-pair synthesis, quality checks, and task replay to generate validated simulated and real-world demonstrations.

We develop a shared EEF-state representation for cross-hand transfer and unified latent bimanual policies.

We evaluate generation, latent consistency, and policy performance on coordinated, sequential bimanual tasks.

title: WTR-Drive: World-Task Decomposition with Structured Risk Supervision for End-to-End Driving
authors: Haoyu Xing,Shaobing Ding,Guanglei Zhao,Guanhua Zhao,Nawu Peng,Mingyang Hou
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Intelligent Vehicles Symposium (IV) 2027
abstract:
Proposal-conditioned scene predictions can lack a common object-level
reference across candidate trajectories. Aggregate planning scores also
leave the objects and times associated with violations implicit.
We present WTR-Drive (World–Task–Risk Driving), a Drive-JEPA-based planner that
separates shared scene estimation from proposal-conditioned reasoning.
A proposal-independent World Memory estimates object states, map structure,
and future motion by re-reading the original visual features at each
refinement round. Proposal feedback updates a residual Task branch without
writing back to World Memory. This branch guides refinement through
candidate-specific retrieval and gated visual feedback. A final Task readout
supplies candidate-conditioned features for scoring.
We derive structured risk targets from existing candidate-scoring rollouts
without additional simulator calls.
For at-fault collision and time-to-collision violations, the targets encode
event existence, association with shared object slots, and the first
violation time bin. On the NAVSIM navtest split, WTR-Drive achieves
94.66 PDMS on v1 and 88.24 EPDMS on v2 (expert-frame sequential evaluation).
These scores are 0.96 and 0.44 points
above the published Drive-JEPA values, respectively. Candidate-level
analysis shows that higher best-candidate scores can coexist with lower
selected-trajectory scores, revealing a gap between candidate quality
and selection effectiveness.
Code is available at
https://github.com/xingxing9013605/WTR-Drive.
introduction:
Candidate trajectories represent alternative actions in the same observed
scene. Joint perception–planning systems use intermediate scene
representations [1, 2]. Drive-JEPA combines video pretraining
with multimodal trajectory distillation [3].
iPad [4] retrieves visual features around candidate waypoints.
However, proposal-conditioned predictions
can assign different states to the same object across candidates.
Our approach uses a shared estimate of object states, map structure,
and object motion for all candidates.
Each candidate then reasons about object relevance and potential violations
along its path.

For example, a vehicle may lie outside a lane-keeping trajectory yet
intersect a lane-change trajectory. Aggregate planning scores summarize
trajectory quality but leave the involved object and first violation time
implicit.
Explicit object and time labels supervise candidate–object interactions
and help diagnose object-association and event-timing errors.
iPad and Drive-JEPA already use mapping and collision-related
supervision [4, 3]. We extend this supervision to predict
event existence, association with object slots, and the first violation
time bin for each candidate.

Writing proposal feedback into World Memory would make its updates depend
on the candidate set. We therefore confine this feedback to a residual
Task branch to preserve an observation-based scene estimate for candidate
comparison.
We introduce WTR-Drive (Fig. 1), a
Drive-JEPA-based planner that separates observation-based World estimation
from proposal-conditioned Task reasoning. Structured risk targets from
existing scoring rollouts supervise candidate–scene interactions.
We make three contributions:

A proposal-independent World Memory.
We maintain shared object and map slots that estimate scene structure
and object motion. Each refinement round updates these slots from the
original visual features.

A proposal-independent World Memory.
We maintain shared object and map slots that estimate scene structure
and object motion. Each refinement round updates these slots from the
original visual features.

Residual Task conditioning without World write-back.
We represent proposal feedback as a residual over the shared World slots.
Task reads and gated visual feedback guide trajectory refinement,
while the final Task readout provides features for scoring.
Proposal feedback never writes back to World Memory.

Structured risk supervision.
From existing scoring rollouts, we supervise at-fault collision and
time-to-collision (TTC) event existence, association with World object
slots, and the first violation time bin, without additional simulator calls.

title: Lift, See, Act: Hierarchical Robot Policy Pretraining with 3D Foundation Models
authors: Yiyuan Ge,Changxing Ding,Ziyu Hao,Zijie Zheng,Xiangmin Xu
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
abstract:
Robot policy pretraining based on human videos is crucial for improving the policy’s generalization ability. One main challenge for this task is the lack of explicit action-relevant representations in such unlabeled data. Recent works tend to estimate 3D hand motion trajectories from videos using 3D foundation models (3D FMs). However, they keep solely the sparse trajectories as supervision, ignoring the rich, fine-grained information produced during the trajectory extraction process. To address this issue, we propose LSA, a hierarchical robot policy pretraining framework that includes three phases: Lift, See, and Act. Specifically, the Lift phase elevates 2D video observations into dense 3D representations by adaptively aligning features in the policy’s shallow layers with the intermediate representations extracted from multiple 3D FMs. Building upon these lifted representations, the See phase equips the policy with explicit geometric and interactive awareness through dual guidance. It introduces depth-map reconstruction to help the model comprehend 3D spatial layouts and utilizes hand region cues to explicitly supervise the encoder’s attention toward task-relevant interaction hotspots. Empowered by the dense 3D representation learning and precise spatial guidance, our policy achieves robust and accurate robotic manipulation in the Act phase. Extensive experiments on diverse simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that LSA significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. The project page is available at:
https://yiyuan00.github.io/Lift-See-Act.
introduction:
Large-scale pretraining is crucial for improving the generalization ability of machine learning models [1, 2]. In robotics, pretraining is equally important for policy learning, since high-quality manipulation data are expensive to collect and therefore difficult to scale up. Human videos are a key source of pretraining data, as they cover a wide range of real-world manipulation scenarios and contain rich manipulation knowledge [3, 4]. However, using human videos to pretrain robot policies remains a challenge, as such data inherently lack action-relevant representations [5].

Existing methods for extracting explicit action-relevant representations from human videos can be divided into two categories. The first category of methods extracts 2D
visual primitives from video frames, such as contact points [6, 7], contact heatmaps [8], and object bounding boxes [9], to characterize where contact occurs and which regions are potentially involved in manipulation. However, these methods lack temporal representations of the 3D manipulation process. The second category of methods attempts to estimate 3D hand motion trajectories from videos [10, 11, 12, 13, 14]. These trajectories reflect both the displacement of the hand in the 3D space and the temporal evolution of that displacement; therefore, they are more in line with the robot’s action prediction space. Recently, with the development of 3D foundation models (3D FMs) [15, 16, 17, 18], the accuracy of the estimation of 3D hand motion trajectories has improved substantially [12, 13, 14].

However, as illustrated in Fig. 1, the latter category of approaches only keeps the estimated hand motion trajectories as supervision for robot policy pretraining. They ignore more fine-grained knowledge, e.g., rich geometric representations and depth maps, produced by the 3D FMs during the hand motion trajectory prediction process. This dense knowledge is fundamental for a robot policy in predicting the 3D motion of the end effector. This insight motivates us to study how to make the best use of multi-tiered knowledge from 3D FMs to promote robot policy pretraining.

Consequently, we propose LSA, a hierarchical framework for robot policy pretraining based on three phases: Lift, See, and Act. Specifically, in the Lift phase, our goal is to lift 2D video observations into rich 3D representations. We first construct a 3D hand motion trajectory extraction pipeline utilizing multiple 3D FMs to process unlabeled human videos. This pipeline not only extracts the motion trajectories, but also keeps dense intermediate representations and depth maps produced by these 3D FMs. We then enforce the shallow-layer representations of the policy to align with the intermediate representations of each 3D FM, respectively. We also propose a strategy to adaptively adjust the weights of these alignment losses. This process effectively lifts the policy’s 2D representations into 3D, endowing the policy with more fine-grained geometric knowledge.

Building upon these lifted representations, the See phase equips the policy with explicit geometric and interactive awareness. While the Lift phase establishes a dense 3D representation space, these representations are implicit. Robot manipulation inherently requires an intuitive and precise understanding of the structure of the physical scene, along with a distinct visual focus on the manipulation objectives. To achieve this, the See phase provides dual guidance: explicit structural guidance and attentive guidance. First, leveraging the extracted depth maps, we introduce depth map reconstruction as an auxiliary task, providing explicit 3D geometric constraints to enable the model to comprehend 3D spatial layouts. Second, we utilize the hand region as a cue to guide the encoder’s attention toward task-relevant interaction hotspots.
Specifically, we encode 2D hand keypoints into a Gaussian heatmap to represent the hand region. We then select the attention map most similar to this heatmap across all heads in the shallow layers as our target, and finally use it to supervise the mean attention of all heads within a layer.
The above dual guidance ensures the policy explicitly Sees the 3D scene structure and concentrates on the task-relevant interaction regions.

To the best of our knowledge, LSA is the first approach to leverage multi-tiered 3D information extracted from 3D foundation models for hierarchical robot policy pretraining on human videos. Empowered by the dense 3D representation learning in the Lift phase and the dual guidance in the See phase, our policy predicts 3D hand motion trajectories in the Act phase, ultimately achieving robust and accurate robot manipulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our design and show that LSA outperforms state-of-the-art methods on various simulation and real-world tasks.

title: ReRead: Wrong Predictions, Useful Representations - Correcting Frozen Robot Policies by Re-reading Their Own Representations
authors: Xu Su,Shunlong Xiao,Qintao Yi,Mingkuan Zhao,Xinmiao Yu,Yizhe Li,Zihan Wang,Bokui Chen
abstract: When a pretrained robot policy fails on challenging tasks, common remedies include retraining the backbone, adding an external visual encoder, or introducing a memory module. We argue that wrong predictions do not imply wrong representations: a policy can retain the required information yet fail to read it out as the correct action. To test this view, we propose ReRead: with the backbone frozen, a corrector re-reads the current and two previous caches to predict an action residual. The corrector sees no images, is trained solely on offline demonstrations from all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and adds only 4.17% latency. Ablations and interventions show that the correction relies on the backbone’s own representations: none of four external visual encoders adds further gain, and swapping in past caches from other trajectories sharply increases action error. On the 11 hardest RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, ReRead improves the success rates of LingBot-VLA, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and Fast-WAM by 23.45, 13.09, and 8.00 percentage points, respectively. In paired evaluation on all 50 tasks, it raises Fast-WAM’s average success rate from 90.73% to 92.66%. On a Flexiv dual-arm robot, it raises success on a phase-ambiguous task from 0% to 36%.
introduction:
When a pretrained robot policy fails on challenging tasks, common remedies include retraining the backbone, adding an external visual encoder, or introducing a memory module [6, 18, 13].
These remedies share an implicit assumption: if the predicted actions are wrong, the policy’s representations must lack task-relevant information.

But failure has another possible cause: the policy already has the information it needs, yet fails to read it out as the correct action.
Similar findings in image recognition show that retraining only the classifier can improve accuracy while keeping the learned representations fixed [11, 12].
Robot tasks have a further property: the current frame is often insufficient to determine the action, because the action also depends on the current task phase.
The information needed to distinguish phases is not in the current frame, but it may already reside in the internal representations of the policy’s previous decisions, which are discarded once the actions are output.

We therefore argue that wrong predictions do not imply wrong representations.
The attention keys and values (K/V) cached by the backbone, the robot state, and temporal information form an internal memory, and we call its task-relevant information the representation.
(In Figs. 1 and 2, “R” stands for “Representations”.)
The process that maps the internal memory to an action is the readout, and the action finally returned is the prediction.
A backbone error may arise because the required information was never in the caches, or because it is in the caches but is not read out as the correct action.
In the latter case, it is the readout that needs to be improved, and the backbone need not be retrained.
This corresponds to the classical decomposition under squared loss: the prediction error equals the representation error plus the readout gap.

To test this view, we propose ReRead (Fig. 1): with the backbone frozen, a new corrector re-reads the representations cached by the backbone.
The backbone generates candidate actions as usual, and ReRead stores the native visual and action K/V from each of its decisions.
Using the candidate action as the query, the corrector reads the caches of the current and the two previous decisions and outputs an action residual, which is added back to the candidate action.
The corrector sees no images, does not retrain the backbone, and does not re-encode the history.
It is trained solely on offline demonstrations with an action MSE loss and adds 11.66 ms of latency per decision (4.17%).

We train ReRead on offline demonstrations from all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0 [4].
Fast-WAM [23] has a reported average success rate of 91.83% on these tasks, but its failures are concentrated in a few tasks: the 11 tasks with the lowest published success rates (Hard11) account for about 66.5% of the failures.
We use Hard11 as an evaluation subset to analyze cases in which the policy retains the required information but predicts the wrong action, and evaluate the overall effect of re-reading on all 50 tasks.

The experiments are organized around four questions.

First, when the backbone errs, is the required information still in the caches? Re-reading the current cache alone reduces the native candidate’s open-loop MSE by 61.45%. With ReRead, the success rates of LingBot-VLA, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and Fast-WAM on Hard11 improve by 23.45, 13.09, and 8.00 percentage points, respectively. In our paired evaluation on all 50 tasks, Fast-WAM’s average success rate rises from 90.73% to 92.66%.

Second, can prediction and representation be evaluated separately? Intervention experiments show that the corrected action is determined mainly by the caches: increasing the error of the candidate action 2-fold increases the error of the corrected action by only 12.08%, whereas replacing the past caches with those from other trajectories of the same task increases it 12.37-fold.

Third, do backbone failures stem from insufficient perception? None of the four external visual encoders outperforms ReRead, whereas replacing the past caches markedly changes the corrected action. These results do not support the perception-bottleneck explanation.

Fourth, when the current frame cannot distinguish phases, where is the required information? On a phase-ambiguous task, ReRead raises the success rate from 2% to 50% in simulation and from 0% to 36% on a real Flexiv dual-arm robot. Swapping in caches from the opposite phase moves the corrected action toward the other phase, indicating that the required information lies in the caches of previous decisions.

Our contributions are as follows:

We propose a new perspective: wrong predictions do not imply wrong representations. We decompose the prediction error into the representation error and the readout gap, and estimate the part that re-reading can eliminate.

To test this perspective, we propose ReRead, which freezes the backbone and trains a corrector solely on offline demonstrations to re-read the backbone’s cached representations and correct the actions. Our training and inference code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/tan2355/reread.

Interventions and ablations show that the correction relies on the backbone’s own caches. Phase information also remains in the caches of previous decisions. Prediction and representation can therefore be evaluated separately.

1. We propose a new perspective: wrong predictions do not imply wrong representations. We decompose the prediction error into the representation error and the readout gap, and estimate the part that re-reading can eliminate.

2. To test this perspective, we propose ReRead, which freezes the backbone and trains a corrector solely on offline demonstrations to re-read the backbone’s cached representations and correct the actions. Our training and inference code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/tan2355/reread.

3. Interventions and ablations show that the correction relies on the backbone’s own caches. Phase information also remains in the caches of previous decisions. Prediction and representation can therefore be evaluated separately.

title: Stochastic Self-Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Jingru Guo,Alessandra Russo,Joey Bose,Christos Ziakas
abstract: Flow-based vision–language–action (VLA) models achieve strong performance in robotics through imitation learning, yet fine-tuning them with on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is limited. In group-based RL methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), every rollout step requires multi-step ODE integration, and the sampler’s limited stochasticity leads to rollout groups with low variance. We propose VLA-SSD, which addresses both high inference latency and limited stochasticity. In particular, our method self-distills a pretrained flow-matching action head into a stochastic one-step policy by conditioning a single-jump generator on a Brownian path. We derive a conditional action density via our stochastic one-step policy, enabling efficient post-training via likelihood-ratio RL algorithms. We show that distilling VLA-SSD from the π0\pi_{0} VLA reduces the action head’s forward-pass time by a factor of 7.7, at the cost of a 5.5% relative decrease in the success rate on the LIBERO benchmark. However, by leveraging the increased sample diversity of VLA-SSD during group generation, post-training a π0.5\pi_{0.5} VLA using GRPO yields a 20.6% relative improvement.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models have achieved significant advances by leveraging knowledge from pre-trained vision–language models in robotics (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024). However, state-of-the-art VLAs have yet to achieve comparable generalization to other foundation models due to their reliance on imitation learning from expert demonstrations for adaptation to embodiments and environments (Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025). Frontier flow-based VLAs generate continuous action chunks with a flow-matching action head (Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). Yet, enabling them to improve via on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is still limited by the inference time of multi-step ODE integration and a lack of stochasticity.

To improve efficiency, one-step flow-based policies have been introduced for continuous control (Zhan et al., 2026; Ziakas et al., 2026), replacing multi-step ODE integration with a single transport step learned via self-distillation (Song et al., 2023; Boffi et al., 2024; Geng et al., 2025; Boffi et al., 2025). However, in RL methods using multi-sample advantage estimation, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), the baseline is derived directly from a group of trajectories given the current state. Because flow-matching rely entirely on the initial random noise draw for stochasticity, they restrict the action diversity within the sampled group, resulting in a degraded training signal (Shao et al., 2024). To enable exploration, existing approaches increase sample diversity by introducing an external noise network or reverting to multi-step samplers that inject noise at each integration step (Chen et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026).

In this work, we address both the efficiency and stochasticity limitations of current VLAs by learning a stochastic one-step policy via self-distillation. We propose VLA-SSD, a method that utilizes Itô flow maps (Pan et al., 2026) to distill a multi-step flow-matching VLA head into a one-step stochastic policy. In contrast to prior work, we introduce stochasticity directly through self-distillation rather than relying on an external noise network or a multi-step sampler. To enable likelihood-ratio policy optimization such as GRPO, we derive a conditional action density that requires only a single additional Jacobian-vector product to approximate. In our experiments, we first distill VLA-SSD from π0.5\pi_{0.5}, achieving a 7.7×7.7\times faster action head with a 0.30.3-point drop in success rate, while reducing zero-variance groups from 63%63\% to 35%35\% relative to the original sampler. Leveraging the stochasticity and efficiency of VLA-SSD, we
post-train it with GRPO, reaching 93.0%93.0\% on LIBERO, a
15.915.9-point gain over the SFT checkpoint, and matching four-step
GRPO with πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}} (91.5%91.5\%) while generating each action
chunk 3.2×3.2\times faster during training rollouts.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

One-Step Stochastic VLA Policies: We introduce VLA-SSD, a novel self-distillation framework that converts multi-step flow-matching VLA heads into efficient, one-step stochastic policies using Itô flow maps.

Density Evaluation for Likelihood-Ratio Optimization: To overcome the lack of tractable likelihoods in flow-based models, we derive a closed-form conditional action density that evaluates efficiently via a single Jacobian-vector product.

Efficient Policy Distillation: We demonstrate that distilling VLA-SSD from π0.5\pi_{0.5} yields a 7.7×7.7\times faster action head with a minimal 0.30.3-point performance drop, while mitigating the exploration bottleneck by reducing zero-variance groups from 63%63\% to 35%35\%.

RL Post-Training: When post-trained with GRPO, VLA-SSD reaches a 93.0%93.0\% success rate on LIBERO, a 15.915.9-point gain over the SFT checkpoint, matching the standard four-step πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}} baseline while accelerating training rollouts by 3.2×3.2\times.

1. One-Step Stochastic VLA Policies: We introduce VLA-SSD, a novel self-distillation framework that converts multi-step flow-matching VLA heads into efficient, one-step stochastic policies using Itô flow maps.

2. Density Evaluation for Likelihood-Ratio Optimization: To overcome the lack of tractable likelihoods in flow-based models, we derive a closed-form conditional action density that evaluates efficiently via a single Jacobian-vector product.

3. Efficient Policy Distillation: We demonstrate that distilling VLA-SSD from π0.5\pi_{0.5} yields a 7.7×7.7\times faster action head with a minimal 0.30.3-point performance drop, while mitigating the exploration bottleneck by reducing zero-variance groups from 63%63\% to 35%35\%.

4. RL Post-Training: When post-trained with GRPO, VLA-SSD reaches a 93.0%93.0\% success rate on LIBERO, a 15.915.9-point gain over the SFT checkpoint, matching the standard four-step πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}} baseline while accelerating training rollouts by 3.2×3.2\times.

title: XMimic and XSoma: Learning Humanoid Motion Tracking and Locomotion in Under a Minute
authors: Nico Bohlinger,Jan Peters
abstract:
We present XMimic and XSoma, which learn humanoid motion tracking and locomotion on rough terrain in under a minute of training.
Both follow SuperMimic, which learns a world model of the robot and optimizes the policy with analytic gradients through short rollouts imagined in this model.
Existing implementations of this method do not make use of larger GPUs, as every training iteration is a long chain of small GPU operations that run one after another.
XMimic and XSoma therefore shorten this chain and run the steps of every iteration at the same time on up to four GPUs.
We compile the complete training loop with JAX, including the MuJoCo Warp simulator.
For locomotion, XSoma leaves only the dynamics of the robot to the world model and computes everything else exactly, including the terrain height under the feet.
It learns with a horizon of one second and without a critic.
On four H100 GPUs, XMimic learns to track all 40 LAFAN1 clips with the Unitree G1 in 0.86 minutes, 3.7 times faster than BlinkMimic on one GPU.
XSoma reaches the tracking target that Holosoma’s tests set for FastSAC in 0.77 minutes, 12.3 times faster than FastSAC on one GPU, while needing only an eighth of its environment steps.
The code is available at https://github.com/nico-bohlinger/xmimic and https://github.com/nico-bohlinger/xsoma.
introduction:
Humanoid robots learn to track retargeted human motion [1] and to follow velocity commands on rough terrain [2, 3] with Reinforcement Learning (RL) in simulation, where massively parallel GPU simulation has reduced the training time from days to minutes [4].
SuperMimic [5] showed that motion tracking can be learned with far less compute when the policy is optimized through a learned world model instead of with model-free RL such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [6].
As in SuperTrack [7] and Dreamer [8], the policy is rolled out for a short horizon in the world model and follows the analytic gradient of the imagined return.
Over such horizons, this gradient has a much lower variance than the likelihood-ratio gradient that PPO estimates from sampled actions [5, 9].
InstantTrack [10] and BlinkMimic [11] then reduced the time to learn all 40 clips of the LAFAN1 dataset [12] on the Unitree G1 to about 3 minutes on a single consumer GPU, down from about 1.5 hours with an unofficial reimplementation of SuperMimic [13].

However, these implementations do not make use of larger GPUs.
BlinkMimic trains barely faster on an NVIDIA H100 than on an RTX 4090, as every training iteration is a long chain of small GPU operations that depend on each other, most of all in the backpropagation through the world model.
The time of such a chain is set by the number of its operations rather than by the compute of the GPU, and spreading each operation over more GPUs does not shorten it either.
Additionally, all of these methods learn motion tracking, where the reference motion gives the policy a target at every step.
For locomotion, Terrain-Grounded Imagination (TGI) [14] recently trained a humanoid policy through a world model to walk over stairs and gaps, using exact heightfield lookups for the terrain in its rollouts, but its training takes hours.
The fastest humanoid locomotion methods are still model-free, such as FastSAC [2], which learns to walk on rough terrain in about 15 minutes on a single GPU.
No method that learns with a world model has come close to this time.

This is why we present XMimic and XSoma (see Figure 1), which learn humanoid motion tracking and locomotion on rough terrain with a world model in under a minute.
XMimic reimplements BlinkMimic with the same algorithm and hyperparameters, while XSoma learns the velocity-tracking task of Holosoma [3] for the G1.
Following InstantMimic [15], which learns physics-based skills in seconds by keeping the complete training loop on the GPU, we compile the whole training loop with JAX [16] instead of PyTorch and run the MuJoCo Warp simulator [17, 18] through MJX.
We also restructure the policy update to shorten its chain of operations.
As the policy and the world model change only slightly from one iteration to the next, data collection, world-model update, and policy update can use an older policy and world model instead of waiting for each other.
XMimic therefore runs these three steps at the same time on separate GPUs, while XSoma, which spends most of its iteration on policy updates, computes the gradients of consecutive updates at the same time on separate GPUs.
For locomotion, XSoma leaves only the dynamics of the robot to the world model and computes everything else exactly, including the terrain height under the feet, which it looks up as in TGI.
It learns with a horizon of one second and without a critic.

XMimic learns to track all 40 LAFAN1 clips in 0.86 minutes on four H100 GPUs, 3.7 times faster than BlinkMimic on one, and it is already 1.3 times faster on a single GPU.
XSoma reaches the tracking target that Holosoma’s tests set for FastSAC in 0.77 minutes on four H100 GPUs, 12.3 times faster than FastSAC on one, as it needs only an eighth of the environment steps.
Even on a single GPU, XSoma is 3.8 times faster than FastSAC and ends with a lower velocity error, while Holosoma’s PPO does not reach the target within an hour.

title: Making Koopman Control Guarantees Hold on Robots
authors: Abulikemu Abuduweili,Changliu Liu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
comment: this https URL
abstract:
A Koopman controller can stabilize its learned latent-space linear model yet fail to stabilize the nonlinear plant. The learned model propagates predictions in latent space, while the deployed controller repeatedly re-encodes the measured physical state. We show that nominal closed-loop stability transfers to the nonlinear plant when the learned and true closed-loop dynamics agree to first order on the embedding’s tangent space at the target. We derive a robustness margin for approximate matching and show that a stable open-loop latent model cannot exactly match an unstable equilibrium.
We introduce Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and enforces first-order matching to this estimate. TIK recovers the fitted LQR gain at the target, while a bilinear predictor captures state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. Across four simulated unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers have stable latent closed loops, but their deployed nonlinear systems are locally unstable. In contrast, all 40 TIK controllers locally stabilize their respective nonlinear plants. An offline stability test using empirical curvature estimates identifies stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole systems, but is inconclusive under high noise. Under explicit model-error and curvature bounds, an invariant terminal set guarantees constraint satisfaction after entry under local feedback. TIK achieves 88% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with a 0.25 ms planning budget and controls simulated seven-joint arms within 1–5 ms per step.
introduction:
Koopman models approximate nonlinear dynamics with linear dynamics in a learned latent space, enabling efficient model-based control (Williams et al., 2015). However, a controller designed on these learned dynamics may fail to stabilize the nonlinear plant. The learned model propagates its own predictions in latent space, while the deployed controller repeatedly re-encodes the measured physical state (Assumption 1a,b). Consequently, a stable latent closed loop does not guarantee stability of the deployed nonlinear system. In the double cart-pole example in Assumption 1c, Standard Koopman predicts recovery from a 0.6∘0.6^{\circ} tilt, while the simulated plant falls.

c Double cart-pole

d Tangent action at the target

Koopman models lift nonlinear dynamics into a higher-dimensional space, using fixed dictionaries or learned
observables (Lusch et al., 2018, Shi and Meng, 2022). With linear lifted dynamics, quadratic costs, and linear
constraints, model predictive control (MPC) is a convex quadratic program (QP) (Korda and Mezić, 2018). Near a target inside the constraints, a Riccati terminal cost makes its feedback law coincide with lifted linear-quadratic regulation (LQR).
The nominal stability test checks whether the lifted closed-loop matrix 𝐀cl\bm{\mathrm{A}}_{\mathrm{cl}} is Schur, with all eigenvalues inside the unit circle.
Local plant stability depends on the physical Jacobian 𝐅\bm{\mathrm{F}}, which also involves the encoder’s derivatives. A model with low prediction error can
still give the wrong stability verdict.

What is required for a nominal stability certificate to remain valid after re-encoding? The answer lies in the tangent space of the learned embedding. If the latent closed-loop dynamics reproduce the physical closed-loop Jacobian on this space, every physical closed-loop eigenvalue also appears in the latent model (Assumption 2). We also give a margin for approximate matching, and we show that a latent model
that is open-loop stable cannot match an open-loop unstable equilibrium (Assumption 3).

We then build the matching into the model. Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK) enforces the two first-order equations
𝐀𝐉θ=𝐉θ​𝐀^f\bm{\mathrm{A}}\bm{\mathrm{J}}_{\theta}=\bm{\mathrm{J}}_{\theta}\hat{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{f} and 𝐁=𝐉θ​𝐁^f\bm{\mathrm{B}}=\bm{\mathrm{J}}_{\theta}\hat{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{f}, where (𝐀^f,𝐁^f)(\hat{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{f},\hat{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{f}) is a local plant linearization fitted from
offline transitions (Assumption 4). For fixed 𝐉θ\bm{\mathrm{J}}_{\theta}, these equations are linear in 𝐀,𝐁\bm{\mathrm{A}},\bm{\mathrm{B}}. The fit determines
the local feedback: TIK’s gain equals the LQR gain on the fit. The learned predictor models dynamics away from the target,
including state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. We also give a stability test that accounts for estimation error (Assumption 6) and an invariant
terminal set under explicit curvature and noise assumptions (Assumption 8).

In four simulated open-loop unstable benchmarks, all 4040 Standard Koopman controllers pass the nominal test but have unstable physical closed-loop Jacobians; all 4040 TIK controllers have Schur physical Jacobians. Further experiments evaluate offline stability verification, constrained maneuvers, and control under short planning budgets.

title: High-Speed Forward and Reverse Tractor-Trailer Driving with Learned Vehicle Dynamics
authors: Aaron Chen,David Shen,Taekyung Kim,Kaleb Ben Naveed,Dimitra Panagou
comment: The first three authors contributed equally to this work. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Tractor-trailer systems are difficult to control, especially unstable during reverse motion, and their dynamics depend on difficult-to-measure factors, including road friction and suspension coefficients. We introduce a learned dynamics model for tractor-trailer control and compare it with a reduced-order dynamics model with Fiala tire forces as an analytic baseline. Specifically, we compare a model predictive path integral (MPPI) controller that uses the learned dynamics model to an MPPI controller that uses the analytic model, as well as to three additional baseline controllers. In the main closed-loop tracking experiments across four simulated environments, MPPI with learned dynamics achieves mean speeds closer to the target magnitudes and lower root-mean-square (RMS) hitch angles than MPPI with the analytic model at every tested setpoint, with higher completion rates in seven of eight reverse configurations.

introduction:
Despite advances in autonomous vehicle control [1, 2], uncertain dynamics remain challenging [3]. Particularly, Model Predictive Control (MPC), which uses predictions from a system model to optimize a finite-horizon control sequence subject to input and state constraints, is a common control framework applied to vehicle control. As MPC relies on predicted costs and constraint violations determine the selected inputs, model errors can degrade closed-loop performance [3, 4].

These challenges are particularly pronounced in tractor-trailer systems, whose coupled dynamics are nonlinear [5]. Tractor-trailers are unstable, especially in reverse, and trailer motion must be controlled indirectly through tractor control [6]. At high speeds, the controller must anticipate the vehicle, tire, and hitch behavior while tracking the target velocity and path and avoiding jackknifing. Changes in road friction alter available tire forces, while terrain, load transfer, and suspension motion introduce effects that two-dimensional models struggle to capture. Prediction is challenging when these vehicle states and environmental parameters are only partially observed.

Recent approaches to handling uncertainty have focused on designing MPC schemes with learned dynamics, reducing the reliance on a fixed analytic dynamics prior [3, 7, 8, 9, 10].
Another approach is policy adaptation: Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) augments a base policy with a latent representation of the operating conditions [11]. The policy is trained in simulation with additional environmental information not available in operating conditions. At deployment, an adaptation module infers the latent representation from recent state-action history, while the base policy weights remain fixed. This approach has also been extended to bipedal robots [12]. Safe Deep Policy Adaptation combines an adaptive reinforcement learning policy with learned dynamics and a control barrier function (CBF) filter [13].
We focus on a different approach: we learn the dynamics of the system directly rather than adapting a control policy online.

Learning-based MPC addresses model mismatch by learning vehicle dynamics directly from data [14, 9] or learning a residual correction to an analytic model [15]. Gaussian processes (GP) are commonly used for the learning framework, as they provide native uncertainty quantification output and have been shown to be effective estimators in low-data regimes [10]. More recently, however, neural dynamics have arisen as an alternative [3, 7, 16] because they
scale to large offline datasets and can use finite histories of state–action pairs to infer latent operating conditions and mitigate partial
observability [14, 9].

Recent tractor-trailer methods address forward and reverse parking using barrier-rate-guided MPPI [17], navigation using learned geometric distance estimates within MPPI [18], and safety-critical trajectory planning for general NN-trailer systems [19]. High-speed studies have used analytic models for lateral stabilization and forward trajectory tracking, including active trailer steering [20] and tube MPC for robustness to model uncertainty and disturbances [21].
Learned vehicle dynamics have also been used to improve robustness to state-estimation error and environmental variation, including in towing tasks [22].
Here, we address high-speed reverse tracking of a tractor-trailer system, which requires jointly tracking the target velocity and path and regulating the hitch angle under uncertain vehicle and environmental dynamics.

We propose a predictive control framework for high-speed forward and reverse tractor-trailer tracking under uncertain dynamics, combining a compact history-conditioned dynamics model with MPPI to balance velocity tracking, path following, and hitch-angle regulation. Our main contributions are:

We integrate a learned dynamics model that takes a fixed-length state-action history as input with MPPI for high-speed forward and reverse tractor-trailer control under uncertain vehicle and environmental dynamics.

We integrate a learned dynamics model that takes a fixed-length state-action history as input with MPPI for high-speed forward and reverse tractor-trailer control under uncertain vehicle and environmental dynamics.

We derive a reduced-order tractor-trailer dynamics model using Fiala tire forces without constant longitudinal velocity assumptions to accurately characterize the forwards and reverse driving of tractor-trailers.

We demonstrate high-speed forward and reverse tracking in high-fidelity simulation across friction and terrain variations, the latter of which is absent from the training data.

1. We integrate a learned dynamics model that takes a fixed-length state-action history as input with MPPI for high-speed forward and reverse tractor-trailer control under uncertain vehicle and environmental dynamics.

2. We derive a reduced-order tractor-trailer dynamics model using Fiala tire forces without constant longitudinal velocity assumptions to accurately characterize the forwards and reverse driving of tractor-trailers.

3. We demonstrate high-speed forward and reverse tracking in high-fidelity simulation across friction and terrain variations, the latter of which is absent from the training data.

title: NF-VLA: A Normalizing-Flow Baseline for Vision-Language-Action Learning
authors: Ruichen Deng,Qinyu Zhao,Yong-Hyun Park,Mutian Tong,Liang Zheng,Jiatao Gu
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026 G2A Workshop
abstract: Autoregressive normalizing flows (NFs) provide a tractable density for learning and sampling continuous robot actions. We show that a single maximum-likelihood objective can train vision–language–action (VLA) policies competitive with leading methods on manipulation benchmarks. We present NF-VLA, which combines conditional autoregressive normalizing flows with score-based action refinement. Its deep–shallow architecture concentrates visual, language, and proprioceptive prefix conditioning in a high-capacity deep block, while unconditioned shallow blocks provide a shared invertible action transformation. The vision–language backbone and flow are jointly trained by exact maximum likelihood on Gaussian-smoothed action chunks. The same learned density supplies a single score-based correction at inference, refining generated actions to account for training-time smoothing without a separately trained denoiser. Trained on LIBERO from a pretrained vision–language backbone without robot pretraining, NF-VLA achieves 98.35% success across the four standard suites and 72.6% on LIBERO-Plus using the same checkpoint without further fine-tuning. Ablations show that deep-only prefix conditioning and score-based refinement both improve closed-loop success. Together, these results establish carefully structured autoregressive flows as a competitive approach to VLA control, with one learned density supporting policy training, action generation, and refinement.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect pretrained visual and linguistic representations to robot control, allowing policies to generate actions from images and language instructions [1, 2].
A central design choice is the action model: it determines how observations condition the action distribution and how that distribution produces executable commands.
Existing approaches include discrete action prediction, continuous regression, diffusion, and flow matching [2, 3, 4, 5].

Normalizing flows (NFs) offer a formulation in which an invertible transformation defines both a continuous density and a sampling procedure.
Their tractable change-of-variables likelihood allows direct maximum-likelihood training [6, 7].
TARFlow [8] and the STARFlow family [9, 10, 11] demonstrate the potential of Transformer autoregressive flows for visual and multimodal generation, with STARFlow introducing a deep–shallow architecture for scaling latent image generation.
These developments motivate a study of conditioning and sampling in autoregressive-flow VLA policies: where and how to inject multimodal context, and whether the learned density’s score can improve actions after sampling.

Recent work establishes normalizing flows as capable robot policies. NinA [12] introduces coupling-based action decoders for VLAs, emphasizing efficient generation, while RoMAN-Flow [13] develops autoregressive-flow policies for offline reinforcement learning and one-step policy distillation. Building on this progress, we focus on the manipulation performance obtainable from likelihood-based imitation learning itself. The central design question is how to organize multimodal conditioning and sample refinement within a single continuous-density model.

We present NF-VLA, a VLA policy that combines conditional autoregressive flows with score-based action refinement. Building on the deep–shallow architecture of STARFlow [9], we concentrate visual, language, and proprioceptive conditioning in a high-capacity deep block, while shallow blocks provide a shared invertible transformation between action coordinates and intermediate latents.
The vision–language backbone and action model are trained jointly with a single exact maximum-likelihood objective on Gaussian-smoothed actions.
At inference, the same learned density supports flow inversion and a single Tweedie denoising correction computed from its own score [14, 8].
Learning, sampling, and refinement therefore share one density model, without a separately trained denoiser or an additional training objective.

Starting from a pretrained vision–language backbone, NF-VLA is trained jointly on the full LIBERO dataset without robot pretraining or reinforcement-learning post-training. It achieves 98.35% success across the four standard LIBERO suites [15], including 97.8% on LIBERO-Long. The same checkpoint achieves 72.6% on LIBERO-Plus [16] without further fine-tuning, demonstrating strong aggregate performance under benchmark perturbations. These results place NF-VLA competitively alongside leading VLA policies in the benchmark comparisons. Ablations support the two design choices: concentrating prefix conditioning in the deep block improves average LIBERO success by 1.20 percentage points over all-block prefix conditioning, and a single score-based refinement step improves success by 1.90 percentage points using the same trained checkpoint.

Our contributions are threefold:

We present NF-VLA, an autoregressive-flow VLA baseline trained end to end with a single likelihood objective and using the learned density for both sampling and score-based action correction.

We evaluate conditioning placement and mechanism, finding that deep-only prefix conditioning achieves higher average success than all-block conditioning in our tested configurations. We additionally quantify the control benefit of self-score correction and report the inference costs of the evaluated designs.

We evaluate the resulting policy on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, reporting strong standard-task performance alongside a perturbation-dependent robustness profile.

1. We present NF-VLA, an autoregressive-flow VLA baseline trained end to end with a single likelihood objective and using the learned density for both sampling and score-based action correction.

2. We evaluate conditioning placement and mechanism, finding that deep-only prefix conditioning achieves higher average success than all-block conditioning in our tested configurations. We additionally quantify the control benefit of self-score correction and report the inference costs of the evaluated designs.

3. We evaluate the resulting policy on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, reporting strong standard-task performance alongside a perturbation-dependent robustness profile.

title: Ontology-Compiled Control Barrier Functions for Heterogeneous Robot Teams
authors: Peng Wu,Seyede Fatemeh Ghoreishi,Nathan Bastian,Mohsen Imani,Tian Lan,Mahdi Imani
abstract:
Safety filters for heterogeneous robot teams fail because of missing constraints, overestimated braking capabilities and conflicts between individually satisfiable constraints.
We present OntoCBF, which compiles a domain ontology with a class taxonomy, typed relations, safety axioms and a dynamics profile per robot class into a control barrier function filter with one quadratic program per agent.
Description-logic entailment supplies the constraints of any team online, including those that follow from chains of relations and from classes defined by what a robot carries, so the existing safety axioms cover new robot classes, payload classes and combinations.
We prove that a subclass may reuse the braking capability of its parent whenever it can produce every velocity of the parent, a property separate from subsumption.
For box-bounded double integrators this property is also necessary, and every loss of safety then begins with a conflict.
Once three robots interact, the safe set of pairwise barriers contains states from which a collision is unavoidable, and such states persist in larger teams under any fixed capability reduction.
In a simulated warehouse where humans ignore the robots, a filter written for the design classes violates safety in 89–100 % of the episodes with unseen classes.
In all scenarios, including one with 32 robots, OntoCBF violates safety in 20–70 % of the episodes, each time after a conflict, with a median deepest intrusion of 10–17 % of the keep-out distance.
A multi-agent PPO policy trained with the filter in the loop lowers the rate of infeasible quadratic programs, nearly all of them conflicts, by 18–41 %.
introduction:
Warehouses, hospitals and construction sites increasingly operate heterogeneous robot teams in spaces shared with people.
Their safety requirements depend on what each entity is and on how the entities are related.
A drone keeps farther from a person than a ground robot does, a carrier is responsible for the distance between its payload and nearby people, and ground robots avoid restricted zones that drones may cross.
Industrial standards state such requirements in the same terms, through separation distances that depend on the type of machine and on its stopping performance (ISO, 2016; ISO, 2023).
Safety filters based on control barrier functions (CBFs) enforce requirements of this kind on top of a learned or hand-designed controller with minimal changes to its commands (Ames et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017), and they are a common safety layer for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) (Cai et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2025b).

In existing multi-agent safety filters, the constrained pairs, the keep-out distances and the braking capabilities are fixed at design time for the robot types known at that point (Wang et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2021; ElSayed-Aly et al., 2021).
Learned graph CBFs for collision avoidance generalize across team sizes and, empirically, across robot models (Zhang et al., 2025b; Kim et al., 2026a).
Semantic safety filters query language models for constraints, which leaves the completeness and consistency of the constraint set unverified (Brunke et al., 2025; Ravichandran et al., 2026).
Robot fleets change over their lifetime, and whenever a team gains a new robot model, payload type or task combination, an engineer has to determine by hand which constraints apply to the new entities and whether the existing safety certificate still holds.

We let a domain ontology, of the kind already standardized for robotics (IEEE, 2015), carry the safety specification.
A filter for a heterogeneous team can miss a constraint for a new entity, overestimate the braking capability of a robot, or contain constraints that are each satisfiable and exclude each other.
In our warehouse ontology (Fig. 1), the taxonomy states that a 𝖫𝗂𝗀𝗁𝗍𝖣𝗋𝗈𝗇𝖾\mathsf{LightDrone} is a 𝖣𝗋𝗈𝗇𝖾\mathsf{Drone} and that every 𝖣𝗋𝗈𝗇𝖾\mathsf{Drone} is 𝖠𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖺𝗅\mathsf{Aerial}.
A safety axiom states how far an 𝖠𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖺𝗅\mathsf{Aerial} agent stays from a 𝖧𝗎𝗆𝖺𝗇\mathsf{Human}, and a property chain relates each carrier to the people near its payload.
Entailment removes the first failure, because the constraints of unlisted classes, payloads and combinations follow from these statements.
The second failure depends on dynamics, because a 𝖧𝖾𝖺𝗏𝗒𝖣𝗋𝗈𝗇𝖾\mathsf{HeavyDrone}, a 𝖣𝗋𝗈𝗇𝖾\mathsf{Drone} that brakes less strongly, inherits every constraint of 𝖣𝗋𝗈𝗇𝖾\mathsf{Drone} and needs a braking capability of its own.
A test on the dynamics profiles in the ontology, together with classification, decides when a subclass may reuse the capabilities, and with them the certificate, of its parent.
We prove that the third failure is intrinsic to pairwise barriers.

Our contributions are the following.

We formulate safe control of heterogeneous teams whose active constraints are entailed by an ontology and switch online. Our method, OntoCBF, compiles these entailments into a CBF filter with one quadratic program (QP) per agent and trains a shared multi-agent PPO (MAPPO) policy with the filter in the loop.

Theorem 4 shows that a subclass inherits exactly the constraints of its parent under a classification test, and its capabilities under dynamic subtyping, an inclusion of velocity sets that braking barriers of box-bounded double integrators require.

Propositions 5–7 show that, with capabilities assigned this way, safety is lost only after a conflict, and that some states with positive pairwise barriers lead to a collision under every input, for three robots and, under any fixed capability reduction, for large enough teams.

Experiments in a simulated warehouse with unseen classes and up to 32 robots show that OntoCBF removes the first two failures, that every remaining violation follows a conflict, and that the learned policy lowers the rate of infeasible QPs by 18–41 % (Section 6).

title: DexFormer 2.0: Towards a Cross-Embodiment Foundation Policy for Dexterous Grasping
authors: Lixin Xu,Ke Zhang,Xinyu Liu,Jie Tan,Senming Tan,Jiaju Yin,Yating Feng,Xiaoyi Lin,Xiyue Dong,Renjing Xu
abstract:
Dexterous grasping policies are usually trained for one arm paired
with one hand. Every new pairing then needs its own policy, and the number
of policies grows with every arm and hand added. We ask whether a single
policy can control many arm–hand combinations and transfer to pairings
and hands it has never seen. This is hard because robots differ in the
number, layout, and dynamics of their joints, so their observations and
actions share no common interface. We present DexFormer 2.0, a single
reinforcement learning policy for cross-embodiment dexterous grasping. It
maps every robot to a canonical joint interface with validity masks,
encodes each joint’s morphology with attention biased by the kinematic
tree, and uses a Transformer-XL memory to infer embodiment-dependent
dynamics from recent interaction. Trained on 18 combinations of four arms
and six hands, it reaches 89% stable success on seen combinations and 51% on six held-out arm–hand pairs, outperforming GRU and DexFormer 1.0 baselines. Without
fine-tuning, it also grasps with four new hand types and, through
retargeting, with parallel grippers. Ablations show that memory, the
kinematic-tree bias, and broader pairing coverage each matter for
transfer. On a physical Flexiv arm, distilled students transfer zero-shot
from simulation with two hands, including a held-out pair.
introduction:
Dexterous grasping policies are commonly developed for a fixed robotic
embodiment: one arm, one hand, and one carefully matched action space.
This specialization makes policy development expensive as hardware
diversifies. Replacing either the arm or the hand changes the kinematic
chain, reachable workspace, joint limits, control response, and contact
geometry; replacing both compounds these changes. A straightforward
solution is to train a separate policy for every arm–hand pairing, but
the number of policies grows with the Cartesian product of available
arms and hands, preventing knowledge sharing across related embodiments.

Learning one policy across heterogeneous arm–hand systems is challenging
for three reasons. First, different hands expose different numbers and
arrangements of active joints, so their observations and actions do not
naturally share a fixed interface. Second, the same action value has a
different physical meaning under different joint axes, limits, link
placements, and kinematic depths. Third, morphology alone is insufficient:
closed-loop grasping also depends on contacts and embodiment-specific
dynamics that must be inferred over time.

We present DexFormer 2.0, a morphology-aware recurrent policy for
cross-embodiment dexterous grasping (Figure 1). We represent every robot through a
canonical set of 29 joint slots—seven arm joints and up to 22 hand
joints—together with validity masks. Each joint receives a 16-dimensional
morphology descriptor encoding its axis, attachment position, joint and
velocity limits, semantic role, and kinematic depth. Our MorphNode encoder
adds an attention residual biased by the robot’s kinematic tree and joint
roles, and a Transformer-XL maintains a 16-step temporal context over the
fused features. A shared actor head then produces a masked Gaussian
policy over the canonical action space, using the same network across all
arm–hand pairings.

We study a single policy over four robot arms and six dexterous hands,
forming 24 arm–hand combinations. We randomly select 18 combinations for
training and reserve the remaining six for testing. Evaluation on both training and held-out arm–hand pairs uses the same ten object identities, isolating
embodiment generalization from object-identity generalization. The policy
reaches 89.01% stable success on the seen combinations and 51.18% on the held-out pairs, and it keeps 48.85% on held-out pairs when the
objects are ten unseen YCB objects [4]. Without
fine-tuning, it also grasps with four hand types that never appear in
training, and its actions can be retargeted to four parallel grippers.
Our contributions are:

We introduce a joint cross-embodiment training paradigm:
one policy is trained on many arm–hand embodiments together, through
canonical joint slots and validity masks. The policy, without
fine-tuning, transfers to held-out pairs and to hand
types absent from training, and even to parallel grippers.

We develop a topology-aware recurrent policy architecture
that combines per-joint physical descriptors, a gated spatial-attention
residual, Transformer-XL memory, and a shared actor head.
The architecture conditions control on morphology without using a
dedicated policy or output head for each embodiment.

We show that temporal memory, kinematic-tree bias, and
pairing coverage each matter for transfer: removing memory or the
tree bias roughly halves success on held-out pairs, and training
on 18 instead of 12 combinations raises it from 5.65% to 51.18% at
a matched interaction budget.

title: Right Goal, Wrong Body: Re-grounding Frozen VLAs under Actuation Shift
authors: Umer Siddique,Peilang Li,Yongcan Cao
comment: Accepted at the SPAIS Workshop at CoRL 2026
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are capable of producing desired robotic behaviors in ideal settings. However, they often fail when the robot’s actuation changes at deployment. For example, remounting, mechanical wear, or command latency changes can lead to failed tasks and unsafe behaviors. To address the inevitable actuation shift, we propose ReGround, an inference-time method that keeps the VLA frozen and re-grounds its intended motion. ReGround learns the deployed robot’s dynamics from task-agnostic motor babbling, and then tracks the policy’s intended motion while staying close to the policy’s own plan. ReGround activates only upon detecting a shift, and needs no rewards, demonstrations, or retraining. We show via two VLAs, eight LIBERO tasks, and five shift settings that ReGround can restore near-oracle success, such as raising π0.5\pi_{0.5}’s success from 0.16 to 0.90 under 400 ms latency, while remaining safer than a linear-calibration baseline. Project website and open-source code: umersiddique94.github.io/ReGround.
introduction:
Recently, vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance across diverse robotic manipulation tasks by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and vision-language
representations to map observations and language instructions directly to actions [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8].
However, a VLA is typically trained assuming a particular relationship between its action commands and the robot’s resulting motion.
Changes in the action coordinate frame, controller gains, or command latency can alter this relationship, causing the same action predicted by the VLA to produce a different physical motion.
We refer to this mismatch as actuation shift, where the task and observations remain unchanged, but the mapping from the VLA’s action commands to the robot’s physical motion has changed.
A natural solution is to retrain or fine-tune the policy on the deployed robot, but this requires additional task demonstrations, computation, and access to model weights [9, 10, 11, 12].
This motivates our central question: At deployment, how can a frozen VLA remain effective and safe when the robot’s actuation has changed?

Actuation shift is not only a performance issue but also a safety concern [13]. A VLA may still be able to identify the correct task and target object while producing actions that lead to unintended robot motion, resulting in overshoot, unintended contact, object displacement, or other unsafe behavior.
Existing work on VLA robustness has primarily studied changes in visual observations [14], while adaptation to changes in robot actuation generally relies on additional fault data, demonstrations, or policy updates [15].
Training-time approaches, such as rapid motor adaptation and meta-learning, improve robustness by exposing policies to variations during training or adapting them after deployment [16, 17].
More recently, test-time methods have also shown that frozen policies can be steered without parameter updates by using reward, value, or verifier signals to guide action selection [18, 19, 20]. Closest to our work is the
inverse-dynamics transfer, which maps intended motion to actions under changed execution dynamics [21]. However, these methods were not designed for frozen VLAs that output action chunks, nor do they address actuation shift.

We address this gap with ReGround, an inference-time method for adapting frozen VLAs under actuation shift.
Our key insight is that actuation shift changes how the robot executes the VLA’s actions, while the frozen VLA still knows what motion is needed to complete the task.
ReGround therefore recovers the motion intended by the VLA under the training-body dynamics and computes new actions that reproduce this motion on the deployed robot.
To achieve this, a model of the training body rolls out the VLA’s action chunk to obtain a reference trajectory. A deployed-body model learned from task-agnostic motor babbling is then used to determine how the robot should act to follow this trajectory under the changed dynamics. A trust region then keeps the corrected actions close to the VLA’s original plan, while a residual monitor activates ReGround only when an actuation shift is detected.
On π0.5\pi_{0.5} across eight LIBERO tasks and five shift settings, ReGround restores 0.90–0.98 success, including 0.16 to 0.90 at 400 ms latency. For both VLAs, ReGround reduces unsafe episodes relative to linear calibration.
