title: AgenticJevNav: Agentic Object Search and Navigation via Event-Driven Verification
authors: Shuning Zhang,Shuli Zhang,Yunheng Wang,Wei Lu,Jiaxi Zhang,Yihang Kang,Tao Wang,Xiangyu Chen,Yixiao Feng,Kai Sheng,Renjing Xu
comment: . Project page:this http URL
abstract:
Agentic navigation must maintain goals despite incomplete evidence, execution failures, and delayed inference. We present AgenticJevNav, integrating goal-directed planning, evidence memory, event-triggered verification, and bounded execution. The Agent plans from RGB, odometry, memory, and feedback, retains goal ownership, and authorizes candidate actions. Jev reviews structured evidence after blocked or failed execution, or two consecutive low-progress segments. Version, freshness, and once-only checks govern execution; a single executor and independent RGB reflex constrain motion. Goal revisions revoke obsolete requests and actions. Across six simulated task families, AgenticJevNav achieves 73.33% SR over 60 trials, 21.67 percentage points above the strongest Agent-only control. A real-world GENISOM L1 quadruped deployment achieves 70.0% success over 30 trials, including bounded search reporting. Together, simulation and physical-robot results demonstrate the architecture’s effectiveness.
Project page: http://106.55.248.254/.
introduction:
Research on embodied navigation spans instruction following and grounding [1, 2], semantic exploration [3, 4], language-model planning [5, 6, 7], and learned navigation [8, 9]. Vision-language models ground natural-language goals in visual observations, while large language models generate structured navigation plans from task descriptions. Learned policies integrate these capabilities into end-to-end systems that map observations to actions. However, these capabilities leave a coordination problem: how should a robot maintain its goal, respond to a lack of progress, and apply delayed decisions as execution and instructions change? When perception is uncertain, when should the system trigger additional verification rather than proceeding with the Agent’s initial judgment? How can the system ensure that decisions produced by remote inference remain valid and authorized when the goal has been revised or execution context has changed?

We study when verification is warranted, whether responses remain valid, and how motion can stop before remote inference returns. AgenticJevNav addresses these questions through a versioned evidence interface. The Agent owns the goal and replans from feedback; Jev reviews only authorized actions. A shared consumer checks versions, authorization, freshness, and once-only consumption before execution. An independent RGB reflex can stop forward motion without remote inference. Here, agentic denotes this feedback-driven planning and delegation loop within one robot. Jev has no independent goal authority.

We make three contributions to agentic navigation through coordinated planning, verification, and execution:

Feedback-driven planning with authorized verification.
Feedback-driven planners use environmental feedback to correct actions [10, 11]. We further specify when to trigger Jev and which authorized actions it may select. Jev reviews only after blocked or failed execution, or two consecutive low-progress segments, choosing from the Agent’s authorized set. This reduces review overhead while preserving goal ownership.

Versioned memory and decision-making for online goal revision.
Interactive planning [10, 6] and latency mitigation [12] address feedback and action continuity, respectively, while semantic-map reasoning [13] and instance-oriented navigation in dynamic environments [14] organize semantic information for acting. We address the complementary issue of temporal validity after online goal corrections. We bind evidence to mission, revision, skill, and snapshot, and revoke stale requests upon correction. This isolates obsolete responses and maintains authorization consistency with the current task context.

Execution that separates remote semantic decisions from local motion constraints.
Inference latency affects action continuity [12]. We integrate RGB veto checks, skill leases, command time-to-live (TTL), and task versions within a single executor. This enables stop/veto actions without waiting for remote responses, and limits the application of invalid commands through revocation and expiry.

title: DiffWAM: Learning World Action Model from Consecutive Visual Difference
authors: Xinheng Zhang,Haoyu Xiong,Chao Jing,Xiaohan Zhang,Linshan Li,Hongbang Fan,Xingyu Chen
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as an important paradigm in robot learning, jointly predicting future scene states and robot actions from current observations and instructions. However, future states entangle task-related changes with large amounts of task-irrelevant content, such as static backgrounds, which weakens the model’s ability to capture changes relevant to task execution. To address this, we propose Difference World Action Model (DiffWAM), a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that enhances world representations by jointly learning future-state prediction and consecutive visual difference prediction. We define consecutive visual differences as differences between the latent representations of consecutive observations, providing an explicit learning signal for temporal variation. The framework comprises a World Expert for future frame prediction, an Action Expert for action generation, and a Diff Expert for predicting these latent differences along the trajectory. A structured unidirectional attention mask conditions the Diff, World, and Action Experts solely on the current-frame representation while blocking attention between experts. This design allows both the World and Diff Experts to be removed during inference, introducing no additional inference overhead. DiffWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks and substantially improves over FastWAM on real-world manipulation tasks. Specifically, it attains average success rates of 98.8%, 92.65%, and 88.3%, outperforming the state-of-the-art baseline (i.e., FastWAM) by 1.75, 1.55, and 15.0 percentage points, respectively.
introduction:
Learning task-related representations is crucial for robotic manipulation, as a robot must understand scene content and changes relevant to task execution. Two main paradigms have emerged to this end. Vision Language Action models (VLAs) [1, 2] map observations and instructions directly to actions, which is simple and efficient but lacks explicit modeling of scene evolution during task execution [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. In contrast, World Action Models (WAMs) [10, 11], building on the predictive world modeling paradigm [12], learn by predicting future scene states alongside robot actions, thereby acquiring a predictive understanding of task-related scene dynamics [13, 14, 15, 16].

Despite recent progress in WAMs [17, 18, 19, 20, 21], a key question remains: is future-state prediction alone sufficient to learn world representations that capture task-related changes? As illustrated in Figure DiffWAM: Learning World Action Model from Consecutive Visual Difference, much of the scene content persists across consecutive observations, while task execution involves changes such as robot motion and object interactions. The full-state prediction objective supervises these changes together with persistent content, without providing a separate learning signal for temporal variation. Thus, the representation of task-related changes relies on what the model learns implicitly from predicting complete future states.

This observation suggests a principle of visual foresight: a WAM should model not only what the future scene will look like, but also how it changes over time. Future-state prediction captures scene structure, object appearance, and spatial relationships, while consecutive visual difference prediction provides a separate target for temporal variation. We define a consecutive visual difference as the difference between the latent representations of two consecutive observations. Predicting this quantity, also referred to as diff prediction, provides explicit supervision for temporal variation without requiring additional motion annotations. By jointly modeling future states and their consecutive visual differences, a WAM can develop a more comprehensive world representation that integrates scene understanding with task-related dynamics for action generation.

In this paper, we propose DiffWAM, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that jointly learns future-state prediction, visual difference prediction, and action generation. A shared Observation Encoder encodes the current visual observation into world representations, which are used by a World Expert to predict future states, a Diff Expert to predict differences between consecutive frame latents, and an Action Expert to generate actions. A structured unidirectional attention mask allows each expert to attend to the current-observation representations while blocking attention between experts. This architecture integrates state and visual difference modeling into the world representations used for action generation, while keeping the prediction pathways separate. At inference, both the World and Diff Experts are removed, retaining only the Observation Encoder and Action Expert without additional inference overhead. Across LIBERO [22], RoboTwin 2.0 [23], and real-world manipulation tasks, DiffWAM achieves average success rates of 98.8%, 92.65%, and 88.3%, respectively, outperforming FastWAM [15] by 1.75, 1.55, and 15.0 percentage points.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce joint future-state and visual difference modeling in WAMs, enabling world representations to capture both scene content and task-related dynamics for action generation.

We propose DiffWAM, a Mixture-of-Experts framework with a shared Observation Encoder and dedicated World, Diff, and Action Experts. A structured unidirectional attention mask separates the expert pathways, allowing the World and Diff Experts to be removed at inference without additional overhead.

We validate DiffWAM on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness across simulated and physical settings. DiffWAM reduces the optimization steps required to reach 95% average success on LIBERO by 28.1%. Ablation studies validate the benefits of joint state and visual difference modeling.

1. We introduce joint future-state and visual difference modeling in WAMs, enabling world representations to capture both scene content and task-related dynamics for action generation.

2. We propose DiffWAM, a Mixture-of-Experts framework with a shared Observation Encoder and dedicated World, Diff, and Action Experts. A structured unidirectional attention mask separates the expert pathways, allowing the World and Diff Experts to be removed at inference without additional overhead.

3. We validate DiffWAM on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness across simulated and physical settings. DiffWAM reduces the optimization steps required to reach 95% average success on LIBERO by 28.1%. Ablation studies validate the benefits of joint state and visual difference modeling.

title: EasyNav: A Modular Architecture for Real-Time Navigation Across Heterogeneous Robot Environments
authors: Francisco Martín Rico,Francisco Miguel Moreno,Juan Sebastián Cely Gutiérrez,Esther Aguado,Miguel Ángel De Miguel Paraíso,José Miguel Guerrero
comment: . Code:this https URL
abstract:
Most robot navigation stacks implicitly bind mapping, localization, planning, and control to
specific representations and data flows, yielding architectures hard to extend, compare
experimentally, or reason about end-to-end timing. This is critical in heterogeneous scenarios,
where multiple spatial representations, sensing modalities, and coordinate frames coexist and
evolve at different rates.
This paper presents a navigation architecture centered on an explicit, shared navigation state that
serves as the sole interaction interface between modular components. Constraining mapping,
localization, planning, and control to operate over this shared state enables interchangeable,
representation-agnostic pipelines under explicit compatibility and timing contracts. We realize
this architecture as EasyNav, an open source ROS 2 framework, and
validate it through real-robot experiments, including indoor navigation with laser sensing and
large-scale indoor-outdoor navigation with GPS and 3D LiDAR across multi-level routes. Compared
with Nav2 under matched conditions, EasyNav reduces reaction latency from 377 to 33 ms indoors and
from 71 to 8 ms outdoors, while also using less CPU and memory.
introduction:
Autonomous robot navigation has matured into a core capability of modern robotic systems, yet the
architectural principles underlying most navigation stacks have evolved far more slowly than the
sensing, mapping, and learning techniques they integrate. Contemporary
frameworks [1], built on ROS and its successor
ROS 2 [2, 3], typically intertwine environment representations,
localization, planning, and control through implicit data flows, ad hoc interfaces, and callback
execution order. This coupling hampers systematic comparison, complicates reuse across robots and
domains, particularly when navigation spans indoor and outdoor environments or combines metric,
semantic, and topological information, and, most critically, leaves end-to-end latency and
time/frame consistency as emergent properties of scheduling rather than design objectives, making
reactivity and determinism hard to guarantee.

This paper presents a navigation architecture organized around an explicit navigation state that
captures, in a unified and temporally consistent form, all information required by mapping,
localization, planning, and control. By enforcing interaction exclusively through this shared state
rather than through direct dependencies, navigation components remain modular and interchangeable
under well-defined compatibility and timing constraints, elevating time and frame management to
first-class design concerns and enabling explicitly ordered reactions to new information. We
realize this architecture as EasyNav11
1
https://github.com/EasyNavigation
and validate it on real robotic platforms spanning indoor
navigation with laser sensing and large-scale indoor-outdoor navigation with GPS and 3D LiDAR
across multi-level routes,
showing that architectural clarity and temporal rigor can coexist with practical, real-time
deployment.

This work makes four primary contributions to the design and implementation of robot navigation
systems:

An explicit, shared navigation state through which mapping, localization,
planning, and control interact exclusively, eliminating implicit data dependencies and
decoupling navigation functionality from any specific environment representation.

Real-time behavior, freshness, and frame consistency as enforced properties of
the navigation state, rather than emergent effects of execution order, allowing end-to-end
latency to be explicitly instrumented, characterized, and controlled at the architectural
level.

Native support for heterogeneous, coexisting environment representations, such as
costmaps, multi-level navigable surfaces, and volumetric models, within a single pipeline, with
components remaining interchangeable as long as they satisfy the shared state’s temporal and
compatibility constraints.

EasyNav, a fully open source, documented, and extensible ROS 2 realization of
these principles, with a diverse set of ready to use plugins and a low barrier of entry for
third party contributions.

1. An explicit, shared navigation state through which mapping, localization,
planning, and control interact exclusively, eliminating implicit data dependencies and
decoupling navigation functionality from any specific environment representation.

2. Real-time behavior, freshness, and frame consistency as enforced properties of
the navigation state, rather than emergent effects of execution order, allowing end-to-end
latency to be explicitly instrumented, characterized, and controlled at the architectural
level.

3. Native support for heterogeneous, coexisting environment representations, such as
costmaps, multi-level navigable surfaces, and volumetric models, within a single pipeline, with
components remaining interchangeable as long as they satisfy the shared state’s temporal and
compatibility constraints.

4. EasyNav, a fully open source, documented, and extensible ROS 2 realization of
these principles, with a diverse set of ready to use plugins and a low barrier of entry for
third party contributions.

title: Drone Navigation for Fast, Safe Emergency Response
authors: Pranav Nedunghat,Jeffrey Mao,Praveen Merumugumala
comment: Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
abstract: In 2025, there was a total of 358 weather-related disasters worldwide affecting millions of people. For unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to autonomously aid these people, they need to be able to navigate around complex obstacles and reach their destinations to deliver supplies or quickly locate survivors in disaster-stricken areas. Our research addresses this need by providing a method to compute minimum-time trajectories in real time while providing guarantees of obstacle avoidance along the trajectory. Previous approaches treat the problem of computing time-optimal trajectories without considering obstacle avoidance. Our work not only includes obstacle avoidance constraints, but also improves overall mission time for navigation. We define mission time as the sum of planning time and traversal time. In time-sensitive emergencies, rapid trajectory planning is essential to ensure the prompt delivery of critical medical aid. As such, we consider the combined planning and traversal time as the key metric for how quickly the vehicle can reach a survivor. We show a sample mission in Fig. 1 where the quadrotor navigates through multiple canyon-like obstacles to deliver aid; during most of this trajectory, it is applying the near-maximum thrust.
introduction:
Aerial robots have seen success in search and rescue [1] and the delivery of vital medical supplies. These tasks need to be accomplished as quickly as possible while safely navigating obstacles in complex environments. Our research focuses on generating time-optimal trajectories in real time while also respecting safety constraints and accounting for drag. A key challenge is that time-optimal trajectory planning methods can require multiple seconds [5], [6] of computation each planning instance. Long trajectory-computation times can substantially delay mission completion, even when the resulting flight path is fast. For this reason, practical performance must account for both traversal time and planning time.

Other works have addressed this problem by using a simplified model such as a point-mass model (PMM). For example, recent work [2] uses separate acceleration limits for each axis to compute minimum-time trajectories in real time. However, constraining acceleration independently along each axis does not fully utilize the vehicle’s collective thrust capability and can therefore produce suboptimal trajectories. This simplification can produce unnecessarily conservative and therefore slower trajectories.
Our work seeks to bridge the gap between accurate methods with long computation times and fast methods that rely on simplifying approximations. We propose a time-optimal trajectory formulation that accounts for drag, actuator thrust limits, and obstacle avoidance while retaining the computational speed needed for real-time planning. Building on the framework proposed by Mao et al. [3], this work uses Bernstein polynomials to formulate our time-optimal trajectory, model drag dynamics, and formulate the thrust constraint. Using Bernstein polynomial basis functions allows the problem to be solved more quickly, but polynomial representations are often considered poorly suited for time-optimal trajectories. This is because, in a straight line, the time-optimal trajectory exhibits bang-bang behavior, whose discontinuous switching cannot be represented exactly by a finite-order polynomial. Our method addresses this issue by representing the trajectory as a sequence of polynomial splines and optimizng the endpoints over the coefficients. This representation allows our method, as shown in Fig. 1 to approximate bang-bang trajectories while incorporating drag and multi-axis collective-thrust constraints.

In this paper, we provide the following key contributions:

We provide a time-optimal trajectory-generation method that considers both collective-thrust and obstacle-avoidance constraints using Bernstein polynomials.

We provide a time-optimal trajectory-generation method that considers both collective-thrust and obstacle-avoidance constraints using Bernstein polynomials.

We propose a method to modify a polynomial trajectory representation to incorporate drag dynamics directly into the optimization. This method is applicable to both Bernstein and regular polynomials.

We demonstrate that our approach achieves superior mission time compared with other state-of-the-art-methods [2, 4] when both planning time and traversal time are considered.

1. We provide a time-optimal trajectory-generation method that considers both collective-thrust and obstacle-avoidance constraints using Bernstein polynomials.

2. We propose a method to modify a polynomial trajectory representation to incorporate drag dynamics directly into the optimization. This method is applicable to both Bernstein and regular polynomials.

3. We demonstrate that our approach achieves superior mission time compared with other state-of-the-art-methods [2, 4] when both planning time and traversal time are considered.

title: DynLimit: A Simulation Benchmark for Dynamics-Critical Planning and Control
authors: Yang Xiao,Yongzhi Liu,Sunan Zhang,Kang Wang,Guodong Yin,Weichao Zhuang
abstract:
Experiments near vehicle handling limits must keep three questions apart: what a maneuver requests, what the closed-loop system executes, and whether the task is completed.
We present DynLimit, a simulation platform that organizes this process end to end.
Scenarios are composed from road, friction, obstacle, and reference objects; planners and controllers attach through a shared observation and control interface; a vehicle adapter runs either a license-free four-wheel model or an external dynamics solver; and synchronized records feed task evaluation, replay, and response inspection.
The platform carries a task-oriented evaluation method that pairs a prescribed reference demand with a sampled passing set and event-aligned diagnosis.
Across eight task families, three friction environments, and three reference-assisted baseline chains we executed 450 runs: 360 nominal, 18 locally refined, and 72 with prescribed initial offsets.
Method differences depend on the task family, equal aggregate pass counts arise from different passing cells, and local refinement narrows two sampled transitions without locating a continuous boundary.
Two case comparisons show why sideslip or tire-utilization peaks cannot replace task constraints.
The three views therefore stay distinct in every reported run: an outcome can be traced from the prescribed demand, through the executed response, to the task rule that decided it.
Code is available at https://github.com/Yang2581/dynlimit.
introduction:
Evaluation of planning and control near the vehicle handling limit rests on three kinds of evidence that are easily conflated.
First, the prescribed maneuver fixes what the road and the reference demand: a speed profile, a curvature, and the resulting accelerations.
Second, the closed loop yields the executed response: the vehicle states and tire forces produced, together with the commands applied to obtain them.
Third, the task rule decides the outcome: whether the vehicle met its goal without leaving the road, striking an obstacle, missing a gate, or exceeding its deadline.
Because the three are recorded on different objects, none follows from another, so a pass count alone neither explains a failure nor locates the condition at which behavior changes.
The two same-scenario pairs in Section V-D show how far the views can diverge: in the first, the chain with the larger peak sideslip completes the task while the other violates a geometric constraint.

Obtaining this evidence repeatedly is a systems-engineering problem as much as a modelling one.
Each trial is assembled from road geometry, a friction field, obstacles, an initial state, reference information, and an algorithm.
The loop must run at declared rates, with controls and states recorded on a common timeline, and each outcome must be decided by the same task rules online and offline.
Simulators supply vehicle models and scenario formats, and planning benchmarks supply scenario sets and metrics [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
The layer between them, an experiment process that keeps these pieces aligned across tasks and algorithms, is still reassembled for most studies and has only recently begun to be automated in parts [6].

This paper presents DynLimit, a simulation platform for dynamics-critical planning and control experiments, together with the task-oriented evaluation method embedded in it.
DynLimit is the platform: it owns the scenario objects, the algorithm and vehicle interfaces, the execution schedule, and the records.
DynLimit-Bench is the method embedded in that process: reference demand organizes the test set, goals and constraints decide outcomes, and event-aligned records support diagnosis.
The quantitative experiments use reference-assisted control, in which every chain receives the same task description and reference while a shared longitudinal controller supplies speed commands; the platform interface itself is not restricted to this setting.

The contributions are threefold.
Platform design for dynamics experiments: one experiment interface connects scenario composition, algorithm attachment, vehicle adaptation, execution scheduling, and record inspection, and we describe the interfaces and trade-offs behind it, including how interactive and scripted operation share scenario, controller, and vehicle components.
A task-oriented evaluation method embedded in that process: each record is reduced to a demand-indexed passing set and a first-failure diagnosis, with stated sampling and tie-breaking conventions.
Systematic experiments and case analyses: eight task families, 360 nominal runs, and 90 supplementary runs show batch comparison, local refinement of sampled transitions, and inspection of failures in the recorded response.
All quantitative statements are conditional on the declared model, configurations, and finite samples.

title: Recovery-Guided Model-Based Diffusion for Safety-Critical Legged Locomotion
authors: Lei Zheng,Shivam Sood,Mithun Vanniasinghe,Guillaume Sartoretti,Armin Lederer
abstract: Safety-critical high-speed legged locomotion requires motion planners to balance safety foresight with online computational efficiency. Although short prediction horizons reduce rollout costs, they provide limited safety foresight, and strict safety constraints severely restrict the feasible trajectory space. We propose a recovery-guided model-based diffusion (MBD) framework for safety-critical legged locomotion. It incorporates a learned terminal recovery critic into short-horizon trajectory optimization. Specifically, the critic approximates the worst-case future clearance margin along rollouts of a designated recovery policy. We introduce a feasibility-guided refinement strategy that combines within-horizon constraints and terminal recoverability at each sampling stage, while retaining feasible elites to mitigate sampling-support loss. Across 50 paired randomized Unitree Go2 obstacle-avoidance trials, our approach achieves zero collisions and 98% strict-clearance success, while requiring substantially less computation than long-horizon MBD baselines. A project page is available at https://zack4417.github.io/rg-mbd/.
introduction:
Safety-critical legged locomotion in contact-rich environments requires controlling high-dimensional, nonlinear hybrid systems while satisfying stringent physical constraints (He et al., 2024; Liao et al., 2023; Sood et al., 2024). The resulting trajectory optimization problem is highly nonconvex and admits distinct motion strategies, making diffusion models attractive for exploring multimodal trajectory distributions (Janner et al., 2022; Chi et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2026). However, conventional diffusion-based planners typically rely on offline trajectory data, making performance sensitive to dataset coverage and quality. In addition, they represent system dynamics implicitly through data rather than explicitly enforcing them through
model rollouts.

Recent methods address this limitation through incorporating explicit dynamic constraints (Huang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026c), dynamics-aware trajectory scoring (Li et al., 2024), or projection into reachable sets (Bouvier et al., 2025). Nevertheless, maintaining strict dynamic feasibility remains challenging for high-dimensional legged locomotion. Model-based diffusion (MBD) circumvents these challenges by constructing generative updates from explicit model rollouts and task objectives (Pan et al., 2024). Consequently, sampled trajectories remain dynamically consistent with the model without requiring task-specific diffusion training.
DIAL (Xue et al., 2025) extends model-based generative refinement to online full-order legged locomotion using massively parallel model rollouts.
However, finite-horizon planning does not ensure safety beyond the prediction horizon. While longer horizons provide greater foresight, they incur substantially higher computational costs. In contrast, shorter horizons are computationally efficient but can produce trajectories that satisfy within-horizon constraints while terminating in states from which safe recovery is no longer possible (Yin et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026a).

Addressing this horizon limitation raises two coupled challenges. First, the planners require scalable estimates of whether a terminal state admits a safe continuation. Learned reach–avoid and barrier values have been used for policy switching (He et al., 2024), safety filtering (So et al., 2024), and enforcing beyond-horizon constraints in optimal control (Yin et al., 2025).
Although these approaches extend safety foresight through learned safety values and constraints, they do not incorporate terminal recoverability into the successive generative refinement stages of MBD, where such guidance can actively shape trajectory distributions to preserve feasible candidate support during the diffusion process. More recently, Yang et al. (2026b) incorporate Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability values into diffusion guidance and reactive shielding. However, this grid-based HJ computation scales poorly with state dimension, limiting its direct applicability to full-order legged dynamics.

Second, incorporating terminal recoverability alongside within-horizon safety and physical constraints further restricts the feasible set of control sequences, potentially leaving too few feasible samples for reliable refinement under finite sampling budgets. Recent constrained MBD methods improve sampling efficiency through progressive barrier enforcement (Mishra and Manchester, 2026) and adaptive constraint handling with feasibility projection (He et al., 2026). However, these methods primarily focus on constraint satisfaction during refinement, without explicitly addressing how terminal recoverability constraints affect the preservation of feasible candidates across successive MBD stages. Thus, a framework is needed to jointly address beyond-horizon recoverability and feasible-support preservation.

In this paper, we propose a recovery-guided MBD framework that encodes long-horizon recovery information offline and exploits it during short-horizon MBD. A neural terminal recovery critic is trained from closed-loop rollouts under a designated recovery policy to approximate the worst-case future clearance margin along induced trajectories. During online planning, this critic is combined with within-horizon clearance and physical-feasibility checks to guide each diffusion-style refinement stage.
The main contributions are:

We introduce a learned terminal recovery critic and exploit it as a terminal criterion in short-horizon MBD. This extends the effective safety foresight horizon without costly long-horizon online rollouts at each planning step during high-dimensional legged robot locomotion.

We develop a feasibility-guided MBD refinement strategy that integrates within-horizon constraints with terminal recoverability, using feasible-first weighting and safe-elite retention to mitigate feasible-support loss under finite sampling budgets.

We validate the proposed framework in simulation on the Unitree Go2 over 50 paired randomized obstacle-avoidance trials. The proposed 10-step planner achieves zero collisions and 98% strict-clearance success, compared with a 58% collision rate and 22% strict-clearance success for 50-step DIAL, while requiring substantially less planning time.

1. We introduce a learned terminal recovery critic and exploit it as a terminal criterion in short-horizon MBD. This extends the effective safety foresight horizon without costly long-horizon online rollouts at each planning step during high-dimensional legged robot locomotion.

2. We develop a feasibility-guided MBD refinement strategy that integrates within-horizon constraints with terminal recoverability, using feasible-first weighting and safe-elite retention to mitigate feasible-support loss under finite sampling budgets.

3. We validate the proposed framework in simulation on the Unitree Go2 over 50 paired randomized obstacle-avoidance trials. The proposed 10-step planner achieves zero collisions and 98% strict-clearance success, compared with a 58% collision rate and 22% strict-clearance success for 50-step DIAL, while requiring substantially less planning time.

title: JEPA4R: Embodied JEPA World Models with 4D Point Planning
authors: Jiarui Dong,Zhiheng Liang,Yanjun Li,Zeyu Zhang,Heejeong Nam,Haoyu Chen,Hao Tang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Code:this https URL, Website:this https URL
abstract:
Joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) world models predict future embeddings instead of pixels and plan in latent space.
Two challenges remain: 2D images leave the metric geometry that manipulation acts on implicit and entangled with appearance, and what these models imagine stays hidden, as they are mostly judged in simulation by short-horizon latent planning.
We present JEPA4R, a JEPA world model that observes single-depth-camera point clouds, predicts and plans in their latent space, and acts through a policy head on its frozen latents; we call this 4D point planning.
A decoder on the frozen world model shows what it imagines as 4D point clouds, with a mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 steps.
Under the policy-learning protocols of OGBench and CortexBench, JEPA4R leads pixel JEPA models on OGBench Cube-Single, Cube-Double, Cube-Triple and Scene, and ranks first on MetaWorld and Adroit Relocate with 98.4% and 88.0%, above the runner-up, R3M, at 96.0% and 65.3%.
Trained only in a digital twin, JEPA4R and its policy heads run zero-shot on the real arm with both a gripper and a dexterous hand.

introduction:
World models built on joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict how a scene’s latent changes under an action and plan toward the latent of a goal [4, 110, 79].
However, current JEPA world models have two significant challenges in robot manipulation, which hinges on metric 3D geometry:

First, most JEPA world models read 2D input. Point-cloud JEPAs mostly pretrain encoders without actions [75, 27, 36, 113] or forecast LiDAR occupancy [112], so metric geometry rarely reaches the model that predicts and acts.
An image entangles metric geometry with appearance and perspective, so a pixel model must infer depth, whereas a point cloud from the same camera records visible surfaces at their metric positions (Fig. 3).
Even web-scale 2D foundation features show limited 3D awareness [18].
LeWM [50], trained from pixels without pretraining, has its lowest success on OGBench Cube [61], where it trails DINO-WM [110] on frozen DINOv2 features (74% vs. 86%) [50].
Its authors relate this gap partly to the 3D nature of the scene [50].

Second, what these models imagine stays hidden. JEPA latents are trained to be predictable, not reconstructive. Existing tools only decode them to images [110, 50] or audit them indirectly [50, 84], so the imagined 3D scene stays out of sight, which hampers debugging and real-robot safety checks. Scores do not reveal it either.
JEPA world models are mostly scored in simulation by short-horizon goal reaching [110, 79, 50], where a sampling-based planner such as the cross-entropy method [15] searches a few action blocks for the predicted latent closest to a goal latent.
Such search tests the predictor over short, in-distribution horizons, not how well the latents serve the policies robots learn. For example, LeWM latents that plan well transfer poorly to policy learning [45], and the model is evaluated only in simulation [50].
Frozen-encoder imitation on established suites such as CortexBench [51] asks instead how well a representation lets a policy learn a skill from a few demonstrations, which matters when robot data are scarce. However, JEPA world models rarely face it.

To address these two challenges, we propose JEPA4R, a JEPA world model designed to see metric geometry and to show what it imagines, so that a robot’s predictions can be checked before it acts. It reads a single-camera point cloud through a parameter-matched encoder (Fig. 2).
Every point cloud is paired with an image from the same eye-to-hand camera, so the 2D JEPAs are trained or evaluated on the same trajectories and viewpoint.
To evaluate how JEPA4R performs in robot policy learning, we train a policy head on the frozen latents under established protocols. Specifically, we use goal-conditioned policy learning on OGBench [61] and imitation on CortexBench, where JEPA4R is ranked among published representations and 2D JEPAs evaluated on the same data.
JEPA4R predicts, plans and acts in the 4D point latent space of its encoder, and we call this 4D point planning. An imagined rollout is the latent sequence that the predictor generates autoregressively from context frames and actions. A decoder attached to the frozen world model shows this imagination by turning every imagined rollout into a decoded 4D rollout (a).
All world models train in simulation. The RM75-B twin, a digital twin of the RealMan RM75-B arm, lets JEPA4R’s twin-trained world models and policy heads run zero-shot on the real arm.
Notably, we evaluate policy learning on manipulation suites with colored point clouds from a pipeline that also runs on the real arm, while previous work [58] evaluates planning alone with xyz-only raycast point clouds and finds the two modalities on par.

JEPA4R leads the 2D JEPAs on OGBench Cube and Scene and ranks first on CortexBench, above every published representation (Tabs. 1 and 2, Fig. 4). Its decoder recovers the observed scene from encoded and predicted latents alike, so even long imagined rollouts stay close to the observed point clouds (Tab. 3, Fig. 7). On the real arm, JEPA4R’s twin-trained policies run with both a parallel gripper and a dexterous hand.

In general, our paper can be summarized in the following three points:

4D point planning: we propose JEPA4R, which predicts, plans and acts in the latent space of realistic single-depth-camera point clouds, to bring the metric 3D geometry that 2D inputs leave implicit into JEPA world models.

4D point planning: we propose JEPA4R, which predicts, plans and acts in the latent space of realistic single-depth-camera point clouds, to bring the metric 3D geometry that 2D inputs leave implicit into JEPA world models.

Latent-space reconstruction: we propose a decoder attached to the frozen world model that turns every imagined rollout into 4D point clouds, to show what JEPA world models imagine, which their latents keep hidden. The decoded imagination keeps a mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 environment steps, so it can be inspected for debugging and real-robot safety checks.

Experiments on benchmarks and in the real world: we learn policies on OGBench and CortexBench in a paired 2D/3D evaluation, where JEPA4R’s point-cloud features rank first on CortexBench, above every published representation and 2D JEPA. JEPA4R transfers zero-shot to the real arm with both a gripper and a dexterous hand, after training only in a digital twin.

1. 4D point planning: we propose JEPA4R, which predicts, plans and acts in the latent space of realistic single-depth-camera point clouds, to bring the metric 3D geometry that 2D inputs leave implicit into JEPA world models.

2. Latent-space reconstruction: we propose a decoder attached to the frozen world model that turns every imagined rollout into 4D point clouds, to show what JEPA world models imagine, which their latents keep hidden. The decoded imagination keeps a mean point error within 1.1 cm over 200 environment steps, so it can be inspected for debugging and real-robot safety checks.

3. Experiments on benchmarks and in the real world: we learn policies on OGBench and CortexBench in a paired 2D/3D evaluation, where JEPA4R’s point-cloud features rank first on CortexBench, above every published representation and 2D JEPA. JEPA4R transfers zero-shot to the real arm with both a gripper and a dexterous hand, after training only in a digital twin.

title: M-CROSS: A Multisensor Simulation Dataset for SLAM across Water--Land Transitions
authors: Yan Dong,Tianyi Wu,Junyu Yang,Shaoqiang Qiu,Zefeng Yan,Tao Zhang,Bin Han
comment: Submitted to ICRA 2027
abstract:
Water–land cross-domain robots require continuous localization across land, transition and underwater phases, where sensor characteristics and availability change abruptly. Existing datasets and conventional metrics are not designed to capture transition-induced degradation and failures. We present M-CROSS, to the best of our knowledge, the first multisensor simulation dataset and benchmark for SLAM across continuous water--land transitions. It provides synchronized LiDAR, sonar, stereo camera, IMU, DVL, and depth measurements; 6DoF pose ground truth; sensor-wise medium-state annotations; and medium-dependent sensor degradation models. We establish a transition-aware protocol comprising the Trajectory Completion Rate (TCR), Piecewise Absolute Pose Error (PW-APE), Transition End Error (TEE), and Transition Survival Period (TSP), which measure trajectory completion, single-domain accuracy, transition-induced error, and localization survival under prolonged partial immersion, respectively. Experiments with 6 representative SLAM systems show that existing methods fail to maintain both localization accuracy and trajectory continuity across the full set of water--land transitions, exhibiting transition-induced drift, trajectory discontinuities, and tracking failures. M-CROSS is publicly available11

introduction:
Amphibious robots have demonstrated the ability to operate across terrestrial, water-surface, and underwater environments. Representative platforms include AQUA [1], AmphiHex-I [2], and the tracked amphibious robot presented in [3]. These platforms employ flipper-based locomotion, transformable flipper-leg propulsion, and tracked locomotion, respectively. Visual and multimodal perception have also supported underwater tasks such as diver following, robot tracking, inspection, and autonomous exploration [4, 5, 6]. However, most existing studies focus on locomotion, control, or perception within individual media. Continuous localization across the air–water interface remains insufficiently investigated, although sensor characteristics and availability change substantially during this process.

A major limitation is the lack of datasets designed for continuous cross-domain localization. KITTI [7], EuRoC [8], and TUM RGB-D provide standardized measurements and ground truth for terrestrial, aerial, or indoor environments [9], while AQUALOC [10], FLSea [11], and AquaticVision [12] focus on underwater visual or visual–inertial perception. These datasets are largely confined to a single physical medium. Real-world cross-domain data are difficult to collect under repeatable conditions, and continuous 6DoF ground truth spanning terrestrial, partially immersed, and underwater phases is particularly challenging to obtain. Simulation offers a controllable alternative: TartanAir supports photorealistic visual SLAM evaluation [13], while Stonefish [14], DAVE [15], and OceanSim [16] provide underwater optical, acoustic, hydrodynamic, and navigation-sensor simulation. Nevertheless, existing resources do not jointly target continuous land–interface–underwater trajectories with complementary terrestrial and underwater sensors, robot- and sensor-level medium annotations, medium-dependent sensor models, and transition-aware evaluation metrics.

Evaluation is also challenging. Absolute Pose Error (APE) characterizes global trajectory accuracy [9, 17], while existing benchmarks additionally consider cumulative error, incomplete trajectories, and relocalization [18, 19, 20]. However, these measures are not explicitly associated with medium-transition events. Errors concentrated within short transition intervals may be diluted by longer single-domain trajectories, and conventional metrics cannot directly characterize how long localization remains reliable during prolonged partial immersion. A cross-domain benchmark must therefore distinguish continuous completion, single-domain accuracy, transition-induced error, and robustness under sustained interface disturbances.

To address these gaps, we present M-CROSS, a multisensor simulation dataset and benchmark for cross-domain water–land SLAM, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The main contributions are:

We introduce M-CROSS, providing synchronized multimodal measurements, continuous six-degree-of-freedom ground truth, medium-state annotations, and medium-dependent sensor degradation models.

We introduce M-CROSS, providing synchronized multimodal measurements, continuous six-degree-of-freedom ground truth, medium-state annotations, and medium-dependent sensor degradation models.

We establish an evaluation framework comprising TCR, PW-APE, TEE, and TSP to separately assess trajectory completion, single-domain accuracy, transition-induced error, and prolonged-interface robustness.

We benchmark representative visual, LiDAR-based, sonar-based, and multisensor SLAM methods, revealing transition-induced drift, trajectory discontinuities, and tracking failures under changing sensing modalities.

1. We introduce M-CROSS, providing synchronized multimodal measurements, continuous six-degree-of-freedom ground truth, medium-state annotations, and medium-dependent sensor degradation models.

2. We establish an evaluation framework comprising TCR, PW-APE, TEE, and TSP to separately assess trajectory completion, single-domain accuracy, transition-induced error, and prolonged-interface robustness.

3. We benchmark representative visual, LiDAR-based, sonar-based, and multisensor SLAM methods, revealing transition-induced drift, trajectory discontinuities, and tracking failures under changing sensing modalities.

title: Cooperative Transport of Unknown Objects by Distributed Effort Regulation in Multi-agent Systems
authors: Tamzidul Mina,Shyam S. Kannan,Wonse Jo,Shaocheng Luo,Galen B. King,Byung-Cheol Min
comment: supplementary video available atthis https URLsubmitted to ICRA 2027
abstract:
A distributed multi-robot object transportation strategy is proposed for objects of unknown shape, size, geometry, mass and mass distribution without any prior knowledge about the object or number of robots involved in the transportation process.
Robots follow the boundary of the object and dynamically determine viable pushing points.
A novel object-model-free heading-error-driven pushing effort regulation method is proposed to promote goal-directed object motion; robots regulate their pushing effort using individual and collective heading errors.
Robots dynamically relocate around the object boundary if a pushing point is lost or the required pushing effort exceeds its capability to correct its heading.
The proposed method is validated using simple and complex shapes with convex and non-convex boundary regions and dynamically changing weight distribution of objects.
Detailed analysis on the effects of robot distribution and initial object pose on the transportation performance in terms of required time and path efficiency is also presented.
Scalability analysis revealed that object transportation time is dependent on the number of pushing surfaces available which in turn depends on the object size, shape, and set inter-robot safety distance.
The proposed system yielded highly efficient object paths with consistent elapsed transport times over several trials robust to external disturbances such as non-uniform friction between contacting surfaces and robot wheel slip.
introduction:
Object transportation by robotic systems has a rich potential for application in warehouse logistics, path clearing in search and rescue, evacuation scenarios, and the construction industry.
Multi-robot teams can provide redundancy in enabling reconfiguration, distributed sensing and action at scales that are impractical or expensive with a single unit.
Traditional approaches often frame the necessity of multi-robot configurations around the pooling of physical force to move large payloads.
In contrast, this work emphasizes that the primary value of a multi-robot system lies in utilizing multiple independent contact locations to enable the distributed regulation of object motion despite unknown geometry, unknown center of mass, non-uniform surface friction, and continuous external disturbances.

Multi-robot object transportation can generally be categorized into caging/grasping, towing, and pushing strategies.
Caging and grasping require a minimum number of robots, graspable features, and are limited to convex shapes [1, 2], while towing requires attachable points for cables [3].
Pushing strategies offer versatility and robustness [4] but face inherent goal-occlusion challenges.
While occlusion-leveraging strategies work for simple geometries [5], complex shapes often cause significant drift making identification of correct pushing surfaces critical for path efficiency.

Pushing strategies often integrate force feedback for motion contribution and path keeping [6].
Coordination ranges from centralized systems that lack fault tolerance [7] to decentralized leader-follower models requiring no communication [8].
Analytical pushing strategies [9] and data-driven models [10] have been explored, yet they remain limited by rigid assumptions [11].
Recent advancements utilizing Distributed Model Predictive Control (DMPC) [12], multi-objective optimization under distributed control [13], rigid formation architectures [14], or event-driven collaborative frameworks [15] introduce heavy computational overhead, depend heavily on strict prior object geometry tracking, or require explicit modeling constraints to safely capture payload dynamics. Consequently, combining applied force regulation requirements with fully distributed, model-free coordination strategies that adapt to arbitrary object physical configurations online has been a significant challenge [16].

In this paper, we propose a scalable multi-robot pushing strategy for transporting objects of unknown shape, size, mass, and center of mass.
The method requires no prior knowledge of the object or robot count and remains robust against imprecise contact and non-uniform friction effects.
Using individual assessments within a limited field-of-view (FOV), robots:

identify potential pushing surfaces on the perceived object boundary and initiate pushing minimizing the risk of physical damage to the object, and

regulate their pushing effort based on a proposed object-model-free strategy such that their combined action creates a resultant motion of the unknown object in the intended direction.

1. identify potential pushing surfaces on the perceived object boundary and initiate pushing minimizing the risk of physical damage to the object, and

2. regulate their pushing effort based on a proposed object-model-free strategy such that their combined action creates a resultant motion of the unknown object in the intended direction.

title: AlphaTruck: A Platform for High-Speed Off-Road Autonomy on Unstructured Terrain
authors: Rwik Rana,Adam J. Thorpe,Jesse Quattrociocchi,William Ward,Goktug Poyrazoglu,Adam Uccello,Christian Ellis,Rahul Moorthy Mahesh,Yukang Cao,Nathan Tsoi,Garrett Warnell,Volkan Isler,Ufuk Topcu,Joydeep Biswas
abstract:
Progress in autonomous navigation in off-road environments requires not only advances in algorithms, but also robust and capable physical platforms suited to both development and deployment.
Today, off-road autonomy is typically developed and tested at one of two extremes of vehicle scale, each with different drawbacks.
Full-size vehicles are capable but expensive, require large logistic infrastructure for deployment and maintenance, and expensive when pushed beyond their limits. RC-scale vehicles are small and inexpensive, but limited in the terrain they can traverse and the payload that they can carry, which includes their sensors and compute. We present the AlphaTruck platform, which leverages recent advances in compact sensing and compute to integrate multimodal sensing, embedded CPU-GPU compute, and an onboard autonomy stack for high-speed, off-road navigation, all integrated into a large-scale, 1/5th RC vehicle chassis. AlphaTruck is designed as both a research testbed and a field-deployable platform for commercial and defense missions such as survey, search and rescue, and agriculture, with the capacity to carry task-specific payloads. At 1/5 scale, the autonomy stack, sensors, and batteries all compete for the same mass, power, and cooling budget, so the platform must balance five needs: mobility over rough terrain, rich sensing, onboard computation, payload capacity to carry the autonomy stack while leaving room for task-specific equipment, and practical operation and repair. Thus, AlphaTruck navigates off-road environments autonomously at 6–10 m/s using only onboard sensing and compute.
introduction:
Off-road autonomous driving requires a vehicle to sense, localize, plan, and act on natural terrain, where rocks, roots, ruts, slopes, dirt, and vegetation affect where it can travel and how it responds to steering and throttle. Moreover, GPS and communication are often unreliable in off-road areas, so the full autonomy stack must run onboard. At high speed there is less time to read the terrain ahead and react to bumps or lost traction, so perception, planning, and control must all run quickly.

For this problem, generally two platform sizes have been used (Table 1). At the large end are drive-by-wire conversions of full-size off-road vehicles and purpose-built UGVs. These platforms carry multimodal sensors and powerful onboard computers and handle rough terrain, but they are costly to transport, support, maintain, and repair, and their mass and speed increase the consequences of a crash, making testing at their limits difficult. At the other extreme, small-scale platforms make experiments inexpensive, portable, and repeatable, but their size limits ground clearance, suspension travel, sensor placement, and onboard computation. After the autonomy hardware is installed, little room may remain for task-specific payloads. Computation can instead be offloaded off the vehicle, but the resulting dependence on a communication link and its latency is unsuitable for long-range missions.

To support rapid experimentation while remaining field-deployable, a platform between these two extremes is needed. In this paper, we present AlphaTruck, a rugged 1/5-scale platform and autonomy stack for high-speed off-road navigation. By field-deployable, we mean a platform that can (i) traverse uneven natural terrain—rocky trails, dirt, roots, ruts, etc.—as shown in Figure 2, (ii) run its full autonomy stack onboard, (iii) carry mission-specific payloads beyond that stack, and (iv) hold enough onboard energy for kilometer-scale missions. Kilometer-scale missions benefit from sustained speed, so we target 6-10 m/s. The autonomy stack limits speed to about 10m/s, beyond which sensor smearing degrades odometry and sensing range limits reaction time. With newer embedded compute and better sensors, AlphaTruck targets unstructured off-road terrain as both a research testbed and a field-deployable platform, driving autonomously off road at 6–10 m/s with the full stack onboard.

title: Sim-to-Real Room-Mediated Object-Goal Navigation with ROS 2 and Nav2
authors: Matthew Chua,Adam Scicluna,Gavin Paul
comment: . Accepted to ACRA (Australasian Conference on Robotics and Automation) 2026
abstract: Although object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) approaches are usually evaluated in simulation, which offers scale and repeatable environments, real-world deployments are rarely examined beyond feasibility demonstrations. This paper presents the deployment of Room-Mediated Co-occurrence, an ObjectNav policy that reasons over Room Probability Vectors (RPVs), on two robotic platforms (Boston Dynamics Spot and Clearpath Robotics TurtleBot 4) through a robot-agnostic ROS 2 bridge. We study how these semantic priors generalise to physical environments and describe the adaptations required to transfer RPV from simulation to hardware, covering sensing, localisation, and the action interface. Across 66 trials on Spot, searching for 11 object categories from two starting positions in a university postgraduate research facility, RPV achieves a raw Success Rate (SR) of 0.455. Our analysis identifies undetected glass walls, entry into off-limits areas, limited usable depth range, target size, and mismatch between the room lexicon and physical layout as plausible contributors to the 8.4-percentage-point gap between the real-world SR and the reported simulated SR of 0.539. Code is available at https://github.com/Matthew-K-Chua/rpv-ros2-bridge.
introduction:
Zero-shot Object-Goal Navigation (ObjectNav) [20] is a foundational problem for general-purpose robotics, requiring an agent to find an instance of a specified object in an initially unseen environment without domain-specific fine-tuning. Large datasets provide the scale and visual fidelity needed to test ObjectNav approaches while abstracting several failure points that become apparent on a real robot, including synchronisation, locomotion, and sensor noise. For example, the RPV simulation benchmark uses 2,000 episodes across 20 HM3D environments [14] within Habitat [15, 16]. Physical deployment is then needed to establish how the method behaves outside those simulated assumptions.

Recent work on Room-Mediated Co-occurrence [16] extends Vision-Language Frontier Maps (VLFM) [21] with Room Probability Vectors and reports a 3% relative improvement over the VLFM baseline on the HM3D validation split in simulation. Although VLFM has also been demonstrated on the Boston Dynamics Spot platform, the literature still lacks detailed analysis of how such policies behave and fail when transferred to physical environments.

In this paper, we deploy and evaluate RPV on a Boston Dynamics Spot and demonstrate portability to a Clearpath Robotics TurtleBot 4. Rather than coupling the semantic policy directly to a robot-specific SDK, we communicate through the open-source Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) [11] and standard navigation interfaces. This design lowers the effort required to evaluate embodied-AI ObjectNav pipelines on different physical robots. Figure 1 illustrates one successful Spot trial.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

A modular ROS 2 bridge implementing RPV on Boston Dynamics Spot and Clearpath Robotics TurtleBot 4.

An analysis of the adaptations required to transfer the simulation pipeline to physical control.

Real-world evaluation and analysis of RPV over 66 trials on Boston Dynamics Spot.

title: Cache or Denoise Less? Residual Reuse in a Flow-Matching World Action Model
authors: Abhinav Gupta,Nissan Pow
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: Honorable Mention at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Efficient Foundation Models for Real-Time Embodied AI (EEAI). Code and data available atthis https URL
abstract:
Flow-matching robot policies generate each action chunk through repeated network evaluations, one per denoising step.
Cross-cycle caches such as C3ache reuse computation from earlier replanning calls, but whether they beat simply taking fewer steps is unclear.
We compare the two in Fast-WAM, a 6B-parameter world action model, on LIBERO-Goal.
Two uncached steps keep the success of ten: on all 500 initial states they are non-inferior within two percentage points, for one checkpoint and noise seed.
Under PyTorch’s default compile mode, they also cut a replanning call on an RTX A6000 from 202 to 92 ms.
This leaves little room for caching. A cache that keeps two fresh steps cannot be faster than two uncached steps: every call still encodes the images, runs the video expert and computes those two steps. Caching the first of two steps, refreshed every fourth call, saves at most 11–14% of a call by our cost model.
Cached policies are also fragile. Their losses tracked the share of the flow path the cached steps cover: under Fast-WAM’s current time shift, C3ache’s eight cached steps cover 80% of the path instead of 44%, and the cached policy succeeds on 63% of states against 95% uncached. Resampling the noise on every call cost caches covering 60% or more of the path 14–40 points.
These results argue for fewer-step baselines and for testing reuse under the deployed sampler and noise settings.
We release our evaluation harness, logs and a checklist.
introduction:
Diffusion and flow-matching policies [6, 3, 2] and world action models [25, 24] produce each action chunk by integrating a learned flow from noise, one network evaluation per step.
A ten-step replanning call of Fast-WAM [25] takes about 200 ms on a desktop GPU, four control steps of a 20 Hz robot, which must pause for each new plan or keep executing an old one.
Distillation [17, 19, 1] and coarser schedules [22] cut the number of steps. Caches reuse computation within a denoising trajectory [15, 20, 13, 16, 14, 10, 23], across chunks [5, 9, 26] or across control cycles [21, 27].

C3ache [27] is a cross-cycle cache for Fast-WAM. A refresh call runs all ten steps and stores the residual that the action transformer adds at each of the first seven or eight. Until the next refresh, every call adds the stored residuals instead of recomputing those steps and runs only the rest in full.
It reports up to 2.5×\times faster inference than ten steps at unchanged success. That baseline has since moved: Yang [22] found that two undistilled steps already reach 95.8% success on LIBERO-Goal.

A cache now has to beat two uncached steps. We compare caches with that baseline on Fast-WAM’s two released LIBERO checkpoints and describe two conditions under which caches lose success. X-Cache [26] reuses residuals across the chunks of a few-step driving world model, gating each block on its input and always recomputing the chunks that write its key–value cache. It notes that resampled noise leaves consecutive chunks dissimilar at the first denoising step, and compares with its own uncached model.
Two uncached steps are non-inferior to ten, and every cache that keeps two full steps is slower, because a reuse call still encodes the images, runs the video expert and computes the last two steps (Sec. 3).
A cache’s losses track the share of the flow path its cached steps cover, a share that Fast-WAM’s latest time shift raised from 44% to 80% for eight cached steps, and the cached policy falls to 63% success (Sec. 4).
The losses grow when the noise is resampled on every call, and a pre-registered control points to the latent changing between calls.
Sec. 5 collects the lessons in a checklist, and code and logs are at github.com/gabhinav001/cache-or-denoise-less.

title: Real-Time Air Pollution Monitoring and Tracking via Adaptive Density-Driven Multi-UAV Coordination
authors: Julian Martinez,Ruchika Singh,Mohammad Afrazi,Kooktae Lee
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Accurate and timely air pollution monitoring and tracking are critical for protecting public health and supporting effective environmental management. This paper presents an adaptive Density-Driven Control (D2C) framework for coordinating multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to track and map dynamically evolving pollutant distributions. The proposed framework extends the D2C strategy to guide UAV trajectories based on predictive pollutant propagation and dynamically updated reference densities. A sensor-driven surrogate plume update mechanism is employed, in which reference samples are propagated using locally sensed concentration gradients and wind estimates through gradient attraction, wind advection, inter-sample repulsion, and stochastic diffusion, enabling UAVs to maintain an accurate spatio-temporal representation of the pollution field. The framework utilizes a coordinated structure where individual UAVs share their local measurements with a central coordinator to maintain a unified set of reference samples, facilitating systematic target allocation and trajectory planning. Simulation results under both mild and strong wind conditions demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of Sinkhorn distance. Specifically, in scenarios where the plume drifts beyond a fixed monitoring domain under high-velocity, time-varying wind fields, the tested baseline methods fail to maintain tracking, whereas the proposed D2C framework successfully adapts to the evolving distribution. These findings highlight D2C as an efficient and resilient solution for atmospheric monitoring in dynamic environments.
introduction:
Air pollution poses significant threats to human health and the environment [1]. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that it causes approximately seven million premature deaths annually [1]. Major pollutants include particulate matter (PM), nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulfur dioxide (SO2), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and carbon dioxide (CO2). These substances are associated with respiratory and cardiovascular diseases, as well as acid rain, photochemical smog, and climate change.

Ground-based stations are commonly used to assess air quality in urban and industrial areas. Although ground-based stations provide continuous local measurements, their fixed deployment restricts the area that can be observed [2, 3]. The problem becomes more pronounced as wind, temperature inversions, and atmospheric turbulence alter the direction and rate of pollutant dispersion [4]. As a result, the movement of pollution plumes may not be adequately captured by measurements from stationary networks.

Satellite remote sensing offers a means of extending atmospheric observations beyond the locations covered by ground stations. Instruments such as MODIS and Sentinel provide measurements across extensive geographical regions [5, 6]. However, their spatial resolution and observation intervals restrict the detection of localized and rapidly changing pollution events. In addition, cloud cover and atmospheric interference can lead to gaps in the collected data [7, 5]. Thus, satellite observations provide broad coverage but remain limited in their ability to follow plume evolution at short time intervals.

UAVs equipped with environmental sensors can obtain pollutant measurements at locations that are not covered by fixed monitoring stations [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. Deploying several UAVs over the same region makes it possible to examine the pollution field from different locations. In this context, pollution monitoring refers to estimating the spatial distribution of pollutant concentrations, whereas pollution tracking concerns the temporal changes in plume position and distribution. Both functions are important when investigating pollution phenomena that vary across space and time.

A major issue, however, lies in the way measurement routes are assigned. Many existing coordination schemes prescribe the flight paths in advance, commonly using lawnmower or grid-based patterns [14, 15]. Once assigned, these paths provide little flexibility for responding to variations in pollutant levels or plume movement. UAVs may therefore spend measurement time in regions that no longer reflect the areas of interest. Allowing flight paths to change with the observed data is consequently an important consideration in multi-UAV coordination [8].

To address these challenges, this paper extends the Density-Driven Control (D2C) framework [8, 16, 17, 18] to enable adaptive multi-UAV coordination for real-time air pollution monitoring and tracking. Although the Density-Driven Optimal Control (D2OC) further improved the performance of D2C by considering the optimality, they are mostly limited to the linear time-invariant (LTI) dynamics [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24]. Thus, D2OC
may not be directly applicable to air pollution monitoring missions, where the mobile platforms such as UAVs have nonlinear dynamics.

The proposed approach leverages Optimal Transport (OT) theory [25] to dynamically guide UAVs toward regions having higher pollutant densities, effectively coupling predictive propagation with data-driven adaptation. The framework maintains a dynamically evolving reference density by updating reference samples with local concentration gradients and wind measurements. This enables UAV trajectories to adapt seamlessly to changes in the pollutant distribution.
To achieve this in practice, each UAV uses onboard gas and particulate sensors to obtain localized, point-wise pollutant measurements [26, 27], together with local wind information.
Each UAV collects local wind and concentration-gradient measurements and sends them to a central coordinator. The coordinator uses these inputs to update a common reference distribution. Its evolution is governed by four components: gradient attraction, wind advection, inter-sample repulsion, and stochastic diffusion. The updated density distribution determines the targets for a separate motion-control stage, which generates trajectories while accounting for UAV dynamics.

We evaluate the proposed centralized method against two alternatives: a prediction-only propagation model and a distributed ergodic coverage approach using Gaussian-process field estimation [28]. The latter coordinates multiple agents by matching the time-averaged spatial distribution of their trajectories to a time-varying target distribution.
Comparing against these baselines allows us to isolate and evaluate the distinct performance benefits of our measurement-informed reference updates and centralized coordination over open-loop predictions and distributed ergodic alternatives.

The main contributions of this work are threefold:
1) A centralized density-driven coordination framework for multi-UAV pollution monitoring and tracking, in which a common time-varying reference distribution is used to coordinate individual UAV targets and allocate coverage weights across the monitored region. This formulation enables multiple UAVs to distribute their sensing activities according to the spatial characteristics of the pollution field;
2) A measurement-informed reference update mechanism that incorporates locally sensed concentration gradients and wind measurements into the evolution of the shared reference distribution. By accounting for gradient attraction, wind-driven advection, inter-sample repulsion, and stochastic diffusion, the proposed mechanism adjusts the reference samples according to changes in plume distribution and provides updated targets for UAV motion control;
3) A numerical evaluation of the integrated sensing, reference-update, and trajectory-control framework under spatially varying wind conditions. The proposed centralized approach is compared with a prediction-only propagation model and a distributed ergodic coverage method based on Gaussian-process field estimation, allowing the effects of measurement-based adaptation and centralized coordination on pollution monitoring and tracking performance to be examined.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the D2C formulation and the centralized monitoring problem. Section III describes the pollutant propagation model, Section IV develops UAV sensing and reference-sample propagation, and Section V presents the integrated multi-UAV algorithm. Simulation results are discussed in Section VI, followed by conclusions in Section VII.
