title: Physics-Grounded STL Monitoring from Image Observations
authors: Xinpei Ni,Glen Chou,Samuel Coogan
abstract:
Robotic manipulation missions must satisfy timed and conditional requirements that can be expressed in signal temporal logic (STL). While a practical means of monitoring these requirements is from camera images, this is challenging because STL robustness depends on physical margins, such as distances and clearances, that are not directly observed. Rather than learning a separate visual monitor for each formula, we learn a shared latent representation from multi-view images and decode physically meaningful margins for individual predicates.
Co-training the encoder with predicate decoders increases the certification rate from 58.7% to 96.3% compared with a frozen encoder, despite nearly unchanged predicate sign accuracy.
STL semantics then compose these margins into robustness estimates for any bounded formula over the trained predicates, without retraining. We further calibrate the decoding errors of selected STL clauses using conformal prediction, yielding two-sided intervals that certify both satisfaction and violation and propagate through interval STL to any formula composed from the clauses.
In simulated kitchen missions (LIBERO), our monitor correctly predicts satisfaction or violation in 98.9% of 4662 evaluations across 18 unseen formulas. For missions lasting up to 17 min, calibrated bounds establish satisfaction or violation for 96.9% of missions without incorrect conclusions. A single calibration also provides simultaneous 91.0% coverage across all 255 conjunctions of eight clauses, allowing new formulas without recalibration.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation tasks often impose temporal or conditional requirements in addition to a terminal outcome.
Kitchen tasks, for example, bound how long a cooking step may last, so that the food is neither under- nor over-cooked.
Signal temporal logic (STL) is a formal language for such requirements (Maler and Ničković, 2004), and its quantitative semantics assigns each trajectory a robustness value, whose sign indicates satisfaction or violation and whose magnitude is the margin (Donzé and Maler, 2010; Fainekos and Pappas, 2009).
In this work, we monitor STL specifications over minutes-long manipulation missions that are observed only through camera images.
This setting is demanding because the robustness depends on physical quantities, such as distances and clearances, that are not measured directly and must be inferred from the images.

Concretely, a monitor for this setting faces three challenges.
First, robustness must be estimated from images, whereas classical STL monitors compute it from perfect state information (Donzé and Maler, 2010; Fainekos and Pappas, 2009; Deshmukh et al., 2017), which is rarely available on a robot.
Second, the monitor should be able to support novel unseen formulas, since the requirements of a mission change more often than the perception model can be feasibly retrained.
Third, the monitor should provide calibrated bounds containing the true robustness of these formulas, enabling reliable conclusions about satisfaction or violation.
Existing camera-based monitors face three key limitations.
First, one-sided certificates: Hoxha et al. (2026) certify short-horizon, negation-free formulas from below only, so violations are never certified.
Second, lack of physically meaningful robustness: other visual monitors (Kapoor et al., 2026; Choi et al., 2024) measure similarity to satisfying examples rather than physical margins to constraint violation. Consequently, their robustness estimates do not directly indicate how close the robot is to violating a physical requirement. Third, data-inefficient calibration: conformal prediction (CP) (Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023) provides probabilistic guarantees, but two-sided calibration for a formula does not extend to other formulas. Certified monitoring of many specifications therefore requires separate calibration or conservative union bounds, making guarantees impractical when calibration data is limited.

To address these limitations, we propose an image-based STL monitor that estimates physically meaningful robustness, supports new specifications without retraining, and provides reusable probabilistic guarantees. First, we define each predicate through a signed physical margin computed from the simulator state and train a decoder for each predicate on a shared latent representation of multi-view images, which reduces occlusions. By learning to estimate individual predicate margins rather than the robustness of a particular formula, we can then use STL semantics to compositionally estimate the robustness of any bounded formula over the trained predicates, without retraining. Finally, to avoid recalibrating the monitor for every new formula, our key insight is to calibrate the decoding errors of a fixed set of clauses (STL subformulas) over entire missions, rather than calibrating each formula separately. We propagate the resulting clause-level intervals through STL operators using interval STL (I-STL) (Baird et al., 2023). Assuming the calibration and test missions are exchangeable, we show that a single calibration simultaneously bounds the true robustness of every formula composed from these clauses with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha.

Related work.
Classical online STL monitors bound the robustness of partial trajectories (Deshmukh et al., 2017), but assume direct access to physical state measurements, limiting their applicability to vision-based robotic systems.
Perception-oriented temporal logics (Balakrishnan et al., 2019; Hekmatnejad et al., 2024) specify requirements on perception outputs, while vision-language-based monitors (Liu et al., 2023b; Duan et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025) detect manipulation failures. However, these approaches do not provide physically meaningful STL robustness estimates with calibrated guarantees.
Interval STL (Zhong et al., 2021; Baird et al., 2023) propagates uncertainty through temporal logic operators, but assumes that bounds on the underlying signals are already available.
More closely related are
Hoxha et al. (2026), whose single calibration certifies every formula in a negation-free fragment, but only from below. Formula-level monitors (Lindemann et al., 2023; Cairoli et al., 2023) are two-sided
but formula-specific. Our clause-level calibration is both two-sided and reusable.

In contrast, we learn physically grounded predicate margins from images and calibrate the decoding errors of a fixed set of clauses rather than individual specifications. By composing these margins using STL semantics and propagating clause-level intervals using I-STL, our approach provides two-sided robustness bounds for any formula composed from the calibrated clauses, without retraining or recalibration. This enables reusable probabilistic guarantees for long-horizon missions observed only through cameras.

Contributions.
We make four contributions:

Physically grounded predicate decoding: We develop a multi-view latent encoder with per-predicate decoders that estimate signed physical margins from images (Sec. 3.1).

Composable STL monitoring: By learning predicate margins independently of the specification, our monitor estimates the robustness of any bounded STL formula over the trained predicates, without retraining, for both offline and online monitoring (Sec. 2 and 3.1).

Reusable probabilistic guarantees: We prove that one clause-level calibration, propagated through I-STL, simultaneously bounds the robustness of every formula over the calibrated clauses, including online at every monitored time step. We also identify the image frame determining each robustness estimate to facilitate diagnosis (Sec. 3.3).

Experimental validation: On LIBERO missions (Liu et al., 2023a) with unseen specifications, new scenes, and durations up to 17 min, we outperform visual STL monitors, embedding-based predicates, and vision-language models in monitoring and certification (Sec. 4 and 5). title: Early Readability of Trajectory Quality in Diffusion Driving Planners
authors: Xiang Zhang,Ziyang Leng,Yuxin Bao,Zhihao Zhao,Bolei Zhou,Xugui Zhou
abstract:
Diffusion-based driving planners can generate multiple trajectories for the same scene, but these candidates vary in quality. Can their internal states reveal which candidate will be better before denoising is complete?
We systematically study this question in three pretrained planners: Alpamayo, ReCogDrive-IL, and HDP, using linear probes to predict final trajectory quality from intermediate states and evaluating candidate ranking and selection on held-out scenes.
Across all three planners, we observe that states from the first denoiser evaluation already support informative selection, while further denoising does not consistently improve selection quality.
Further analyses show that readout depends on the representation and reader, and that selection can coexist with limited overall ranking accuracy.
These findings motivate an early-selection method that selects after the first denoiser evaluation and completes only the chosen candidate.
This reduces computation relative to fully denoising every candidate and improves open-loop trajectory quality over random selection across all three planners. In particular, it reduces Alpamayo’s average displacement error by 17.8% and 13.4% in one- and four-camera configurations, respectively. Closed-loop evaluations also show higher mean driving scores and progress.
introduction:
Diffusion-based driving planners generate trajectories by iteratively refining noise [1, 2, 3, 4].
In vision-language-action (VLA) models such as Alpamayo [2], an action expert performs this refinement conditioned on vision-language context.
For the same scene, different noise draws can produce trajectories of substantially different quality.
This variation makes candidate selection important, since generating a good trajectory is useful only if the planner can identify it for execution.

Selecting a good trajectory requires a way to assess candidate quality.
Existing approaches use learned value functions to select actions from pretrained policies [5], or learned and rule-based criteria to score completed driving trajectories  [6, 7].
However, in diffusion planners, applying such selection after full denoising requires completing
every candidate, even though only one trajectory is ultimately executed.
This motivates predicting candidate quality from intermediate
states before denoising is complete.

Since early trajectory previews can change during denoising, it remains unclear how reliably their quality predicts the quality of the completed trajectories. Meanwhile, studies of robot policies show that internal activations can predict task success [8], suggesting that useful outcome signals may be available within the policy itself.
Motivated by these findings, we probe the intermediate states of pretrained driving planners to study whether final trajectory quality can be read out before denoising is complete. Fig. 1 shows a qualitative example in which a candidate selected from an early planner state yields a high-quality final trajectory.

We probe the internal states of three pretrained driving planners,
Alpamayo 1.5 [2], ReCogDrive-IL [3], and
HDP [4], to determine when final candidate quality becomes
accessible to a lightweight readout.
Across all three planners, linear probes can use states from the first denoiser evaluation to select better trajectories than random selection.
Further analyses show that the usefulness of these readouts depends on the representation and probe, and that selection gains do not necessarily imply accurate candidate ranking.
These findings motivate using early planner states for candidate selection before denoising is complete.

Based on these findings, we score candidates after the first denoiser evaluation and complete only the selected candidate. We measure denoising work by the number of function evaluations (NFE), counting each candidate’s denoiser evaluation separately. For NN candidates requiring TT NFE each, this reduces candidate work from N​TNT to N+T−1N+T-1 NFE.
Early selection improves open-loop trajectory quality across all three planners and closed-loop performance for Alpamayo in AlpaSim [9] and ReCogDrive-IL in Isaac Gym [10].

We summarize our contributions as follows:

We discover the early accessibility of trajectory quality.
Across three pretrained driving planners, we show that linear probes of first-evaluation states can select better trajectories among candidates from the same scene.

We discover the early accessibility of trajectory quality.
Across three pretrained driving planners, we show that linear probes of first-evaluation states can select better trajectories among candidates from the same scene.

We conduct a representation and readout analysis to examine how outcome readout depends on denoising evaluation, network layer, action-token representation, and probe capacity, and distinguish useful candidate selection from accurate overall ranking.

We demonstrate open-loop quality improvements across all three planners and closed-loop performance improvements with reduced denoising computation for Alpamayo [2] in AlpaSim [9] and ReCogDrive-IL [3] in Isaac Gym [10].

title: PSK: A Matrix-Free Single-Loop Method for K-Level Physics-Based Control
authors: Zherong Pan
abstract: Physics-based control is central to robot learning, but differentiating through implicit physics steps typically requires Hessian or Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) linear solves; we ask whether gradient steps suffice. Each simulation step minimizes an energy under many contact and collision constraints. Without constraints, we view control over KK steps as KK-level optimization with strongly convex lower levels, recast as one min–max problem. Our Penalized Single-loop KK-level method (PSK) uses only gradients and a projection, updates all levels in parallel, and reaches an ϵ\epsilon-stationary control in O⁡(ϵ−3)O(\epsilon^{-3}) iterations, with a KK-independent exponent but a KK-dependent constant. Contact-rich constraints, however, typically violate a constraint qualification (CQ). We replace each constraint by a smooth wall that acts on a band of constant width. Under mild assumptions that need no CQ, every exact solution of the banded lower levels is then feasible and banded Fritz–John, and PSK keeps the O⁡(ϵ−3)O(\epsilon^{-3}) complexity. Without a CQ that is uniform in the band width, however, a shrinking band loses the KK-independent exponent: with width ϵ\epsilon and fixed K≥2K\geq 2, deterministic zero-respecting methods need Ω(ϵ−(K+3)/4)\Omega(\epsilon^{-(K+3)/4}) calls on a hard instance whose control dimension grows with 1/ϵ1/\epsilon. We prove our assumptions for smoothed kinematic and dynamic multi-robot navigation among segment obstacles. In navigation experiments, PSK, tuned per case, reaches every goal with sixteen levels and, at equal time, reaches a lower loss than tuned unrolling in 17 of 18 cases, while implicit differentiation is lower in 10.
introduction:
Many machine-learning and robotics problems optimize controls over chains of physical-system states: a robot’s actions change states through a physics model. Differentiable physics passes gradients through the simulator to train controls, policies, and physical parameters end to end (Degrave et al., 2019; de Avila Belbute-Peres et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2020; Freeman et al., 2021; Werling et al., 2021). It underpins model-based reinforcement learning (Deisenroth and Rasmussen, 2011; Janner et al., 2019; Hafner et al., 2020; Hansen et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022), physical world models (Battaglia et al., 2016; Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020; Li et al., 2019; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018), and real-to-sim parameter fitting (Ramos et al., 2019; Jatavallabhula et al., 2021; Heiden et al., 2021; Le Lidec et al., 2021). Each physics step is itself an optimization problem: implicit integration minimizes an energy, often under contact or collision constraints. Newton-type solvers solve a Hessian or Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) linear system at every step, but local projections, accelerated fixed-point iterations, and gradient descent reach simulation accuracy without one (Macklin et al., 2016; Wang, 2015; Wang and Yang, 2016). Control, however, needs each state’s derivative with respect to the controls, which implicit-function and adjoint methods obtain from a Hessian or KKT solve (Amos and Kolter, 2017; Amos et al., 2018; Geilinger et al., 2020; Du et al., 2021; Howell et al., 2022). Thus matrix-free simulation need not yield matrix-free control. We ask:

We give an affirmative answer for a constant-band surrogate by reformulating physics-based control as a KK-level optimization problem. We model the KK simulation steps as strongly convex constrained problems driven by one global control, with stage-dependent energies and shared constraints. Our contributions follow.

A matrix-free method. We replace each hard constraint by a smooth wall that acts on a band of constant width, and cast the resulting surrogate as one min–max problem. We propose the Penalized Single-loop KK-level method (PSK), which uses only gradients and a projection onto the control set. It builds no Hessian, Jacobian, or linear system, and its stages update in parallel (Section 4).

A KK-independent exponent for constant bands. We design mild stage assumptions that require no constraint qualification (CQ) and under which every exact surrogate state is feasible and banded Fritz–John. Under these assumptions, PSK reaches an ϵ\epsilon-stationary control of the surrogate in O⁡(ϵ−3)O(\epsilon^{-3}) iterations for every KK; the exponent is independent of KK, although the constant depends on KK (Section 4).

A KK-dependent lower bound for shrinking bands. A CQ rarely holds for contact-rich physics. Without a CQ that is uniform in the band width, we prove a lower bound: when the band width shrinks with the target accuracy ϵ\epsilon, every deterministic zero-respecting method, including PSK, needs Ω(ϵ−(K+3)/4)\Omega(\epsilon^{-(K+3)/4}) oracle calls on a hard instance for each fixed K≥2K\geq 2. Hence the exponent grows linearly with KK. The instance meets all other assumptions (Proposition 40), but its two constraint normals become parallel as the band shrinks (Section 4.3).

Practical assumptions and experiments. Our assumptions hold for kinematic and dynamic multi-robot navigation among segment obstacles with smoothed normals. On four scenes, PSK reaches every goal with K=16K=16 and, at equal time, reaches a lower loss than tuned unrolling in 17 of 18 cases, while implicit differentiation is lower in 10 (Section 5 and 6).

title: Towards Probabilistically Safe Reinforcement Learning: Theory and Deployment on Humanoid and Aerial Robots
authors: Pol Mestres,Varun Gabbita,Jason H. K. Siu,Sergio A. Esteban,Hampus Serneke,Joel W. Burdick,Aaron D. Ames
abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) enables robots to acquire complex skills, but standard RL formulations do not guarantee that learned policies satisfy safety constraints, which limits their use in safety-critical settings. Existing safe RL methods with provable guarantees typically support only restricted classes of constraints and require unbiased estimators of the objective and constraint functions, which prevents their direct integration with state-of-the-art algorithms such as proximal policy optimization (PPO). In this paper, we extend the recently introduced robust safe gradient flow-based reinforcement learning (RSGF-RL) framework to overcome these limitations. Our formulation accommodates a general class of trajectory-level safety constraints, including chance constraints such as collision avoidance with a prescribed probability, and our analysis allows for biased value and gradient estimators.
We show that, with high probability, the constraint violation throughout training is bounded by the estimator bias plus a term that vanishes as the number of rollouts grows, and decays to this level if the initial policy is unsafe. We also establish the convergence properties of the iterates to approximate KKT points of the original safe RL problem. Finally, we show that RSGF-RL implemented with PPO-style estimates enables zero-shot sim-to-real deployment of whole-body control policies on a Unitree G1 humanoid and collision-free waypoint navigation on a Crazyflie drone.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful tool for enabling robots to acquire a wide range of complex skills (Hwangbo et al., 2019; OpenAI et al., 2020; Kaufmann et al., 2023).
However, standard RL algorithms primarily optimize task performance, without guaranteeing that the learned policies satisfy safety constraints, either during training or after deployment.
This lack of formal safety guarantees remains a major obstacle to the adoption of RL in safety-critical applications.

Motivated by this challenge, a growing body of work on safe RL seeks to optimize policy performance subject to prescribed safety specifications (Brunkel et al., 2022; Garcia and Fernandez, 2015; Gu et al., 2024).
A common approach formulates safe RL as a constrained policy optimization problem, where the constraint requires the expected cumulative value of a safety-related cost to remain below a prescribed threshold (Achiam et al., 2017; Chow et al., 2017; Paternain et al., 2019).
Several algorithms have been proposed to solve such problems, including primal-dual methods (Paternain et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2020), constrained policy optimization (CPO) (Achiam et al., 2017), projection-based constrained policy optimization (PCPO) (Yang et al., 2020), and state augmentation (Sootla et al., 2022).
Despite their empirical success, these methods generally do not guarantee constraint satisfaction throughout the learning process, and their convergence guarantees rely on restrictive assumptions.

An alternative approach enforces safety at the level of individual control actions, typically by combining an unconstrained RL policy with a safety filter based on control barrier functions (CBFs) (Bejarano et al., 2025; Alshiekh et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2026; Hsu et al., 2024).
While such methods can provide guarantees on the safety of the resulting closed-loop system, they do not directly address the problem of optimizing a policy subject to safety constraints.

In this paper, we adopt the constrained policy optimization perspective, building on the recently introduced robust safe gradient flow-based reinforcement learning (RSGF-RL) framework (Mestres et al., 2025b; Mestres et al., 2025a).
RSGF-RL provides convergence guarantees to critical points of the constrained RL problem while maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout the learning process with high probability.
However, several limitations restrict its
integration with state-of-the-art RL algorithms and modern robotic systems:

Limited class of safety constraints.
The existing framework considers constraints that require that the expected value of cumulative safety costs remains below a given threshold.
However, many safety specifications arising in robotics are naturally expressed as probabilistic constraints, such as requiring that the probability of colliding with an obstacle during an episode remains below a prescribed threshold, which are not equivalent to the expected cumulative cost formulations.

The existing framework considers constraints that require that the expected value of cumulative safety costs remains below a given threshold.
However, many safety specifications arising in robotics are naturally expressed as probabilistic constraints, such as requiring that the probability of colliding with an obstacle during an episode remains below a prescribed threshold, which are not equivalent to the expected cumulative cost formulations.

Restrictive assumptions.
The theoretical guarantees of RSGF-RL as provided in (Mestres et al., 2025b; Mestres et al., 2025a) require unbiased estimators of the objective and constraint functions and their gradients.
In contrast, modern RL algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017), Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) (Haarnoja et al., 2024), and DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., 2025) employ estimation procedures that can introduce bias.
This limits the integration of RSGF-RL with state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. Additionally, the conditions under which (Mestres et al., 2025a) establishes convergence of RSGF-RL (such as the requirement that the estimated RSGF-RL update law converges to the true one with probability one) are quite restrictive.

Lack of hardware validation.
Previous evaluations of RSGF-RL have been limited to relatively simple simulation environments, leaving open whether its theoretical guarantees can be combined with the computational demands and practical challenges of RL policies for real robotic systems.

In this paper, we develop an extension of RSGF-RL that addresses these shortcomings, and show that the resulting algorithm can be used to train RL policies for a variety of different tasks, with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
Our contributions are as follows.

First, we extend RSGF-RL to a general class of trajectory-level constraints, which includes cumulative
cost and probabilistic constraints. Similarly to the Policy Gradient Theorem (Sutton and Barto, 2018, Chapter 13), we show that gradient estimates for this class of constraints follow from the classical likelihood-ratio method in (Glynn, 1990);

cost and probabilistic constraints. Similarly to the Policy Gradient Theorem (Sutton and Barto, 2018, Chapter 13), we show that gradient estimates for this class of constraints follow from the classical likelihood-ratio method in (Glynn, 1990);

Second, we show that, with high probability, the constraint violation of the RSGF-RL iterates is bounded by the estimator bias plus a sampling-error term that vanishes as the number of rollouts NN used for value and gradient estimation grows.
If the initial policy is safe, this bound holds throughout training; if it is unsafe, the violation decays to this level.
We also show that, almost surely, the RSGF-RL iterates have a limit point that is an approximate KKT point of the constrained RL problem, with the approximation level again given by the estimator bias plus a term that vanishes as N→∞N\to\infty.

Third, we show that RSGF-RL implemented with (biased) PPO gradient estimates enables zero-shot sim-to-real deployment of whole-body motor skills on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot and collision-free waypoint navigation on a Crazyflie drone. Some assumptions of our theoretical results are not met in the practical implementation of RSGF-RL used in these experiments. We discuss this theory-to-practice gap in Section 4.3.

title: ResWAM: Learning What Changes, Not What Stays, for World-Action Models
authors: Chongyu Fan,Gaowen Liu,Ramana Rao Kompella,Jason Corso,Sijia Liu
abstract: World-action models (WAMs) augment vision-language-action policies (VLAs) with future prediction so that the policy can anticipate how its actions will affect the physical world. Existing WAMs supervise complete future observations. However, observations typically change little over an action chunk, so the future loss is dominated by copying static background content rather than learning task-relevant robot and object motion, limiting policy learning. Moreover, existing WAMs rely on large video generation models or separate world models, incurring heavy training and inference compute that hinders closed-loop deployment. To improve policy performance, we propose visual residual learning, supervising only the feature change from the current frame to the future frame in a frozen DINOv3 space. Compared with complete future features, this residual learning target yields a higher feature rank with richer and more diverse representations of scene changes, and spatially concentrates on the robot arm and manipulated objects rather than the background. To further improve computational efficiency, we present ResWAM, a residual world-action model with 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly trains an action branch and a residual branch via conditional flow matching. Without robot pretraining (i.e., pretraining on external robot action trajectories beyond the benchmark demonstrations), ResWAM achieves top average success rates on LIBERO-Plus (81.1%), RoboTwin 2.0 (93.8%), and RoboDojo (9.40% success, 13.41 score) at the lowest training (2.7–4.0 TFLOPs) and inference compute (1.0–1.4 TFLOPs), and leads real-robot Open, Put, and Stack (80.0% average, +10.0%+10.0\% over π0.5\pi_{0.5}) at 92.7 ms latency.
introduction:
As frontier AI models advance rapidly, physical intelligence is emerging as a key frontier for perceiving, reasoning about, and interacting with the physical world (Seed, 2026; Fan et al., 2026c).
Current approaches broadly follow two paradigms: vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs), shown in Fig. 1(a).
VLAs adapt pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to predict actions from visual and language inputs (Black et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2026b; Kim et al., 2025), but train only on action labels without modeling how actions change the physical world.

WAMs add future visual prediction alongside actions so the policy accounts for the physical consequences of its commands (Bi et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). Existing WAMs typically realize this by predicting complete future frames or features via a video generation model or a separate world model (Fig. 1(b)). However, this standard paradigm suffers from two fundamental limitations in supervision target and model architecture.

First, in terms of supervision target, supervising complete future observations weakens policy learning because consecutive frames over an action chunk change very little. For instance, on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), current and future visual features share an average cosine similarity of 0.96; consequently, the future loss is largely satisfied by copying static background tokens rather than capturing how the robot and objects move in response to actions, diluting the auxiliary supervision signal for control. To mitigate this issue, recent studies have explored compact representations of temporal changes.
Yet, these approaches still rely on indirect modeling or additional architectural complexity, such as latent-action encoding and future-feature reconstruction (Zhang et al., 2026a), action inference from latent transitions (Qiu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b), or delta tokenization coupled with video generation (Yan et al., 2026).
Second, in terms of model architecture, existing WAMs incur high training and inference cost from large video generation models or separate world models (Fig. 1(b)). Video-generation WAMs (Bi et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Yuan et al., 2026) fine-tune large video diffusion models with costly 3D video VAEs, while external-world-model WAMs (Chen et al., 2026a; Lin et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026) require separate pretrained world models or multi-stage teachers.

The above limitations (static-background dominance in supervision and heavy backbone cost in architecture) motivate our hypothesis:

To approach (H), we introduce visual residual learning, which shifts WAM supervision from predicting what the future world looks like to predicting how the world changes. Given visual tokens 𝐙t\mathbf{Z}_{t} and 𝐙t+H\mathbf{Z}_{t+H} extracted from the current frame and the frame HH steps ahead using a frozen DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) encoder, respectively, we construct the visual residual target as 𝚫t=𝐙t+H−𝐙t\bm{\Delta}_{t}=\mathbf{Z}_{t+H}-\mathbf{Z}_{t}, capturing temporal changes while suppressing static background content. We identify two key advantages of this supervision strategy, as illustrated in Fig. 1(c). First, visual residuals exhibit higher feature rank than future representations, suggesting richer and more diverse information (Sec. 4.2). Second, visualizing the residuals in image space reveals that they concentrate on the robot and manipulated objects rather than static backgrounds, highlighting action-relevant scene changes (Sec. 4.3). Empirically, supervising 𝚫t\bm{\Delta}_{t} improves average success rate by +2.9%+2.9\% over directly predicting 𝐙t+H\mathbf{Z}_{t+H} at identical compute on RoboTwin 2.0 (Fig. 7).

On the architectural side, we design ResWAM (Fig. 1(b)) to improve computational efficiency. Instead of using a large video generation model or a separate world model, ResWAM has only 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly denoises actions and frozen DINOv3 visual residuals via conditional flow matching, without pixel reconstruction or future decoding. Across all evaluated benchmarks, ResWAM achieves the lowest training compute (2.7–4.0 TFLOPs), inference compute (1.0–1.4 TFLOPs), and inference latency (92.2–99.7 ms). Fig. 1(d) highlights the favorable success-latency trade-off of ResWAM on LIBERO-Plus and its strong performance on RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo.
We summarize our contributions below.

❶ Supervision-wise, to strengthen the supervision signal for higher performance, we propose visual residual learning. We show that this signal exhibits higher feature rank than full future features and concentrates on the robot and manipulated objects rather than static backgrounds, providing a more focused and expressive supervision signal.

❷ Architecture-wise, to improve computational efficiency, we design ResWAM, a residual world-action model with 2.3B parameters in total, including a lightweight 0.5B dual-branch DiT that jointly denoises actions and frozen DINOv3 visual residuals via conditional flow matching in place of video generation models or separate world models.

❸ Experiment-wise, without robot pretraining, ResWAM achieves the highest average success rates on LIBERO-Plus (81.1%), RoboTwin 2.0 (93.8%), and RoboDojo (9.40% success, 13.41 score) at the lowest training (2.7–4.0 TFLOPs) and inference compute (1.0–1.4 TFLOPs), and leads real-world FR3 tasks (80.0% average, +10.0%+10.0\% over π0.5\pi_{0.5}) at 92.7 ms latency.

title: Cooperative Gradient Estimation for Multi-Robot Source Seeking with Heteroskedastic Measurements
authors: Alessandro Renzaglia,Lara Briñón-Arranz
abstract:
This paper proposes a novel approach for localizing the source of a three-dimensional scalar field using a team of heterogeneous cooperative mobile robots. Each robot measures the field intensity at its location and shares the information within the team. Measurement noise is explicitly considered, and heterogeneity arises from robot-dependent sensing accuracies, leading to heteroskedastic data.
The proposed framework combines a weighted centroidal Voronoi tessellation-based formation strategy, defined on a spherical surface and parameterized by sensor noise variances, with a Weighted Least Squares estimator to compute the field gradient at the formation center. By explicitly accounting for sensor heterogeneity in both formation design and estimation, the method achieves robust gradient estimation under noisy measurements.
In particular, we show analytically that this construction is nearly optimal. The covariance of the gradient estimate is derived in closed form, providing a lower bound on the attainable estimation variance for any formation on the sphere, and the proposed tessellation is shown to asymptotically satisfy the conditions under which this bound is attained. The estimated gradient is then exploited within a gradient-ascent strategy to guide the team toward the source location.
Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach compared to alternative strategies and highlight its intrinsic ability to reconfigure online in response to robot failures, thereby enhancing its adaptability.
introduction:
Cooperative source seeking is a critical challenge in multi-robot applications due to its importance in various scenarios, including search and rescue missions, environmental monitoring, and pollution source detection [4], [15], [13]. In this context, an unknown source generates a spatially distributed signal field.
A team of autonomous robots, equipped with sensors capable of measuring the signal intensity at their locations, works together to localize the source by leveraging the collected information.
Despite being a widely studied problem in the literature, efficient and accurate source localization based only on sparse and noisy field intensity measurements remains a challenging problem. As discussed in more detail in the following section, most existing solutions focus on two-dimensional environments and often do not analyze the impact of measurement noise. When noise is considered, it is always assumed that the measurements collected by the robots have equal variance, i.e., the collected data are homoscedastic. This is not always the case in many real-world applications, where heterogeneous robots may be equipped with sensors of different quality and characteristics. For example, a few robots equipped with a high-quality, high-value sensor that provides very accurate measurements can be deployed together with robots equipped with cheaper, less accurate sensors.

In this paper, we translate the source localization task into the problem of accurately estimating the gradient of the generated scalar field from sparse and noisy measurements. Since the reliability of the collected heteroskedastic data varies across sensors, this heterogeneity can significantly affect the quality of the estimated gradient and, consequently, the accuracy of the final source localization. Therefore, such information must be taken into account not only in the estimator design but also during the robots’ planning phase. In particular, determining where each robot should collect its measurements becomes a key decision for maximizing the information gathered at the team level.
To this end, this work incorporates sensor heterogeneity directly into the design of the measurement locations and the coordination strategy. More precisely, we aim to answer the following question:
How should a heterogeneous team of robots be coordinated so that their sensing capabilities are exploited to achieve reliable configurations for efficient and robust source localization?

The main contribution of this paper is to present a new approach to address this issue and to perform the source search within a 3D signal field with a multi-robot system collecting heteroskedastic measurements.
The main novelty of this solution is to propose a coordinated measurement strategy based on multi-robot formations obtained via weighted centroidal Voronoi tessellations on spherical surfaces. The weights, which are related to the noise variance of each robot, allow the formation to incorporate the heteroskedasticity of the data and reflect it in the geometric properties of the multi-robot configuration. As a result, the formation presents a different density of robots depending on sensor accuracy, providing higher spatial coverage near less accurate, and therefore less reliable, sensors. The data collected from this formation are then used to obtain a gradient estimate using a weighted least squares method. Furthermore, we provide an analytical justification of the resulting design in terms of estimation accuracy. We derive a closed-form expression for the covariance of the gradient estimate and a corresponding lower bound on the estimation variance attainable by any formation on the spherical surface, together with the two geometric conditions under which this bound is reached. We then prove that the weighted tessellation satisfies both conditions, up to an approximation error that vanishes as the team size grows, and verify numerically that the resulting formation lies within a few percent of the bound already for small teams.
Additionally, a key feature of the proposed framework is its intrinsic reconfiguration capability. Changes in team composition or sensor variances are directly reflected in the weighting function defining the CVT, leading to a modified set of target measurement locations. As a result, the sensing formation is automatically reshaped through the formation controller without requiring explicit fault handling or redesign.

Source seeking with autonomous robots has been extensively studied in recent years, with numerous solutions proposed for both single and multi-robot systems. However, the majority of these approaches are limited to 2D search spaces, while solutions for 3D environments are still scarce. Existing solutions can be broadly categorized into two classes: gradient-free and gradient-based approaches.

Gradient-free methods have gained popularity due to their simplicity and robustness in environments where gradient information is difficult to obtain, for instance, due to discontinuities in the signal.
In this context, a significant body of work has focused on Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithms. For instance, [36] and [34] proposed PSO-based strategies for efficient source localization in 2D environments.
[19] introduced an adapted version of the Quantum Particle Swarm Optimization (QPSO) algorithm, which proposed leading-following behaviors in a swarm-based approach to improve search efficiency in 2D spaces.
PSO-based solutions, however, can become unstable when individual field measurements are unreliable due to high levels of noise, especially with small-sized multi-robot teams. Single outliers can indeed corrupt personal and global best positions, misleading the entire team and potentially causing the optimization to stagnate or induce significant oscillations.
Other gradient-free approaches draw inspiration from biological systems. A method inspired by schools of fish, where robots adjust their speed based on environmental cues to locate darker areas, is presented in [33]. Similarly, in [30], a novel flocking control strategy is proposed for multi-robot exploration and gas field mapping within a 2D framework.
Building on this idea, [31] presents a collaborative gas source localization strategy employing networked nano-drones operating in unknown and cluttered environments, achieved through hybrid integration of Adaptive Robotic Particle Swarm Optimization (ARPSO) with Bidirectional Brain Emotional Learning (BBEL).
The use of multi-robot formations is then treated in [11], which proposed a gradient-free approach addressing source localization and formation control for ground robots.
Communication can also be a crucial aspect in multi-robot strategies, and [2] introduced a consensus-like perception algorithm that allows estimating the source location without explicit communication.

The second class of solutions leverages an explicit gradient estimation of the sensed field to guide robots toward the source. A key challenge in these approaches is obtaining a reliable estimation from sparse and noisy measurements. To do so, two main, often interconnected, problems usually arise: i) how to get the most accurate estimate of the gradient given a set of sparse noisy measurements at a given time, and ii) where to locate the robots to obtain the set of measurements that will provide the best gradient approximation, given the estimation method. Several techniques have been proposed to address this issue, including consensus-based algorithms [12], cooperative Kalman filters [32], and Least Squares methods [25]. However, these solutions often focus on the estimation problem, overlooking the study and optimization of sensor placement, or present approaches whose use is limited by strict requirements on specific robot formations, which are only defined for a limited number of robots, as in [12], hence reducing their applicability and robustness to robot failures.

To address these limitations, some works have proposed multi-robot formations with specific geometric constraints to ensure reliable gradient estimation with proved guarantees [16, 6]. In [1], the authors showed that more generic swarm configurations can be adopted to estimate an ascending direction instead of the exact gradient.
While most of these works focus on 2D environments, a few have explored 3D scenarios.
In [6], we introduced 3D symmetric multi-robot formations that enable the estimation of both the gradient and the Hessian of the field using simple averages of robot measurements and their relative positions. However, this approach requires an even number of robots and a centralized architecture. In a more recent work [5], we overcome these limitations by proposing a new class of formations based on Voronoi partitions over a spherical surface, enabling more flexible and scalable solutions. However, this solution remains suitable only for homogeneous sensing noise.

A third, more recent line of work replaces the explicit estimation step with a learned one. Reinforcement learning has been applied to derive source-seeking policies directly from sequences of measurements [20], while Gaussian-process regression and Bayesian optimization have been used to build a probabilistic model of the field and to select informative sampling locations [7, 14]. Neural-network field approximation has also been combined with formation control for multi-robot source localization [18], although this line of work assumes a deterministic field with bounded approximation error rather than a stochastic, heteroskedastic measurement model.
These approaches are attractive precisely when the structure of the field or the statistics of the measurement noise are unknown a priori, since they do not require an explicit model of either. The counterpart is the need for training data or for an exploration phase, and the loss of the closed-form error characterization that a model-based estimator provides. The approach proposed here represents a complementary situation, where the noise statistics are assumed known, and this knowledge is exploited to obtain both an analytically characterized estimator and a formation design that is provably close to optimal.

The work presented in this paper represents, to the best of our knowledge, the first solution that explicitly considers a heterogeneous system collecting heteroskedastic measurements in a 3D environment and proposes a novel integration of a robust gradient estimation scheme with a formation control strategy that adapts to the differences in measurement noise variance.

title: Depth-Aware Path Planning and Collision Avoidance for Robotic Nursing Assistants Using Real-Time 3D Vision
authors: Peeyush Thakur,Dharmendra Sharma,Archit Sharma,Sandeep Gupta,Anuj Nandanwar,Laxmidhar Behera
abstract: This paper presents a depth-aware path planning and collision avoidance framework for the safe navigation of robotic nursing assistants in cluttered environments with low-height obstacles. Conventional LiDAR-based navigation systems, while accurate for mapping and localization, fail to detect transparent or low-height obstacles, whereas vision-based systems are prone to noise and occlusion. The proposed framework integrates RGB-D depth sensing, rule-based obstacle avoidance, and the NavfnROS global path planner to drive the robot from an initial point to a goal point. The proposed approach is implemented on the Husky A200 robot, equipped with a Kinova Gen3 arm, to form a complete setup for a robotic nursing assistant. This system features a multi-layer architecture for global planning, perception fusion, and real-time control in the ROS-Gazebo environment. Experimental evaluations in a simulated cluttered environment demonstrate up to 40% higher success rate and 35% improvement in minimum clearance compared with single-sensor baselines. Furthermore, real-world experimental results validate the proposed approach as a computationally efficient and safety-aware navigation solution for autonomous healthcare robots. The code is available at https://github.com/Peeyush331098/Depth-based-obstacle-avoidance.git
introduction:
The rapid advancement of service robotics has opened new possibilities for robotic nursing assistants to support healthcare professionals in performing routine tasks such as medication delivery, patient monitoring, and logistics management. Ensuring autonomous and safe navigation in hospital environments, however, remains a formidable challenge. Unlike structured industrial settings, hospitals are unstructured, dynamic, and highly cluttered, with narrow corridors, movable beds, trolleys, and the constant presence of humans. Under such conditions, reliable path planning and obstacle avoidance are essential to prevent collisions, maintain operational efficiency, and ensure patient safety. Consequently, intelligent perception and navigation algorithms have become the cornerstone of modern healthcare robotics, enabling robots to adaptively plan trajectories, localize themselves, and interact safely with human co-workers in real time.

Among the sensing modalities investigated for autonomous navigation, systems based on LiDAR are the state of the art because of their capacity to provide reliable 3D mapping, high-precision range measurements, and steady performance across a range of lighting conditions. Because of these benefits, LiDAR is an essential part of autonomous wheeled systems and hospital-grade SLAM frameworks [5, 6]. For example, hospital service robots have effectively used 2D LiDAR navigation frameworks for waypoint-based path tracking and corridor following, while 3D LiDAR extensions improve spatial awareness in semi-structured interior spaces [7]. However, safety in patient-care scenarios may be jeopardized because LiDAR-only systems frequently miss challenging features such as translucent partitions, low-height obstacles, or partially occluded objects [18]. LiDAR technology also has inherent limitations, such as a limited vertical field of view, low point density, absence of semantic or color information, and difficulty in recognizing translucent or reflective surfaces (such as glass doors or polished floors) [15]. These limitations hamper reliable perception in reflective or visually complex healthcare environments.

To overcome such limitations, depth cameras have emerged as a powerful complementary sensing approach [16]. By providing dense pixel-wise depth maps integrated with visual cues, depth cameras enable enhanced perception of low-lying, irregular, and specular obstacles often missed by LiDAR alone. Therefore, depth imaging constitutes a promising pathway toward perception-aware and context-adaptive navigation, facilitating safer and more efficient path planning [14] for robotic nursing assistants in cluttered and dynamic hospital environments. Recent studies demonstrate that exploiting the contextual richness of depth imagery significantly enhances both obstacle perception and path replanning under dynamic conditions [18, 6]. Moreover, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been applied to interpret fused sensor data for adaptive, human-aware navigation [7, 11]. Vision-based obstacle avoidance algorithms have been proposed in [1, 13, 2, 21].

In [1], the authors used YOLOv5 for real-time object detection and distance estimation, which is valid only for known obstacles. In real-world scenarios, there are obstacles that are not recognized by such object detection algorithms. Despite these advances, achieving real-time fusion, maintaining computational efficiency, and ensuring safe human–robot interaction remain open challenges. These issues continue to motivate the development of hybrid perception frameworks that exploit the complementary strengths of LiDAR and depth cameras for robust navigation in healthcare settings [5, 11, 18, 6].
Hence, there exists a critical research gap in developing a computationally efficient, real-time hybrid perception and path-planning framework that integrates LiDAR and depth camera sensing for context-aware, safe, and adaptive navigation of robotic nursing assistants in cluttered and dynamic hospital environments. Addressing this gap would significantly advance the reliability and autonomy of service robots in healthcare applications.

This paper presents a hybrid depth-aware navigation framework that uses Navfn global planning and a five-zone depth-based reflex layer to avoid obstacles in real time. The framework automatically detects when the Husky A200 robot is stuck and replans a new route, ensuring safe, collision-free motion in cluttered indoor spaces. Experimental results indicate substantial enhancements in navigation success rates and clearance when contrasted with single-sensor methodologies.

title: Semantics First, Pixels Later: Mission-Driven Event Streams for Drone Video over Bandwidth-Starved Links
authors: Cong Xu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

abstract: A surveillance drone on a bandwidth-starved link cannot send the video its operator would need, yet the operator’s questions are often not about pixels: did three people converge, when, and where? We study what should cross a link of 1 Mbps down to 1 kbps instead, and in what order. BPS, a behavior-primitive stream, sends semantics first and pixels later: it runs a detector and a tracker onboard and sends short records (25 bytes on average) of multi-frame events selected by a mission card of 16–125 bytes, ahead of positions and pictures. An event is opened as soon as it can be decided and closed when it ends. We measure it by what a ground-side language model answers from it, under a preregistered protocol with a held-out set, against H.265 read by the vision fine-tune of the same model, H.265 on which the ground runs our own perception, a stream of quantized tracks, and onboard captions. On the development set (84% of questions about convergence, mostly one location) the event stream answers 74.3% of questions at 0.13 kbps. A reader that receives nothing answers 57.4%, and the video reader 59.6% at 100 kbps and 64.7% on the source frames. When the ground instead runs our perception on the video, video matches the stream at 100 kbps, about 800 times the stream’s rate, and falls behind at 64 kbps and below. A track stream matches it at 96 times the bytes and loses 0.03 at 17 times. On held-out data the result is weaker: with events taken from annotated tracks, an oracle, the stream beats H.265 at 100 kbps (+0.13+0.13), but with onboard perception it does not (+0.01+0.01 [−0.04-0.04, +0.06+0.06]) and is no better than receiving nothing. Sent alone through emulated links the event records answer 0.739 at 1 Mbps and still 0.724 at 0.3 kbps; an every-frame track stream holds down to 1 kbps and video with ground-side perception down to about 100 kbps. On a Jetson Orin Nano the unchanged pipeline runs at 4.5 fps and misses most events.
introduction:
Small unmanned aircraft carry cameras whose output the ground often cannot receive: tactical radios, satellite back-haul and contested spectrum deliver from about a megabit per second down to a few kilobits. A codec with low-latency settings can still push a small picture through ten kilobits per second in time (Fig. 1), but a small picture is not an answer. The operator often asks about behavior over time: whether a vehicle stopped and stayed, whether people converged on one spot, when a quiet area came alive. This paper asks what should be sent instead of video when the answer, not the picture, is what the ground needs.

Our answer, BPS (behavior-primitive stream), moves the perception onboard and sends its conclusions. A detector and a tracker run on the aircraft, a streaming engine turns tracks into multi-frame behavior primitives, and a mission card tells it which primitives, classes and regions matter. A scheduler sends event records of a few tens of bytes ahead of everything else, so the stream degrades gracefully: a narrowing link costs the ground its pictures first, then positions, and the events last. An event is opened as soon as the engine can decide it and closed when it ends, so the ground learns of a convergence about two seconds after it starts.

Sending conclusions instead of evidence is not new: edge analytics systems filter frames by relevance [4, 49], cooperative perception sends object lists [47], semantic communication transmits task features [16, 42], and caption or event-log representations let a language model answer video questions [57, 9]. What is missing is a measurement: how much does a symbolic event stream lose or gain against the video it replaces, against simpler things a drone could send, and on emulated links from 1 Mbps to 1 kbps? We contribute that measurement as much as a method:

A transmission code for aerial behavior. Track-level primitives sent as open and closed records of 14–53 bytes, compact mission cards, and a byte-counted packet format with a strict-priority scheduler and 256-byte fragmentation (Sec. 3). Seven primitives are defined and six run onboard; our data tests one of them, convergence, at scale.

A transmission code for aerial behavior. Track-level primitives sent as open and closed records of 14–53 bytes, compact mission cards, and a byte-counted packet format with a strict-priority scheduler and 256-byte fragmentation (Sec. 3). Seven primitives are defined and six run onboard; our data tests one of them, convergence, at scale.

A preregistered protocol with matched readers and strong baselines. Questions are answered by a text-only language model reading the stream and by the vision fine-tune of the same base model reading H.265 video. Because that video reader turns out to use little of the bitrate, we add baselines that isolate the code from the reader: the video reader on source frames, video on which the ground runs our own perception, and a stream of quantized tracks. Hypotheses were preregistered, and a held-out set with its mission cards stayed sealed until the pipeline was frozen (Sec. 4).

Findings, positive and negative. On development data the event stream at 0.13 kbps answers more questions than the video reader does at any rate, though about three quarters of its margin over H.265 at 100 kbps comes from questions where nothing happened. When the ground runs our perception on the video, video needs about 100 kbps to support the same answers, and a track stream needs 96 times the stream’s bytes (17 times at a loss of 0.03). On a Jetson Orin Nano the unchanged pipeline runs at 4.5 fps; at the frame rate it can keep up with, event recall falls from 0.69 to 0.28 (Sec. 5).

title: Long-Horizon Causal Inertial Odometry in Multistory Buildings
authors: Tianzi Zhang,Yan Wang,Hao Qiao,Jian Kuang,Xiaoji Niu
abstract: In indoor 3D localization inside multistory buildings, an elevator or an escalator accelerates for a few seconds and then cruises at constant velocity for tens of seconds. Gait excitation disappears, the specific force degenerates into a constant gravity reaction, and instantaneous velocity becomes unobservable within a 1–2 s window. The output of short-window learned inertial odometry consequently degrades toward the conditional mean of the training set, and vertical displacement is systematically underestimated. We propose Local-Token Causal Attention (LTCA), a long-horizon architecture that compresses each 1 s inertial window into a 1 Hz motion token and sustains, over a bounded 60 s causal cache, the motion state established at the onset event. We further introduce a pluggable barometer branch that, when online, supplies a direct elevation constraint to the vertical channel through local differential height observations, and we train it with paired online/fallback conditional training so that the barometer also regularizes the representation shared by the two modes during training. On MSIO, our benchmark of nine buildings, the RoNIN and TLIO instances reach 3D trajectory errors (ATE-3D) of 2.83/4.18 m and 2.44/5.12 m on the Seen and Unseen splits, respectively, with the barometer online. With the barometer disabled at inference, the same weights fall back to pure inertial inference and reach 3.24/4.28 m and 2.64/5.23 m, still below every native short-window baseline. We further validate the framework on the public RoNIN and TLIO benchmarks.
introduction:
In GNSS-denied indoor and underground environments, localizing a pedestrian inside a multistory building requires estimating the horizontal trajectory and the inter-floor elevation jointly. Visual-inertial odometry [1] is constrained by illumination, texture, and power budget. Without external observations, a micro-electromechanical inertial measurement unit (IMU) accumulates integration error rapidly [2], and the vertical channel is the worst affected. Conventional pedestrian dead reckoning relies on zero-velocity updates at the foot [3] or on empirical step-length models, and both usually assume a rigidly attached device. Once the device is carried in the hand, in a pocket, or in a backpack, these assumptions no longer hold. Obtaining a continuous cross-floor 3D trajectory from a consumer-grade IMU and barometer alone therefore remains an open problem in indoor localization.

Learned inertial odometry, represented by RoNIN [4] and TLIO [5], regresses instantaneous velocity or displacement directly from high-rate inertial measurements, removing hand-crafted gait rules and mounting constraints. Its physical basis is the periodic foot–ground impact of walking: the impact waveform and the translational velocity share a stable statistical relation, so that a 1–2 s window suffices to map one onto the other. Elevators and escalators break this premise. After a brief acceleration, the transport platform enters a constant-velocity cruise that lasts tens of seconds; the net mechanical acceleration vanishes, the specific force degenerates into a constant gravity reaction, and the local signal becomes indistinguishable from standing still. The current window carries no information about instantaneous velocity, so a window-based estimator has nothing left to condition on. A stateless network with a 1–2 s receptive field possesses no cross-segment history, so its output collapses toward the conditional mean and vertical displacement is systematically underestimated. Recovering velocity therefore requires establishing causal state continuity across the excitation-free gap.

To address this problem, we propose a long-horizon architecture termed Local-Token Causal Attention (LTCA). At its bottom level, a 1 s bounded receptive field compresses the high-rate inertial stream into 1 Hz motion tokens while preserving the residual cancellation property of feed-forward convolution. At its top level, a learnable relative temporal bias is applied over a bounded 60 s causal cache, so that the motion state established at the onset event can be called upon throughout the cruise, and a strict causal mask supports 1 Hz streaming inference. What matters here is not a larger parameter count but keeping the onset event inside the visible history. LTCA introduces no independent absolute observation for the vertical channel, so vertical error still accumulates once an external elevation reference is absent. We therefore attach a pluggable barometer on top of it. At the structural level, identity pass-through and hard gating let one set of weights switch between online and fallback modes through a mask; at the training level, paired conditional training makes the barometer act as a privileged observation that shapes the shared representation, so that the fallback path retains most of the gain.

Compared with prior work, our main line is to restore long-horizon causal state with LTCA and to attach the barometer as a pluggable auxiliary observation within the same framework. Short-window learned inertial odometry [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9] relies on bounded receptive fields to cancel residual errors statistically, but cannot cover the onset event. IDOL [10] extends the training window to 20 s with curriculum learning, yet its bidirectional structure requires the whole window at inference and does not admit strictly causal streaming recursion. Learned multi-sensor fusion [11, 12] mostly assumes that the auxiliary sensors remain available throughout and provides no tolerance for packet loss or low-power sleep. Learning using privileged information (LUPI) [13, 14], together with privileged geometric constraints in robot proprioception [15], shows that training-time observations can shape the representation, but this idea has not yet been combined with the training protocol of pedestrian 3D odometry.

The contributions of this paper are threefold.

For continuous 3D localization involving elevators and escalators in multistory buildings, we attach the LTCA long-horizon structure and a pluggable barometric fusion module to two existing local backbones, RoNIN and TLIO, through their existing interfaces, extending learned inertial odometry from level walking to multistory scenes.

For continuous 3D localization involving elevators and escalators in multistory buildings, we attach the LTCA long-horizon structure and a pluggable barometric fusion module to two existing local backbones, RoNIN and TLIO, through their existing interfaces, extending learned inertial odometry from level walking to multistory scenes.

We explain why short-window learned inertial odometry fails during the constant-velocity cruise of passive mechanical transport: once gait excitation vanishes, the inertial window carries no information about velocity and the estimate falls back to its prior. We further identify the role of causal temporal attention in maintaining motion-state continuity across the excitation-free gap.

We build MSIO, a 3D multistory indoor localization benchmark rich in elevator data, carry out a unified cold-start comparative evaluation on MSIO and on the public RoNIN and TLIO benchmarks, and isolate the role of each component through per-motion-mode and ablation studies.

title: MARS: Dynamic Routing of Reinforcement-Learned Atomic Skills for Multi-Stage Robotic Manipulation
authors: Zequan Zeng,Junqin Yang,Kai Wang
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-task robotic manipulation. However, they still face limitations in control precision and execution stability during critical manipulation stages, such as object grasping, alignment and insertion. To combine general-purpose manipulation capabilities with task-specific fine-grained control, while enabling effective coordination between generalist and specialized policies throughout multi-stage manipulation tasks, this paper proposes MARS (Modular Atomic-skill Routing System), a dynamic routing framework for reinforcement learning-based atomic skills. MARS integrates a frozen generalist VLA policy with multiple independently trained atomic skill policies. Using a shared RL Token state representation and the reference action of VLA, specialized control policies are optimized through reinforcement learning for different cr‘itical manipulation stages. For high-level policy selection, we develop a dynamic router that integrates temporal context and skill semantics. The router employs Mamba-based recurrent encoding and a historical feature window to capture state evolution during manipulation. Skill descriptions of candidate policies are encoded into semantic queries, and attention mechanisms are used to establish correspondences between skill semantics and temporal state features. Experimental results show that MARS achieves an average Macro-F1 score of 90.47% across four LIBERO task suites under fixed-trajectory evaluation, outperforming an MLP-based router by 7.08 percentage points. In the simulated Tube Transport task, the full-task success rate increases from 20.04% to 85.67%. These results demonstrate that stage-specific reinforcement learning and temporal state-aware dynamic policy routing can improve multi-policy coordination and overall task execution performance in multi-stage robotic manipulation.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation tasks, such as multi-object pick-and-place, object transfer, and laboratory sample handling, typically involve a sequence of operations, including grasping, transportation, alignment, placement, and insertion. These stages impose different requirements on the underlying control policy. General-purpose policies are often sufficient for relatively simple operations, such as object transportation and robot resetting, whereas alignment and insertion require higher control precision and execution stability. Consequently, relying on a single control policy throughout an entire manipulation task may make it difficult to simultaneously achieve general-purpose manipulation capabilities and precise control during critical stages. Combining pretrained generalist policies with skill-specific control policies optimized for particular manipulation requirements provides a promising approach to improving multi-stage robotic manipulation. However, different policies have distinct operating conditions and applicable ranges. Selecting an appropriate policy according to the robot state and task progress, while ensuring smooth transitions between policies, remains an important challenge in multi-policy coordination [1, 2].

In recent years, generalist robotic policies, including RT-1, RT-2, Octo, OpenVLA, π0\pi_{0}, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and SmolVLA, have demonstrated promising multi-task manipulation capabilities through large-scale robot data pretraining and joint modeling of visual, language and action information [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. Nevertheless, the performance of these generalist policies varies across manipulation stages, particularly in tasks involving precise alignment and contact-constrained operations, where action accuracy and execution stability remain challenging [11, 12]. To further improve robotic manipulation performance, recent studies have investigated reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training methods for VLA policies. One line of research improves manipulation performance by optimizing the action generation process or updating selected model parameters, as demonstrated by VLA-RL, SimpleVLA-RL, iRe-VLA, and π0.6\pi_{0.6} [13, 14, 15, 16]. Another line of research aims to preserve the core capabilities of pretrained models while enhancing task-specific control through lightweight control modules, residual policies, or independently trained RL policies. Representative methods include RL Token (RLT), PARTS, Object-Centric Residual RL, and VLaRL [12, 17, 18, 19]. These studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of reinforcement learning in improving robotic manipulation from different perspectives and have provided a foundation for integrating pretrained generalist policies with specialized control strategies.

Although reinforcement learning can improve the control performance of VLA models in specific manipulation tasks, optimizing a single policy for an entire multi-stage task remains challenging. When only a binary terminal reward indicating full-task success or failure is available, the policy receives no reward feedback for intermediate actions that contribute positively to task progress. This makes it difficult to accurately estimate the contribution of actions at different stages to the final task outcome, thereby complicating state-action value estimation and policy optimization. One possible solution is to decompose critical stages with clearly defined manipulation objectives into independent atomic skills and optimize each skill separately through reinforcement learning. By assigning local objectives and reward signals to individual atomic skills, specialized policies can be trained to address specific control requirements while reducing their dependence on full-task rewards. However, independently trained atomic skills only improve control performance within their respective stages. Determining when to activate each skill and how to coordinate transitions between specialized policies and the generalist VLA remains a key challenge for multi-policy coordination. Several studies have explored skill organization and dynamic routing mechanisms from different perspectives. AtomicVLA organizes manipulation capabilities through atomic skill modeling and an expert-based architecture, SMoDP introduces semantically structured policy specialization for compositional robotic manipulation, and SWAP enables dynamic selection among multiple VLA policies through policy value estimation [20, 21, 22]. These approaches offer different solutions for atomic skill modeling, policy specialization, and dynamic selection. Nevertheless, for a system consisting of a frozen generalist VLA and multiple independently trained RL-based atomic skill policies, determining which policy is most appropriate at different stages of task execution remains a key challenge. Since individual policies have different control objectives and operating ranges, atomic skill selection should not rely solely on predefined manipulation stages but should also account for state changes throughout the sequential execution process. Meanwhile, descriptions of candidate policies provide policy-specific semantic information that can help the router learn correspondences between candidate skills and temporal state contexts. Motivated by these considerations, we formulate dynamic policy routing from two complementary perspectives: temporal state modeling and candidate policy matching. Specifically, temporal encoding is used to extract contextual information from sequential robot states, while skill descriptions are transformed into conditioned semantic queries that interact with temporal state features. This enables the router to construct policy-specific matching representations and provides a basis for dynamically selecting between the generalist VLA and reinforcement-learned atomic skill experts.

To address these challenges, we propose MARS (Modular Atomic-skill Routing System), a dynamic routing framework for reinforcement learning-based atomic skills in multi-stage robotic manipulation. MARS decouples local skill optimization from high-level policy selection, enabling coordinated control between a generalist VLA and multiple specialized atomic skill policies. For atomic skill optimization, we first construct a shared RL Token adapter based on intermediate features extracted from the frozen VLA backbone. The adapter produces compact state representations that can be reused across different skill policies. Each atomic skill policy then takes the shared state representation and reference action chunks of the frozen VLA as inputs and is independently optimized through reinforcement learning for a specific local manipulation objective. For high-level policy selection, we develop a dynamic router that integrates temporal context and skill semantics. The router employs a Mamba-base recurrent encoder [23] to capture temporal information from robot states and maintains a fixed-length historical feature window to preserve recent state changes. Meanwhile, the skill descriptions of candidate policies are encoded into semantic queries, which are further refined through self-attention to capture inter-skill relationships. Cross-attention is then applied to extract skill-relevant information from historical state features, providing contextual representations for subsequent policy selection. The skill-conditioned features are then used to predict routing probabilities for the generalist VLA and each atomic skill policy.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We propose MARS, a multi-policy coordination framework that integrates a frozen generalist VLA with independently optimized reinforcement learning-based atomic skill policies using shared RL Token representations and VLA reference actions.

We propose MARS, a multi-policy coordination framework that integrates a frozen generalist VLA with independently optimized reinforcement learning-based atomic skill policies using shared RL Token representations and VLA reference actions.

We develop a dynamic policy router that combines Mamba-based temporal modeling and skill-conditioned attention to select appropriate control policies based on temporal state information and candidate skill semantics.

We evaluate MARS through simulation and real-world robotic experiments, demonstrating its effectiveness in atomic skill execution, dynamic policy routing, and full-task manipulation performance.
