title: Residual Reinforcement Learning for Visual Servo Control with Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer
authors: Mahdi Nobar,Alisa Rupenyan,John Lygeros,Jürg Keller
comment: This manuscript is currently under review in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
abstract:
We address tracking a moving object on a conveyor with a Franka Emika Panda robot arm, despite an imprecise digital twin, measurement errors, and noise.
Our novel approach augments a loop-shaped inverse–Jacobian PI controller with a residual policy learned via Soft Actor–Critic in the digital twin.
A delay-compensated Kalman filter fuses out-of-sequence camera measurements to provide latency-aware moving target position estimates.
We compare the achieved performance to a performance bound for a class of model-based controllers derived from a frequency-domain sensitivity analysis, quantifying the minimum achievable error imposed by uncertain kinematic model mismatch.
Simulation and hardware experiments indicate that our residual policy drives tracking error below the bound.
Across conveyor speeds (27.927.9–41.8​mm/s41.8\ \mathrm{mm/s}), our method reduces mean tracking errors from 1.11.1–1.4​mm1.4\ \mathrm{mm} (baseline inverse-Jacobian PI) to 0.30.3–0.7​mm0.7\ \mathrm{mm}.
These results show that learning residual corrections in a limited-fidelity simulator, combined with delay compensation, can substantially improve model-based control under modeling and measurement uncertainties while maintaining reliable sim-to-real transfer.
introduction:
Autonomous manipulation on moving conveyor belts is a pivotal challenge in industrial automation because unmodeled belt and robot dynamics, sensor delays, and kinematic uncertainties hinder precise tracking.
Classical model-based controllers guarantee stability yet degrade under model bias or localization noise [1].
Pure reinforcement learning (RL) approaches are adaptive but data-intensive and impractical to train exclusively on hardware [2].
Hybrid methods alleviate these limitations by combining model-based and data-driven control.
Residual learning enables an RL agent to augment the nominal controller, leveraging model knowledge for stability and sample efficiency while locally compensating for modeling and sensing errors [3].
Learning-based model predictive control has likewise achieved high-precision trajectory tracking on compliant robotic arms by integrating a Gaussian process–based model correction and an online disturbance estimator [4].
Similarly, data-driven trajectory optimization has been shown to improve motion accuracy in precision systems without modifying the underlying low-level controllers [5].
Researchers have also addressed the simulation–to-reality gap by, for example, pairing simulated pretraining with domain randomization across varied parameters [6] or constraining policy updates near nominal trajectories to improve transferability and convergence [7].
Alternative iterative approaches address model mismatch through repetitive control and run-to-run optimization [8], while data-efficient optimization with digital twins accelerates controller tuning by substituting costly real experiments with simulated trials [9].
Learning-based iterative controllers achieve high-precision tracking through compensation across repeated executions [10, 11], and adaptive Bayesian optimization uses Gaussian process models to improve performance over multiple runs [12].
In dynamic grasping and conveyor picking, deterministic planners predict object motion for interception [13], adaptive controllers reconfigure trajectories in real-time [14], and multi-agent RL with replay optimization enables interception on moving platforms [15].

We propose a control framework that augments a nominal inverse-Jacobian PI controller with a data-driven residual Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) policy to address autonomous manipulation on moving conveyor belts.
The proposed framework contributes three elements: (i) a principled architecture that integrates model-based control and reinforcement learning for real-time refinement of the control signal through zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, (ii) a varying delay-compensated Kalman filter for vision-based state estimation under sensing latency, and (iii) a power-spectral tracking error lower bound derived from the closed-loop sensitivity.
The SAC agent is trained entirely in simulation without any real-system data and compensates for modeling and sensing uncertainties, including kinematic bias, unmodeled dynamics, belt flexibility, measurement latency, and noise, by refining the commands generated by the nominal controller.
We validate the proposed controller on a real robot using a vision-based robot cell with a dead–time–compensated Kalman filter and digital twin simulations, achieving sub-millimeter tracking accuracy that surpasses the performance limit on a class of model-based baseline controllers across varying conveyor speeds.

Section II defines the problem and control objective; Section III presents the proposed controller algorithm; Section IV derives a lower bound for the tracking error of the class of controllers; and Section V discusses simulation results and experimental validations.

title: VLN-Flash: Parallel Action Decoding with Adaptive Execution for Vision-and-Language Navigation
authors: Ruizhe Xie,Honghua Chen,Binglin Wang,Tong Guo,Xu Tang,Puti Yan,Shaoxiong Cai
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: When a vision-and-language navigation policy generates an action sequence autoregressively, the robot waits for a chain of dependent predictions. A small discrete action vocabulary makes it possible to score all short-horizon plans in parallel. We introduce VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder that evaluates the complete action-prefix tree in a single forward pass. Branch-specific attention and matched token positions preserve the original policy’s conditional action distribution for each prefix in exact arithmetic. We use the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative at each depth to decide how many actions to execute. The robot then executes the plan with the highest joint score at the chosen depth before observing again. On matched inputs, VLN-Flash achieves a nearly 3×3\times speedup in action decoding over native autoregression on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN. Compared with the native autoregressive decoders, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, VLN-Flash improves navigation success and cuts the mean wait between actions by about 160 ms after subtracting network transmission time.
introduction:
Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow an instruction through an unseen environment using first-person observations. Recent policies fine-tune video-based large language models to emit low-level actions as tokens [27, 23], improving performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE [1, 7, 6]. In autoregressive decoding, each predicted action becomes part of the input for the next prediction. The robot waits for these successive model calls before it can execute the plan. That delay recurs each time the robot uses a new observation to plan its next actions.

Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN predict up to four actions per decision. Uni-NaVid executes at most two [27], while StreamVLN executes the full prediction [23]. In both policies, the execution limit is set in advance, regardless of how strongly the policy favors a particular plan given the current observations. This motivates using the policy’s predictions to decide how much of a plan to execute before observing again.

The small navigation action space lets us enumerate all prefixes needed to score short plans. We introduce VLN-Flash (Figure 1), a training-free decoder that packs these prefixes into a tree and scores them together in one forward pass through the navigation policy. Tree attention lets branches share the observed context while keeping each candidate’s own action history. Matching the visible history and position indices to autoregressive decoding preserves the corresponding conditional distributions in exact arithmetic. The original language-model head reads out the action distribution for every branch.

Scoring the whole tree lets the robot choose how many actions to execute at each decision. Execution length determines when new observations can influence the policy. Longer blocks reduce the number of decisions along a route, while shorter blocks allow earlier replanning with fresh visual feedback. Since the tree already scores all depths, selecting a shorter execution prefix requires no additional prediction pass.

VLN-Flash uses these readouts for joint-probability plan selection and margin-based adaptive execution. Joint probabilities rank candidate action sequences using the policy’s conditional predictions. To determine the execution length, we scan the score margin between the fixed stepwise-greedy branch and its strongest alternative from shallow to deep. The scan stops when the greedy branch’s lead falls below a threshold, or when that branch ends. At the selected depth, the agent executes the highest-scoring branch and then observes again. The same tree scores thus determine both which plan to execute and how long to follow it.

We measure decoding on identical inputs and ablate plan selection and adaptive execution. On Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN, VLN-Flash accelerates action decoding by nearly 3×3\times over native autoregressive decoding and improves success rate (SR) and success weighted by path length (SPL) on both R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with SR gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, the same StreamVLN policy completes 52 of 60 instructions with VLN-Flash versus 49 with autoregressive decoding.

Our main contributions are as follows.

One-pass action-tree decoding. VLN-Flash scores all short-horizon action prefixes in a single forward pass without retraining, preserving autoregressive conditional distributions in exact arithmetic.

Shared scores for planning and execution. Joint probabilities rank candidate plans, and score margins determine how many actions to execute before observing again.

Faster decoding and better navigation. VLN-Flash decodes actions nearly 3×3\times faster, improves SR and SPL on both benchmarks, and reduces action waiting time on a Unitree GO2.

title: HospitalBench: Diagnosing Where and Why Embodied Agents Fail on Long Hospital Task Chains
authors: Gaytri Jena,Kapil Wanaskar,Aman Chadha,Vasu Sharma,Vinija Jain,Amitava Das
abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks fail in ways that end-task success cannot see. HospitalBench is a diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each two unscored warm-up steps followed by a causal chain of five scored sub-tasks in one continuous simulation: the state one step leaves (an object pose, a choice, a fact seen once) determines what the next step must do, unlike benchmarks that place sub-tasks side by side. Vision-language agents act through skill-level tools from camera images. A scripted robot that makes only the calls a model gets is the solvability check of a chore. From each trajectory the benchmark reads where a chain breaks, what the agent did after a failed call, and how far its own position estimate drifts from the true one. This version reports first results only: 15 of 60 planned runs (three models at high effort, one run each on chores T1 and T10 from both start states and T3 from one), with scripted-robot proofs on three of the ten chores. Of the 15 runs, 2 passed all five sub-tasks. Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by a different call and 111 by a call that did not fail. These are first results and not a full benchmark. We will release the scenes, task chains, scripted robot, evaluation harness and trajectories.
introduction:
Where along a chain of dependent chores does an embodied agent’s performance degrade, and why? Long-horizon benchmarks report that success falls as tasks get longer [22, 28], and recent work traces failures to the seams between skills [35, 24], but one end-task score cannot say at which step, at which link or by which kind of failure a chain breaks. A chain shows degradation by carrying only if each step needs the actual result of the one before, or a fact seen earlier: a trolley parked a few centimetres off its mark moves every grasp that follows, whereas a card seen once names the forceps to take and is gone by the time they are needed. HospitalBench is built for this diagnosis: ten chores of five dependent sub-tasks (50 sub-tasks, 40 links) in six simulated hospital areas (Sec. 3, Tab. 2), each link depending on the step before it in one of four ways (Fig. 2). A model sends every robot call and a controller executes it. A walk is one model at one effort tier (the reasoning-effort setting of its API call) running the sub-tasks of one chore in order, with no reset (a chain), from one start state (the initial scene). The scene state is the poses of the robot, objects and people, which every pass term and harm event reads. A walk ends at its first failed sub-task. The number passed before it is its passed in a row score. The scripted robot is a hand-written program that makes only the calls a model makes. The calibration model is the model whose walks were used to choose the version of a chore (Opus 5.5 high), so its results are not held out. Held-out models (GPT-6.1 Terra, GPT-6.1 Sol) were not used for that choice (Sec. 4).

What we find so far (Sec. 5). This version reports first results only. We ran Opus 5.5 high, GPT-6.1 Sol high and GPT-6.1 Terra high once on each of five cells (chores T1 and T10 from both start states, T3 from start 0), 15 runs of the 60 planned, outside the staged protocol of Sec. 4. The scripted robot has a proof on those chores and starts, and on none of the other seven chores. Two runs passed all five sub-tasks, both on T1 (GPT-6.1 Terra from start 0, GPT-6.1 Sol from start 1). Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Every other run ended at its first failed sub-task, and in 7 of those 13 runs this was the first free sub-task T#.02, never the guided T#.01. On T1, 3 of the 6 runs that reached T1.02 failed it. Two took the forceps that a card shown only in the first picture of T1.01 named to keep, and one never picked either forceps. After a failed call the next call differed in 168 of 189 cases and did not fail in 111. With one run per cell there is no interval and no ranking of models, and these are first results, not a full benchmark. The other seven chores have no model run.

Failure modes and harm events. We read four failure modes from a trajectory (Sec. 4): compounding errors per link, recovery, state drift and tool-use breakdowns. This version reports the last three from the 15 runs (Sec. 5.1). Compounding by landing position and harm events are defined but not analysed here. Harm events (an instrument left off the tray, the robot closing in on a person) are simulator proxies and not injuries.

Honest scope. No single task is new: every kind of action in our tasks is in a task prompt of seven existing benchmarks, and five further 2026 benchmarks are in the same comparison (Tab. 1). The design property we add is link dependence, tested link by link (the link test, Sec. 3.2) and through a fact shown once. The link test has been run on 1 of the 40 links, for the scripted robot on an earlier T1 version. The rest have only a paper check on assumed numbers (Sec. 3.2). Only T1, T10 and T3 have model runs. No method has been trained on HospitalBench, and we do not claim it works as a training environment.

Contributions.
(1) A diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores, each five dependent sub-tasks in one reset-free simulation, with the kind of each of the 40 links stated, a link kind for a fact shown once, and 36 named harm events (Sec. 3).
(2) A staged protocol (stage 0 calibration, an alone check M1, held-out stages 1 to 3) that reports the calibration model apart from held-out models, and the first 15 runs, made outside it (Sec. 4).
(3) First results on three chores with per-run records of where a chain ended, what followed each failed call and how far the robot’s position estimate drifted, and a read of the T1.01→\toT1.02 link (Sec. 5.1).

title: Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning for Nonstationary Robot Dynamics
authors: Jungjin Lee,Se Jin Kim,Sung Kwon On,Insoon Yang
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this
must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently
to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this
separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do
not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but
describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two.
Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it
conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot’s
inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions
from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.61.6–3.8×3.8\times over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm’s response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate
its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of
individual Lagrangian components.
introduction:
Human intelligence internalizes the world from brief experience. One
explanation, long held in cognitive science, is that it rests on an innate
a priori structure through which experience is interpreted (Spelke and Kinzler, 2007; Lake et al., 2017).
Here, we focus on causal reasoning about how actions affect motion
through the underlying physical mechanisms (Pearl, 2009; Peters et al., 2017).
We study nonstationary robot dynamics, where hidden physical conditions
change during operation and alter the torque–motion relationship.

A central form this structure has taken is a separation of the intrinsic
properties that define a system from the kinematic state in which it is
observed. The state is only a snapshot: two systems can look identical at a
given moment yet respond differently to the same action, because of
properties such as mass or friction that the snapshot does not
reveal (On et al., 2026; Baradel et al., 2020; Schölkopf et al., 2021). Hidden-parameter
MDPs (Doshi-Velez and Konidaris, 2016) and causal world
models (Schölkopf et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022) make this separation
explicit, and context-based approaches (Rakelly et al., 2019; Zintgraf et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020)
define the intrinsic component as a context vector inferred from a short
window of recent transitions. We adopt this structure, as it mirrors the
human case most directly: limited interaction yields a compact summary of
the system, from which the consequences of potential actions can be
anticipated.

Separating context from state does not specify how physical conditions
change the equations of motion. This matters for adaptation to
within-episode changes and generalization beyond the training range:
a payload change affects both inertial and gravitational responses.
Encoding these relationships provides a physical inductive bias for
context-based prediction (Lutter et al., 2019; Karniadakis et al., 2021).
Physics-informed networks (Greydanus et al., 2019; Desai et al., 2021; Cranmer et al., 2020),
in particular Lagrangian models (Lutter et al., 2019), provide this prior
knowledge, but they bind the law to a single system and cannot tell when that system has changed. CaDeLaC (Schulze et al., 2025) combines a
history-conditioned context with Lagrangian dynamics for adaptation, but presupposes a nominal robot model such as a URDF, taking its knowledge of the system as given rather than drawn from experience.

We introduce Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR) for
nonstationary robot dynamics. PICR infers a dynamics-relevant context
from recent interactions and uses Feature-wise Linear Modulation
(FiLM) (Perez et al., 2018) to condition shared Lagrangian networks.
The context modulates inertia and potential while preserving their
mechanical relationships for each fixed context. Network parameters
are learned offline; adaptation updates only the context from new
observations. Payload labels organize the context during training but
are not required at inference. The model thus exposes how inferred
context changes the mechanical quantities used to predict motion.

We evaluate PICR on a torque-controlled Franka Panda arm carrying a payload
of unknown mass and center of mass in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, against
context-based and physics-structured baselines.

Our contributions are:

A physics-informed causal reasoning framework for nonstationary
robot dynamics, in which interaction-derived context modulates a
shared Lagrangian model to adapt the modeled torque–motion
relationship while preserving its mechanical structure.

An empirical evaluation of within-episode adaptation,
generalization to unseen payloads, and action-effect prediction
through paired torque interventions.

A gray-box analysis linking inferred contexts, learned
mechanical terms, and motion predictions through context substitution
and comparison with simulator-derived references.

1. A physics-informed causal reasoning framework for nonstationary
robot dynamics, in which interaction-derived context modulates a
shared Lagrangian model to adapt the modeled torque–motion
relationship while preserving its mechanical structure.

2. An empirical evaluation of within-episode adaptation,
generalization to unseen payloads, and action-effect prediction
through paired torque interventions.

3. A gray-box analysis linking inferred contexts, learned
mechanical terms, and motion predictions through context substitution
and comparison with simulator-derived references.

title: Continuous Lower-Limb Joint-Angle Estimation from sEMG and IMU: The Conditional Value of Cross-Activity and Cross-Subject Data under Update-Matched Controls
authors: Jiaying Xu(Conamur),Guangyuan Chen(Institute of Neuroscience, Chinese Academy of Sciences),Buyun Gao(Conamur),Zhen Dong(University of California, Santa Barbara)
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
abstract: Intent-driven exoskeleton control needs a continuous, causal estimate of the wearer’s joint kinematics and an answer to a second question: whose data should train the estimator for a new user? Borrowing the user’s recordings of other activities, or other users’ recordings of the same activity, is usually evaluated as “more data” versus “less data,” which confounds the information a source carries with the optimizer updates it adds and hides negative transfer behind averages. We separate these effects for hip, knee, and ankle angle estimation from high-density sEMG and an IMU across six locomotion activities on all ten participants of a public dataset. A compact residual causal TCN–GRU decoder is frozen, and an update-matched replay control prices every added source against the same number of updates on the user’s own data. A user’s own other activities raise R2R^{2} from 0.722 to 0.788, of which +0.048+0.048 is information beyond replay; stair descent is a reliably harmful donor and sit–stand–walk a reliably beneficial one. Other users’ same-activity data help while the user has only the target activity (GT=+0.053G_{\mathrm{T}}{}=+0.053) and half as much once own other-activity data exist (GW=+0.028G_{\mathrm{W}}{}=+0.028); at full calibration, donor value collapses after one to two target records. Per-target gains from the two sources correlate, and leave-one-participant-out gates recover most of the cross-subject value only at low calibration. Data value is hierarchical, state-dependent, and directional; the bottleneck is deciding, without test labels, when to transfer.
introduction:
Lower-limb exoskeletons reduce the metabolic cost of walking [1], and assistance is now personalized by human-in-the-loop optimization of controller parameters [2], by estimating the user’s joint moments with a neural network [3], or by driving the device from the wearer’s own neuromuscular intent [4]. All of these, and the co-adaptive controllers that would let decoder and wearer adapt jointly [5], need a continuous, low-latency estimate of intended joint motion. Surface electromyography (sEMG) carries anticipatory information, inertial sensing (IMU) provides kinematic context, and neural-network regressors—shallow networks for simultaneous lower-limb joints [6], recurrent and convolutional–recurrent networks [7, 8], transfer-learning-based recurrent models for the knee [9]—are the standard tools for mapping them to continuous joint angles. Reported errors depend on protocol and units (hip, knee, and ankle RMSE below 6∘ in treadmill walking [6]; a normalized knee MAE of 8.1% [9]); inter-subject variability remains the recognized obstacle, electrode placement, skin impedance, and recruitment strategy all shifting the sensor-to-output mapping [10]; and although convolutional front-ends before a recurrent decoder are common [7, 8], the marginal value of the convolutional stage [11] is rarely isolated with a control that differs only in that stage.

A second question dominates deployment cost and is rarely posed with the same rigor: whose data should train the decoder for a new user? The user’s recording of the target activity is scarce; the obvious remedies are to borrow the user’s recordings of other activities, or other users’ recordings of the same activity. Both are usually evaluated by comparing “less data” with “more data,” which confounds two things. Adding data adds optimizer updates, so a gain may reflect training budget rather than new information (repeated epochs over fixed data recover much of the value of new data [12]); and the farther the source, the more sample size and distribution shift grow together, so an average gain may be the net of substantial positive and negative transfer [13, 14, 15], where which source helps which target is a directed relation rather than a similarity [16]. Transfer studies in myoelectric control, largely on gesture classification [17], resolve neither confound for continuous multi-joint regression, and the conditional value of other subjects’ data, its interaction with the user’s own calibration budget, and its per-subject safety have not, to our knowledge, been quantified against budget-matched within-subject controls.

This letter addresses the decoder and the data question together in a staged, deliberately conservative design (Fig. 1) on all ten participants of a public high-density sEMG locomotion dataset [18], with one 57-channel set fixed by a pre-specified channel-integrity audit. Its contributions are (i) a compact, strictly causal decoder, RC-TCN–GRU (76,534 parameters), selected under a held-out-trial protocol by three pre-specified contrasts—time-domain features carry the decodable information (Δ​R2=+0.211\Delta R^{2}=+0.211 over frequency-domain features), whereas a residual causal TCN front-end (−0.006-0.006) and IMU fusion (+0.002+0.002) are neutral on average, null results we report rather than an architectural advantage—and then frozen as the measurement instrument; (ii) an update-matched replay control that separates the information gain of an added source from its budget effect, applied to a user’s own other activities (total gain +0.066+0.066, of which +0.048+0.048 is information; stair descent a reliably harmful donor, sit–stand–walk a reliably beneficial one); (iii) the state-conditional value of other users’ same-activity data, GT=+0.053G_{\mathrm{T}}{}=+0.053 when the user has only the target activity and GW=+0.028G_{\mathrm{W}}{}=+0.028 once own other-activity data exist, with a recurring target receptivity across sources (r=0.44r=0.44) that leave-one-participant-out (LOPO) gates identify only partly; and (iv) a full-calibration program in which donor value collapses after one to two target records. The decoder is evaluated offline; no exoskeleton, controller, or assistance outcome is claimed.

title: Self-Calibrating Vision-Agent-Action: Deploying Pick-and-Place to New Robot Cells without Demonstrations or Fine-Tuning
authors: Jae Hun Hwang,Yechan Seo,Hong-In Won
comment: supplementary video in ancillary files
abstract:
In simulation, Vision-Agent-Action (VAA) performs pick-and-place
in robot cells with gripper or base-frame changes without robot
demonstrations or fine-tuning. It uses pre-trained vision-language
and language models for interpretation, measures the command map
and camera geometry from its own motion and fingertips, estimates
lens distortion, and plans grasps from measured object depth.
A controlled study of eight public LIBERO-fine-tuned
vision-language-action models (VLAs) varies robot hardware,
camera geometry, appearance, and base frame. Gripper and frame
changes dominate their losses in the tested fractional design.
Across 18 cells with these changes, frozen VAA achieves
230/360 successes (64%),
the refined VAA 268/360 (74%), and the
strongest released VLA on this subset 76/360
(21%). Paired ablations support the self-calibration
bundle, lens estimation under compounded changes, and the
measured-depth pipeline. On a two-step LIBERO-Goal chain with
object state carried between instructions, VAA completes 54/60
chains in changed cells, while four evaluated VLAs complete none.
introduction:
Moving a manipulation system to another robot cell changes more
than its images. A different gripper changes fingertip geometry
and object contact. A rotated command frame changes the direction
in which an action moves the tool center point (TCP).
Camera pose, lens, lighting, support surfaces, and objects may
also change. Collecting demonstrations and fine-tuning a policy
for each cell adds deployment work.

Public vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tuned on LIBERO
can perform tasks in their training setup. Transfer to a new cell
also requires their commands to produce the intended physical
motion under changed hardware and coordinate frames.
Fig. 1 illustrates this deployment problem.

We first examine where released VLAs lose success in a controlled
cell design. Gripper and base-frame changes dominate their
losses in the tested fraction. Both changes alter the relation
between commands and fingertip or object motion. This diagnosis
motivates measuring the new cell’s geometry before manipulation.

Vision-Agent-Action (VAA) performs this measurement and executes
pick-and-place without robot demonstrations or fine-tuning.
It combines pre-trained VLM/LLM components with self-calibration.
Before the task, the robot observes its own motion and fingertips
to establish a cell model. During the task, language models
identify the relevant objects, while geometric modules determine
where to grasp and where the TCP must move.
Fig. 2 separates these stages.

The study contributes:

A controlled diagnosis identifying gripper and
command-frame changes as dominant VLA transfer factors
in the tested design.

A self-calibrating pipeline combining command and
camera measurement, lens estimation, and measured-depth
grasp planning.

Paired ablations and two-step manipulation testing
the roles of cell measurement and calibration reuse.

in the tested design.

title: Ego2Sim2Humanoid: Agentic Real-to-Sim for Learning Loco-Manipulation VLAs without Robot Demonstrations
authors: Chen Liu,Nikolaus Correll
abstract:
Imitation learning for visuomotor policies typically relies on teleoperated
robot demonstrations, which are costly because every episode requires a trained
operator controlling a physical robot in real time through teleoperation
interfaces and wearable body-tracking hardware.
Egocentric glasses capture human demonstrations without a robot or handheld grippers, yet they track only the
head and in-view human hands, and directly copying human motion to a robot with
different stature, arm reach and hand morphology fails to produce feasible
contacts. E2S2H converts egocentric glasses recordings into physically
verified robot training trajectories. An agentic real-to-sim stage reconstructs
collision and textured visual assets from the recorded RGB-D and head streams,
completes unseen surfaces when needed, and predicts target contact bands on the
manipulated objects. During motion adaptation, a grasp planner turns
each contact band into a feasible robot wrist pose and finger closure, bilevel
stance optimization plans collision-free standing postures that keep hand
targets reachable, and a whole-body motion generator synthesizes lower-body
locomotion and out-of-view arm motion. Two-stage motion correction then blends
visibility transitions kinematically and trains a reinforcement-learning
tracking policy in physics simulation under agent-designed semantic rewards,
completing manipulation phases even when the object leaves the camera view.
Rendering the reconstructed scene through the robot’s onboard camera along the
optimized rollout yields synchronized robot-view images, proprioception and
verified action labels. Fine-tuned exclusively on this converted dataset,
without real-robot demonstrations, GR00T N1.7 performed loco-manipulation tasks
autonomously on a Unitree G1. Project page:
https://robonana.github.io/ego2sim2humanoid/
introduction:
Whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a route to generalist
humanoid policies, yet their performance remains bound by the supply of
action-labelled robot trajectories [34, 35, 9, 44].
Internet text and video pretrain visual and semantic representations, but
mapping observations to coordinated joint commands requires physical
demonstrations. Current pipelines collect these demonstrations through
teleoperation across robots and tasks during pretraining and repeat collection
in the target scene for each deployment [34, 35]. Because every
episode requires a physical robot and a trained operator, data collection scales
poorly across new scenes and tasks.

Human recordings provide an alternative data source without a physical robot,
but existing capture setups omit the whole-body motion required for humanoid
loco-manipulation. Egocentric video corpora supply visual and hand-trajectory
pretraining for models such as GR00T N1, EgoVLA, Being-H0 and
H-RDT [34, 46, 30, 3]. Because an egocentric camera observes
the hands rather than the torso and legs that carry them, policies pretrained on
these videos predict hand and wrist poses and still depend on teleoperated
robot trajectories to ground those poses in whole-body joint
control [46, 3]. Portable manipulation interfaces such as UMI and
smart-glasses capture rigs bypass robot teleoperation for fixed-base arms by
placing the robot’s gripper or camera on the demonstrator [7, 25, 27].
A handheld gripper or head-mounted camera alone records no stance, footstep,
posture change or balance recovery, separating hand manipulation from the body
motion that positions the hand in space.

Because a humanoid differs from a human demonstrator in height, limb length and
hand morphology, direct retargeting leaves the robot’s hand at the wrong
distance from the object, produces infeasible finger contacts, and causes
identical step counts to cover different ground distances. Existing humanoid
transfer pipelines sidestep full-body adaptation rather than resolving this
physical mismatch. Humanoid Policy ∼\sim Human Policy co-trains a shared
human–humanoid action space but restricts the robot to tabletop manipulation
from a fixed stance [36]. EgoHumanoid extends egocentric transfer to
loco-manipulation, yet it reduces lower-body motion to three discrete walking
commands, co-trains with teleoperated robot episodes and translates upper-body
motion kinematically [38]. Such kinematic translation also passes
sensor drift directly into the action labels without verifying whether the
robot maintains balance or achieves stable contact with the object.

E2S2H is, to the authors’ knowledge, the first pipeline to bring real-to-sim
reconstruction to egocentric data generation for humanoid robots, converting
egocentric recordings into executable whole-body robot
trajectories. The glasses record the head trajectory throughout, the
hands while they are in view, and RGB-D streams of the scene in one metric
frame. For daily-life recordings in the wild without
pre-scanning, an agentic real-to-sim stage reconstructs per-episode assets,
optionally completes unseen surfaces, and predicts target contact bands. Motion
adaptation starts from
the robot’s standing pose and projects the head path onto the floor while
planning collision-free stances and upper-body postures so the robot’s arms can
reach the interaction targets. Each hand’s timeline is split by visibility into
tracked in-view segments, where a rule-based grasp planner maps the predicted
contact band to a feasible robot wrist pose and finger closure, and out-of-view
segments synthesized by a whole-body motion generator. Two-stage motion
correction then blends visibility transitions kinematically and trains a
reinforcement-learning tracking policy for dynamic feasibility in physics simulation under semantic
rewards designed by the agent from the contact events, completing manipulation
phases even when the object moves outside the camera view. The resulting
training label is the closed-loop whole-body action token and hand joint
command that physically moved the simulated object while maintaining balance.

To pair these verified actions with the visual observations the robot would
receive, E2S2H renders the reconstructed scene through the robot’s onboard
camera along the accepted physics rollout. Each rendered frame shows the
robot’s own arms, the object at its simulated pose and the scene from the
robot’s camera height. Because images, proprioception and actions come from the
same rollout, vision and control are synchronized without clock alignment. To
demonstrate the fidelity of the converted data directly, whole-body VLA
policies are fine-tuned exclusively on these converted trajectories without any
real-robot demonstrations of the target tasks.

This paper makes five contributions. First, an agentic real-to-sim procedure
reconstructs per-episode collision and textured assets without prior scans,
completes unseen surfaces, and localizes target contact bands on manipulated
objects (Section III-A). Second, a motion
adaptation method combines rule-based grasp planning on the predicted contact
bands with bilevel collision-avoiding stance optimization and whole-body motion
generation across visible and out-of-view hand segments (Section III-B).
Third, a two-stage kinematic and reinforcement-learning motion correction
smoothly blends hand visibility transitions and executes the trajectory in
physics simulation under agent-designed semantic rewards that also guide
out-of-view task phases (Section III-C). Fourth, robot-view rendering along
the accepted rollout synthesizes synchronized onboard images and verified
action labels (Section III-E). Fifth, real-robot experiments on a Unitree G1
evaluate policies fine-tuned solely on the converted data without real-robot
demonstrations (Sections III-E and IV).

title: Distilling Safety Filters for Filter-free Multi-agent RL
authors: Srikar Babu Gadipudi,Somayeh Sojoudi,Claire J. Tomlin
comment: and 6 tables
abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) can teach robot teams to navigate shared spaces, but trial and error causes collisions that real robots cannot afford. Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters prevent these collisions by correcting unsafe actions, yet in a team the filter becomes a centralized optimization whose number of constraints grows quadratically with the team size. We propose an approach that builds the filter’s safety into the RL policy and examine how such a system behaves during filter-free deployment. However, the filter that keeps training safe also hides what the policy must learn: it masks the cost of unsafe actions, which actor-critic methods then overvalue, and it keeps near-collision states out of the training data. Our approach therefore learns only from executed safe actions with implicit Q-learning and distills the filter into the policy at synthetic near-collision states. We prove that filter distillation loss bounds the policy’s constraint violation and hence how far agents can cross their safety margin, so errors never accumulate. When distillation states cover deployed states, the loss also bounds the collision probability at every step. Without a filter and acting only on local observations, our policies have no collisions in 1,8001{,}800 test episodes with multiple agents. A policy trained with three agents transfers zero-shot to teams of twenty at constant per-agent computation and stays collision-free with up to eight agents. We test our policies on Crazyflie quadrotors with up to five flying at the same time.11
1
          
          
          
        Videos of the hardware experiments and code are available at srikarbabug.github.io/ff-safemarl.
introduction:
Robots increasingly work in teams that share space, where each robot must reach its goal while avoiding collisions with other robots and obstacles. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach to learning such behaviours, but its trial-and-error nature causes collisions during training that can damage hardware, so real-world multi-agent RL requires safe exploration from the start. Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters (Ames et al., 2017; Ames et al., 2019) address this challenge: at each step, the filter minimally modifies the actions proposed by the policy to satisfy the collision-avoidance constraints, so only safe actions are executed during training (Fisac et al., 2019a). In multi-agent systems, however, pairwise constraints couple the team into a centralized quadratic program (QP) whose number of constraints grows quadratically with the team size. Solving it requires every agent’s state and proposed action; for 2020 agents, the joint QP takes 16.916.9 ms, a third of the control period, against 0.60.6 ms per agent for our policy (Sec. 5.2). This motivates our objective: use a centralized safety filter to guarantee collision-free exploration during training, but learn a decentralized policy that no longer requires the filter at deployment.

Simply removing the filter after training, however, leads to a fundamental distribution mismatch: the policy is trained under filtered action-to-transition mapping but deployed under an unfiltered one. CBF-RL (Yang et al., 2025) adds barrier-based reward shaping so that single-agent policies, trained with the filter, run without it at deployment. Because the filter maps many raw actions to the same safe action (Markgraf et al., 2025), actor-critic methods such as soft actor-critic (SAC) can overvalue unsafe raw actions: SAC trained with the filter in the loop collides in 98%98\% of episodes when deployed without it (Sec. 5.3).

This observation motivates RL methods that learn only from actions in the data: we extract the policy from the executed safe actions with implicit Q-learning (IQL) (Kostrikov et al., 2022) (Sec. 3.2). IQL alone is insufficient, however: because the filter prevents collisions, the replay buffer lacks the near-collision states that the unfiltered policy may reach. To cover them, off-support safety-filter distillation (OSFD; Sec. 3.3) trains the policy on the actions of the training filter, queried at synthetic near-collision states, without environment interaction. Following centralized training with decentralized execution, only training uses the joint state, and the deployed policy is an attention-based actor on local observations whose parameters do not depend on the team size (Sec. 3.4).

We prove theoretically that this training controls safety once the filter is removed (Sec. 4). The distillation loss bounds a closed-form CBF residual that measures how much the unfiltered policy violates the filter’s constraints, a bounded residual lowers the barrier by a bounded amount uniformly in time, so violations never accumulate, and, when the distillation states cover the deployed states, the loss bounds the collision probability at every step. The training loss thus certifies the safety of the filter-free policy, and every bound held on the 7575 trained policies we audited.

Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) Filter-free multi-agent RL: we propose a novel framework that trains collision-free with a centralized CBF filter and deploys a decentralized policy without it, by combining IQL-based policy extraction with OSFD. (2) Safety guarantees: bounds that tie the distillation loss to the safety of the unfiltered policy under single- and double-integrator dynamics (Sec. 4). (3) Scalable filter-free collision avoidance: our local-sensing policies have no collision in 1,8001{,}800 episodes on the training scenes, where CBF-RL collides in up to 44%44\%, a policy trained with three agents transfers zero-shot to twenty at a constant 0.60.6 ms per agent (Sec. 5), and our policies fly up to five Crazyflie quadrotors without a filter (Sec. 5.4).

title: ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation
authors: Matthias Jammot,Pembe Gizem Özdil
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces.
Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional–derivative (PD) control.
We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping.
We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference.
Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor.
By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot.
The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.
introduction:
Movement is governed by forces, which in locomotion arise from foot–ground contact and determine a sprinter’s acceleration, a patient’s loading asymmetry and a humanoid robot’s balance.
Cameras have made motion datasets abundant (Ionescu et al., 2014; Mahmood et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2026), but force data remains scarce. Force plates confine recordings to the laboratory, and wearable insoles resolve only the normal component and drift over time (Koch et al., 2016).
Recovering forces from motion alone would extend movement analysis into natural, unconstrained settings.

Recent corpora synchronize motion capture with force-plate measurements (Werling et al., 2024), extending beyond steady gait to tasks like cutting, lunging and jumping (Scherpereel et al., 2023).
Learning-based methods use such data to map kinematics to ground reaction forces (GRF), either through direct regression (Mourot et al., 2022) or generative modeling (Tan et al., 2026).
Their predictions can violate physics, for example by loading the ground during flight or placing the center of pressure (CoP) outside the foot, since a loss term at best encourages physical consistency.
The learned mapping is also opaque, going from motion to force directly without modeling the actuation and body dynamics that produce it, and therefore cannot drive a simulated body or robot.

Physics-based motion imitation addresses both limitations.
Tracking a recorded motion in a physics engine yields contact forces that are dynamically consistent by construction (Peng et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2023), and the controller producing these forces is explicitly defined.
However, dynamic consistency does not imply agreement with measured forces.
Most imitation policies output joint-position targets, which a proportional–derivative (PD) controller with hand-tuned gains converts into joint torques to drive the simulated body (Peng & Van De Panne, 2017).
Different gains can track the same motion, yet produce different contact forces.
Recent work incorporates measured force as an observation (Hori et al., 2026) or a reward (Liu et al., 2026), but fixes the gains and reports accuracy either with force sensors available at inference or on a single participant.
Alternative actuation models, including learned gains (Yuan et al., 2021), muscle models (Li et al., 2026) and direct torque control (Cotton, 2025), have not been systematically evaluated against measured forces.

Here, we present ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning imitation policy that outputs per-joint stiffness, damping and position setpoints, supervised by reference kinematics, force-plate GRF and CoP.
On 129 participants, nine datasets and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms fixed-PD, direct-torque, muscle and existing imitation controllers on kinematic and force accuracy.
To our knowledge, no prior controller reproduces measured per-foot contact forces across subjects and activities, including unseen ones, without force at inference.
We contribute:

Action-space bounds on force recovery.
We derive a lower bound on stiffness, set by the torque the reference force demands, and an upper bound on damping, set by discrete-time stability, which oppose each other between contact and swing.
Empirically, a fixed-gain policy forfeits either motion or force tracking, whereas learned impedance satisfies both, extending the action-space analysis of Peng & Van De Panne (2017) to force.

A morphology-agnostic controller.
Expressing impedance as a scaled inertia prior, our policy, trained on 107 subject-specific models without anthropometric input, transfers zero-shot to 22 subjects and a simulated humanoid robot (G1).
To our knowledge, this is the first physics-based imitator to transfer across unseen biomechanical and robotic embodiments.

Learned impedance encodes motor state.
The learned gains form a low-dimensional, interpretable representation in which stiffness scales with load and damping anticipates unloading. It generalizes to withheld activities better than fixed action spaces and identifies the activity from a single cycle of gains. This representation carries over to unseen subjects.

An open benchmark.
We release code, checkpoints and splits for a benchmark spanning 129 participants and six activities, with ablations, fixed-PD, direct-torque and muscle action spaces, and the existing methods PHC (Luo et al., 2023), SimPoE (Yuan et al., 2021) and GaitDynamics (Tan et al., 2026).

introduction:
Autonomous driving is turning to vision-language-action models (VLAs), vision-language models (VLMs) trained end to end as driving policies [3, 4, 2, 5, 1].
They bring broad visual knowledge.
Such a policy reads camera frames and the ego state and outputs a trajectory for the next few seconds.
A VLM answers by decoding, and current driving VLAs produce this trajectory step by step as well (Fig. 1a,b): they write waypoints as text or action tokens, one per forward pass [6, 7, 8, 2], or denoise it over several steps with a planning expert that reads the VLM’s features [5, 1].

Every step is another forward pass, and the passes add up.
On one H200 GPU at batch size one, Qwen-Drive-1.0 [1] spends 518 ms of GPU time on a plan over 11 passes, and 1,213 ms when also writing short reasoning (, left).
The car keeps moving while the policy thinks, so the plan arrives late (Sec. 4.3).
A human driver plans at a glance, with the fast, automatic thinking known as System 1 [9].
Faster designs mostly move planning out of the VLM into a separate planner or smaller student (Sec. 2), leaving the VLM’s abilities behind.
So far, a fast driving VLA that answers questions either plans outside the VLM or regresses one trajectory from query tokens [10].

Yet before a VLM writes its first token, it has already read the scene into one hidden state.
We show that, once trained, this hidden state is enough to drive and to answer questions about what the model sees.
VLMs became decoder-only to write free text; a plan is not free text.
BERT [11] and GPT [12] classify from one hidden state with a small head, as did early vision-language transformers.
We bring this classification approach to driving, with candidate trajectories as the classes, so a plan takes one forward pass.

We present SuperGlance, which turns a decoder-only VLM into an encoder-style driving policy that plans in one forward pass (, left; Fig. 1c).
A linear Policy Head on the last hidden state at the answer position, [ANS], scores a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories, most of them cluster centers of human trajectories (Sec. 3.1).
As the set is fixed, every candidate’s reward in every training scene is computed once, offline.
Training has three stages (Fig. 2).
Stages 1 and 2 train on multiple-choice questions to keep the VLM’s visual abilities in one forward pass and carry them to questions about driving scenes.
Stage 3 trains the policy, first toward a supervised target that weights the candidates by reward.
This target can still leave much probability on unsafe candidates (Fig. 3), so reinforcement learning (RL) raises the expected reward, computed exactly over all candidates without sampling, and lifts NAVSIM’s no-collision and time-to-collision scores.
The language-model head is kept and question data stays in training, so the final model still answers questions at almost no cost to planning.
With no decoding, denoising or separate planner, the VLM itself plans at a glance, as a human driver does.

We test our final RL checkpoint on NAVSIM, WOD-E2E, PAI-AV and Language2Drive, and in AlpaSim closed loop [13].
With each plan’s GPU time charged as delay, it drives 3.9 times as far per at-fault incident as Qwen-Drive-1.0 ().
Without delay, it still leads, as does every one-pass variant in our ablations (Sec. 4.3).

SuperGlance plans from one hidden state of a decoder-only VLM by scoring a fixed candidate set, so RL maximizes the exact expected reward over all candidates.

Multiple-choice training keeps the VLM’s visual abilities in one forward pass and carries them to driving scenes.

One checkpoint plans in 84 ms, 6.2 times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0, and at least as well on NAVSIM, WOD-E2E, PAI-AV and AlpaSim; it answers visual multiple-choice questions as well as its base VLM does by decoding.

title: Wireless Edge-Assisted Adaptive Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models in Physical AI
authors: Fatih Temiz,Melike Erol-Kantarci
comment: submitted to IEEE ICC
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable embodied artificial intelligence (AI) by translating visual observations and language instructions into robotic actions. Emerging use cases in physical AI are expected to drive the need for efficient inference and communication, as the computational demands of the VLA models pose challenges for real-time control with limited onboard resources. Test-time scaling through latent reasoning allows these models to refine hidden representations without generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, but introduces a trade-off between task success, inference latency, and energy consumption. In this paper, we address the efficient collaborative inference under a realistic communication scenario. We propose a wireless edge-assisted framework for adaptive latent reasoning (WEALR) that augments onboard computation with edge computing. A decision-making agent jointly selects the execution location and latent-reasoning convergence threshold. We formulate this joint adaptation as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP).
A Lagrangian-constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) approach, namely trust region policy optimization Lagrangian (TRPO-Lag), learns to balance task performance and resource consumption under varying wireless conditions and task requirements. We evaluate the framework using LIBERO manipulation tasks, profiled VLA inference costs, and ray-traced wireless channels. Experimental results demonstrate that TRPO-Lag achieves up to 23% higher feasibility-weighted task success rate compared to benchmark CDRL methods.
introduction:
Physical artificial intelligence (AI) brings perception, reasoning and action into embodied systems that interact with the physical world
[1]. Vision-language-action (VLA) models, such as OpenVLA [2], support this capability by translating visual observations and language instructions into robotic actions. Advances in these models create opportunities for generalizable physical AI, but their computational demands challenge deployment on resource-constrained robots. Task performance must therefore be balanced against onboard computation, energy consumption, and latency requirements [3, 4]. In particular, timely robotic control requires communication and inference to jointly satisfy a latency service-level objective (SLO). We refer to robots capable of visual perception, instruction understanding, planning, reasoning, and action execution as physical AI devices (PADs) in this paper.

Edge computing augments limited onboard computation by enabling PADs to offload inference to nearby edge servers, but its benefits depend on wireless propagation conditions [5]. This deployment perspective aligns with the vision of using radio access network (RAN) infrastructure to support AI applications at the network edge, such as mobile switching offices (MSO) [6].
However, faster edge computation comes at the cost of wireless transmission delay. In indoor environments such as homes and warehouses, blockage and multipath propagation create heterogeneous line-of-sight (LOS) and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. Changes in PAD position affect achievable uplink (UL) rates and can offset the computational advantage of edge execution. Effective offloading must therefore account for wireless conditions alongside computation and control-latency requirements. Evaluating this tradeoff requires environment-specific channel models that capture blockage, multipath propagation, and spatial variations in link quality, which ray tracing can provide [7, 8].

Reliable physical interaction requires VLA models to interpret diverse visual observations and language instructions and generate appropriate actions across tasks of varying difficulty. Supporting these capabilities motivates increasing model capacity through parameter scaling or allocating additional computation during inference.Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enable parameter scaling while limiting computation per input by activating only a subset of model parameters [9]. However, their memory and computational requirements can still challenge deployment on resource-constrained PADs. Test-time scaling offers a complementary approach that adjusts computational effort within a fixed model, making it particularly attractive for wireless edge deployment, where available resources and latency requirements limit inference costs [5].

Unlike explicit reasoning methods such as chain-of-thought (CoT), which generate intermediate text through sequential decoding, latent reasoning refines hidden representations without producing intermediate text tokens, potentially reducing the decoding overhead and latency associated with textual reasoning. The recurrent-depth architecture in [10] enables large language models (LLMs), which serve as backbones of VLAs, to vary computational depth through shared parameters, offering adjustable inference effort within a fixed model footprint. For robotic inference, recurrent-depth VLA (RD-VLA) applies a related principle through a weight-tied recurrent action head and a convergence-based stopping criterion to adapt the number of reasoning iterations across observations [11]. For example, grasping a small object may
require more reasoning than moving through an unobstructed
region. A single convergence threshold can therefore yield different reasoning depths across stages of a task and different tasks. Additional reasoning may improve action quality but also increases inference latency and resource consumption, motivating adaptive control of reasoning effort.
These considerations motivate jointly selecting VLA execution location and reasoning effort under wireless, energy, and computation constraints.

Related studies address complementary aspects of collaborative inference. The device-cloud framework in [12] uses resource-constrained reinforcement learning (RL) to select LLM inference locations and multimodal inputs. Also, the EcoVLA approach proposed in [13] selects energy-efficient VLA
co-inference schemes under real-time constraints,
adapting to network fluctuations and edge workload
variations. The authors of [14] propose MORES, a reasoning-as-a-service framework that distributes recurrent hidden-state updates between devices and servers, jointly adapting reasoning computation and latent-feature pruning under heterogeneous wireless conditions. While conversational LLM services typically prioritize response quality, VLAs must deliver actions within deadlines imposed by ongoing physical control [3].

Meeting these deadlines requires balancing task success against communication delay and resource consumption. Cumulative budgets couple decisions across requests, and shared edge resources couple decisions across PADs, motivating a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) formulation. Constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) addresses such problems by separating performance objectives from explicit operating limits [15]. This motivates the use of CDRL methods, including Lagrangian variants of proximal policy optimization (PPO) and trust region policy optimization (TRPO), as well as constrained policy optimization (CPO), for resource management in wireless networks. In particular, PPO-Lag has been adopted for joint unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) altitude control and Internet of Things (IoT) channel access [16].

In this paper, we propose Wireless Edge-Assisted Adaptive Latent Reasoning (WEALR), a framework that jointly adapts VLA execution location and reasoning effort. For each robotic task request, an agent selects local or edge execution and a reasoning convergence threshold. This threshold governs termination of the latent reasoning loop while allowing the realized reasoning depth to vary across observations within the task.
We use TRPO-Lag, which learns the policy and constraint multipliers, connecting adaptive latent reasoning with wireless offloading and cumulative resource management.
The key contributions are as follows:

We develop WEALR to jointly select VLA execution location and reasoning threshold according to task requirements, wireless conditions, and available resources.

We formulate a CMDP with per-PAD energy, shared edge-reasoning, and SLO constraints, and apply TRPO-Lag to optimize robotic task success.

We evaluate task success, feasibility, and policy behavior using LIBERO manipulation tasks [17], profiled VLA inference costs, and ray-traced channels under varying wireless conditions and resource budgets.

title: Leaning Over to Reach Far-Away Objects
authors: Allen Devaraj,William Xie,Nikolaus Correll

abstract: We study supported reaching to extend a humanoid robot’s workspace by bracing against the environment for stabilization using a straightforward yet capable whole-body model predictive control (MPC) approach, exclusively with local sensing and fiducial markers. While typical solutions for whole body humanoid control aim at avoiding or accommodating contact, contact is explicitly required to reach objects placed on surfaces far out of normal reach. We employ sampling-based MPC for whole-body leaning, bracing, reaching, and recovery on a Unitree H1-2 humanoid. The controller runs in real-time at 34Hz on a laptop, transfers sim-to-real, extends reach by ≈50\approx 50cm beyond the unbraced standing workspace, and sustains the loaded posture for over four minutes, before pose estimation drifts. The controller reaches the commanded target in 89% of trials and completes the full reach-and-recovery cycle in 81%, across 54 trials spanning six targets and three table heights. We further characterize why such a small real-time sampling budget is sufficient, finding that temporal persistence of sampled actions and exploration scale strongly govern success, while CEM provides the widest operating region over planning rate and model mismatch. These results establish a real-world baseline for online, contact-rich humanoid manipulation. Code, videos, and full hardware details are available at https://h12leaner.github.io/
introduction:
Recent progress in whole-body humanoid control has increasingly relied on large-scale reinforcement learning or specialized trajectory-optimization and control pipelines, typically with unwieldy motion-capture systems to bypass state estimation noise and drift. These approaches enable remarkable behaviors, but can require task-specific training data, predefined motion references, or specialized optimization machinery [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

In parallel, recent work has shown that comparatively simple model-predictive controllers built directly on mature rigid-body simulators can transfer surprisingly well to real legged robots [6, 7, 8]. In this work, we investigate whether the same philosophy extends to multiple-contact planning and control (MCPC) on humanoid platforms for one representative task: supported reaching to far-away objects, which couples manipulation with balance. For example, in industrial battery disassembly [9, 10], many parts are not accessible without leaning into the battery. Humans overcome this challenge quite easily, and can intuitively move beyond their foot-only support region, acquire and load an upper-body support contact, regulate the resulting long-lever posture, accurately and precisely reach a desired target, and subsequently unload and recover [11, 12]. These transitions further depend on contact timing and friction with noisy proprioception. All these challenges combined make the task a demanding test of online whole-body control for legged robots.

We present a sampling-based model predictive control framework for whole-body leaning, bracing and reaching, and recovery on a Unitree H1-2 humanoid. The resulting controller transfers sim-to-real, extends the robot’s reachable workspace by more than 5050cm beyond unbraced standing, sustains the loaded posture for more than four minutes, and completes 7373% of maximum-extent reaches and, across six commanded positions and three table heights, 8989% of commanded reaches. We further study the whole-body stability, target-tracking error, and steady-state jitter of the controller, as well as the component-level contribution of planner costs and four sampling-based planners.
